case_summary.text: IT : Where all members of assessee-trust were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and as regular time teachers and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools and were not being paid any extra salary for management work, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11

INCOME TAX : Assessee-trust formed for limited purpose of managing statutory obligations in form of gratuity payable to employees of parent trust would fall within ambit of advancement of general public utility and, hence, its activities was to be considered as a charitable as defined under section 2(15) and, accordingly, assessee was to be granted registration under section 12AA

INCOME TAX : Where funds of assessee-charitable trust were managed by member of trustees headed by District Collector and audit report was submitted before competent authorities before completion of assessment proceedings, since there was sufficient compliance to claim exemption under section 10(23C)(v), claim could not be denied merely on ground that assessee generated surplus income

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust established with main object of establishing educational institutions and providing scholarships, was also running Kalyan Mandapam within boundaries set out in trust deed and surplus generated out of this activity had been utilized by assessee in furtherance of other charitable purposes viz., payment of school fees, contribution to relief funds etc.,

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust entered into an agreement with a private limited company for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to it, since object of transfer agreement was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally and purpose of charity was not violated, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 could not be denied

IT-I: Where assessee, a trust registered under section 12A, received money from trustees for carrying on of its activities and those monies had been repaid to them or to their nominees as and when funds were available with assessee-trust, there was no violation of section 13(1)(c) and, therefore, assessee's claim for exemption under section 11 was to be allowed
AO can't deny exemption if trust entered into agreement to ensure that hospital was managed professionally: ITAT
Excess of income over exp. can’t be a reason to hold that trust isn’t engaged in charitable activities: HC

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust made payments out of income accumulated under section 11(2) to other institutions registered under section 12AA and described such payments as project implementation or service charges, since section 11(3)(d) was concerned with amounts 'paid or credited' to another trust and not purpose or nomenclature of such payment, amounts constituted deemed income taxable hands of assessee-trust

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed as withdrawn against order of High Court that where assessee-trust failed to produce any application or other documents to prove that advance given to proprietary concern of wife of managing trustee was for purchase of timber for proposed construction of a medical college, it could be concluded that there was a diversion for personal benefit of an interested party as mentioned in section 13(3) and, thus, amounts so advanced was rightly treated as income in hands of assessee
IT: Where genuineness of trust and objects of trust being charitable had not been disputed even if trustees had mismanaged or misutilised funds, exemption under section10(22) could not be denied

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust established with main object of establishing educational institutions and providing scholarships, was also running Kalyana Mandapam within boundaries set out in trust deed and surplus generated out of this activity had been utilized by assessee in furtherance of other charitable purposes viz. payment of school fees, contribution to relief funds etc., assessee's claim of deduction under section 11 could not be usurped merely on finding that assessee's activities resulted into surplus funds for assessee
CIT(E) can’t doubt genuineness of activities of trust based on extent of spending or surplus generated: ITAT

INCOME TAX : SLP granted against High Court ruling that where assessee-trust, engaged in business of publishing newspaper, did not run any school or college but utilized surplus of income from business for donation to a trust which was running educational institution, earnings of assessee being spent for charitable purpose, registration granted to it could not be cancelled

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that where assessee-trust, involved in identifying, enrolling, and allotting work to private workers at certain dockyard, used its surplus to further its charitable purposes and moreover, there was no violations of sections 11(5) and 13(1)(c) regarding investments and loans as amounts in question were eventually repaid with interest, assessee would be eligible to exemption under section 11

INCOME TAX: Where assessee trust was running a medical dispensary wherein it was providing free medical treatment to patients and annual income of assessee trust was out of interest income from investment which had been made of surplus lying with it and there being no allegation that assessee trust was involved in any activity for profit or did not exist for philanthropic purposes, assessee Trust was within its rights to accumulate receipts as per its requirement and thus, would be eligible for exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiae) even though it had incurred only 12 per cent of receipts for philanthropic purposes and accumulated 88 per cent of its receipts
CIT can’t deny registration without providing evidence suggesting trust's non-charitable activities: HC

IT: Exclusion of amounts received by virtue of section 10(22A) is not subject-matter of section 13(1) or any of its further conditions where assessee society duly registered under Indian Societies Act was entitled in law to claim exemption of its income under section 10(22A), fact that managing trustee/founder director in trust was participating in profits of income of trust would not disentitle institution to claim aforesaid exemption

IT: Where assessee-trust spent 85 per cent of its income for construction of building to be used for educational purpose, mere fact that it advanced certain amount to its sister concern out of surplus accumulated which remained at its disposal, there was no violation of provisions of section 11(2) and, thus, assessee's claim for exemption of income was to be allowed

IT : SLP granted against High Court's ruling that merely because assessee-trust incurred expenditure in excess of income in relevant previous year for charitable purposes out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a)

IT : Director (Exemption) having allowed accumulation of income of assessee-trust in terms of section 11(2) after being satisfied with objects of trust, exemption under section 11 could not be denied to assessee on ground of non-application of income for charitable purpose

IT : Where assessee-trust had been formed on basis of transferring of assets of sole proprietorship concern of one 'M' and 'M' was also managing trustee of trust, this fact in no way interfered with granting of registration under section 12A to assessee
No denial of sec. 10(23C) relief merely because trust incurred only 12% of its receipt for philanthropic purposes – ITAT

IT : Where assessee-turst invested funds in a company in which its trustee was managing director and his wife was a director, it was a case of violation of section 13(1)(c) and exemption under section 11 would not be available to assessee

INCOME TAX : Where High Court upheld Tribunals order holding that assessee being a charitable trust within meaning of section 2(15), was entitled to benefit under sec. 10(23C)(iv), SLP filed against said order was to be granted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-association of third party administrators (ATPA) was engaged in primary aim and objective to organise and arrange all licensed third party administrators (TPAs) to be members of trust for mutual betterment of TPA business, merely because certain benefits accrued to TPA members and certain objects of trust were for advancement of business of TPA, it would not ipso facto render trust to be non-charitable

IT: It is permissible under law for charitable trusts to donate for charitable or religious purpose and apply its income for said purpose but benefit of application cannot be claimed if it is found that funds are being diverted for non-charitable purposes

INCOME TAX : Where assessee trust was established with objective to develop world class gems and jewellery park to provide common facilities required to promote exports of diamonds from India and it was not carrying out any trade, commerce or business and only dealt with its members to attain its objects of general public utility, it would not be hit by first proviso to section 2(15), hence, benefit of section 11 could not have been denied

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust, involved in identifying, enrolling, and allotting work to private workers at certain dockyard, used its surplus to further its charitable purposes and moreover, there was no violations of sections 11(5) and 13(1)(c) regarding investments and loans as amounts in question were eventually repaid with interest, assessee would be eligible to exemption under section 11

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that exemption under section 11 could not be denied to assessee-trust running a canteen in hospital and making profit out of it unless it was brought on record that such surplus generated had not been utilized for charitable purposes or had been utilized for non-charitable purposes

IT : Donation given by one public charitable trust to another public charitable trust is permissible in section 11 as application of income and said payment is not in violation of section 13(1)(c) because payment is not made for benefit of any person either directly or indirectly referred to in section 13(3)
No denial of exemption if surplus earned on incidental activities was ploughed back for use towards trust’s object: ITAT
Charitable trust registered under sec. 10(23C)(iv) won't be hit by sec. 40(a)(ia) disallowance

INCOME TAX : Where income of assessee charitable educational institution was brought to tax as 'income from other sources' for reason that assessee was not registered as charitable trust under section 12AA, all incidental expenditures laid out by assessee wholly or exclusively for purpose of making or earning such income were also to be allowed under section 57(iii)
ITAT directs CIT(E) to grant registration as exp. claimed by trust proved that it was related to charitable activities
Section 167B not applicable to charitable trust if it was carrying out charitable activity as per trust deed: ITAT

IT : Where there was no prohibition for trust to take services of persons specified under section 13(3) and Assessing Officer failed to collect evidence to establish violation of section 13(1)(c) and section 13(3), exemption under section 11 could not be denied
Charitable trust entitled to sec. 11 exemption as funds were used for charitable purposes without misappropriation:HC

IT : Once income derived from property held under by assessee-trust was applied in accordance with charitable objects in view of specific exemption granted by a special order issued by CBDT, there would be no violation of section 13(1)(d) so as to deny exemption

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against High Court's ruling that exemption under section 11 could not be denied to assessee-trust running a canteen in hospital and making profit out of it unless it was brought on record that such surplus generated had not been utilized for charitable purposes or had been utilized for non-charitable purposes

IT : When primary purpose of assessee-trust was to afford relief to poor education and medical relief, means employed by exploiting its assets to earn income to achieve objects could not defeat claim of assessee under section 11
Trust was entitled to sec. 10(23C) exemption in respect of additions assessed u/s 68 by AO: ITAT
SC granted SLP against ruling that a charitable trust was entitled to sec. 10(23C)(vi) exemption

INCOME TAX : Where assessee educational trust had advanced a certain sum to proprietory concern of wife of Managing trustee and claimed that amount had been advanced for purchase of timber for proposed construction of a medical college but had not produced any application or other documents submitted to Governmental authorities or Medical Council of India for proposal for setting up of medical college, it could be concluded that in garb of purchase of timber, advance amounts had been diverted for personal benefit of an interested party as mentioned in section 13(3), thus, amounts so advanced had rightly been treated as income of assessee-trust
Running petrol pump was incidental to attainment of educational objects of trust if surplus was used for charitable activities: ITAT

INCOME TAX :Where assessee-trust made donations to other charitable trusts out of accumulated income, since said donations were in any case reversed and had been advanced only for an extremely short duration, same would not be hit by provisions of Explanation 2 to section 11(1) as same applies only to amounts credited or paid to certain categories of institutions

INCOME TAX: Where government-formed registered trust applied interest income for purchasing disaster mitigation equipment as per trust objects, furnished bank certificates showing transfer of funds and vendor invoices in name of State Disaster Management, with no finding of misappropriation or misuse of funds, exemption under section 11 was allowable and violation of section 13 was not established.

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed against High Court's ruling that mere generation of huge surplus could not be a reason for disallowing claim of exemption under section 11 to assessee-trust on ground that intention of trust was profit making

IT : Words used in section 10(23C) is 'any income' received by any trust is exempt, therefore, income of assessee-trust assessed by Assessing Officer by making addition under section 68 would also qualify for exemption
CIT(E) can’t deny sec. 80G approval merely because trust reported surplus every year which was not utilized towards charitable purposes: ITAT

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether section 4(3)(i) relates to income from business held under trust and section 4(3)(ia) relates to income from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution where that business itself is not held on trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where business of managing agency was held in trust, it could be concluded that business carried on by trustees fell under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

On reference:

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1948-49 - Assessee executed a deed of trust whereby they settled certain amount on various charities and appointed themselves as trustees - Later, in accordance with terms of trust deed, trustees assessees were appointed as managing agents of a company - Before Income-tax authorities, trustee claimed that income derived from managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Revenue authorities, however, held that income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Whether word "property" in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend "business," and if question fell to be decided solely on terms of that sub-section, managing agency formed by assessees/trustees must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether fact that trustees had option at any time to throw up managing agency was no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

FACT: 'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

SC).

The provisions of section 4(3)(i ) confer an exemption of income from property only where the property itself is held under a trust or other legal obligation. It does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created in respect of any property, but only the income derived from any particular property or source is itself held in trust as where it is set apart or charged for a charitable purpose. That is clear upon the terms of the section itself and upon the authorities. In the instant case, all the income which the assessee derived or received was in the shape of grants and subscriptions from members which could not possibly have been received by it except from its business. Therefore, the entire income of the assessee must be held to be income derived from its business which was its property. If this contention was correct, then it was further submitted that there could be also no doubt upon the terms of its memorandum of association and its purposes and objects that the assessee was holding the business in trust for charitable purposes.

Supreme Court in J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that "Business" would undoubtedly be property in the connotation in which it is used in section 4(3)(i). In the light of this pronouncement of the Supreme Court it is clear that "business" itself can be property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) and upon that principle the business of the assessee in the instant case would be "property" held by the assessee.

Under the circumstances, the view taken by the Tribunal was the correct view and the income of the assessee would be exempt under the provisions of section 4(3)(i).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from properties held under - Assessment years 1947-48 to 1958-59 - Assessee trust was formed for benefit of public in general without distinction of caste, creed or colour in advancement of education, commerce, industry, public health and medical relief - Under trust deed, trustees were at liberty to apply corpus of said trust fund or any portion thereof as they might from time to time think fit for any one or more of above objects - Trustees might take over superintendence, management and administration of any trust or institution having allied objects whether endowed or not by settlor on such terms and conditions as trustees might in their absolute discretion think fit - Trustees were also entitled accept donations and/or contributions from any person, company, firm or institution upon such terms and conditions as they might deem proper and could apply any portion of income of trust fund for purpose thereof - Assessee claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act but same was denied by ITO - Whether trust deed merely empowered trustees to take over superintendence, management and administration such trust or institution whose object were similar or consistent with objects of assessee trust and they would not ,therefore, by reason of power reserved to them be entitled to take over any trust or institution whose objects were not charitable purposes - Held, yes - Whether donations and/or contributions that trustees might receive would be donations and contributions to trust fund and they would be received as and by way of accretions thereto, and since trust fund and trust property were themselves stamped with objects of trusts, donations and/or contributions which would be accepted by trustees as accretions to trust fund would also be similarly stamped with objects of trusts - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, trust fund as also accretions could not be used in any manner contrary to objects of trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: By an indenture of trust dated 28-7-1945, ‘B’ settled certain shares and certain immovable properties upon certain trust therein more particularly set out. By another indenture of trust dated 2-8-1945, he conveyed, transferred and assigned to the trustees certain immovable properties belonging to him and certain shares and securities standing in his name upon the trust set out therein. Clause 5 of the trust deed provided that the trustees would spend and apply the net balance of the income of the said trust fund and trust property for the benefit of the public in general and of the State within its geographical limits without distinction of caste, creed or colour in the advancement of education, commerce, industry, public, health and medical relief. The clause gave power to the trustees to apply the corpus of the said trust fund or any portion thereof as they might from time to time think fit for any one or more of the above objects. Clause 12 empowered the trustees to take over the superintendence, management and administration of any trust or institution "having allied objects whether endowed or not by the settlor on such terms and conditions as the trustees might in their absolute discretion think fit" and might thereafter superintend, manage and administer the same and might apply such portion of the income of the trust fund as they might in their absolute discretion think fit for the support and conduct of such trust or institution. Clause 13 provided that the trustees might accept donations and/or contributions either in cash or in kind from any person, company, firm or institution upon such terms and conditions as they might deem proper and might carry out such terms and conditions and might apply any portion of the income of the trust fund for the purpose thereof.

indirectly used or applied for the benefit of trustees. In this case, there was no such finding from the Assessing Officer that the income was used or applied for the benefit of trustees. The only allegations is that the trust has given loans to two persons without any security or interest and further said persons are in the nature of managers by whatever name called as referred to under section 13(3)(cc) and thus, said payments violates sections 13(1)(c). [Para 15] The findings of the Assessing Officer to bring two loans within the ambit of section 13(1)(c) read with section 13(3)(cc) could not be accepted. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer has denied the benefit of exemption under section 11 for the simple reason that there is violation of section 13(1)(c) read with section 13(2), insofar as interest free advances given to KVR and SV, on the ground that the assessee has allowed direct/indirect benefit of trust income/property to interested persons referred to under section 13(3)(cc). The provisions of section 13(3)(cc) refers to any trustee of the trust or manager (by whatever name called) of the trust as interested persons under section 13(3). Therefore, it is necessary to examine whether those two individuals are managers as defined under section 13(3)(cc) or not to decide, is there any violation referred to under section 13(1)(c). The legal dictionary Bakshi's Law Lexicon has defined the term 'manager' as per which 'manager has to be a person, has to be in the overall management of the company or trust, very importantly should be noted that, manager specifically for trust is not just a word of art, it is a very serious word comprising of meaning of a overall management.' The term manager is very wide. Thus, in order to bring any persons within the term manager it is essential to see their position in the organization and duties and works performed by them. In this case, the Assessing Officer has treated those two individuals as managers of the trust in terms of section 13(3)(cc), by considering the nature of work required to be carried out by them in terms of their letter of appointment. According to the Assessing Officer, those two persons are tasked with setting up core team to explore changes that are taking place in respect of rules and regulations formulated by the Government. They are required to directly report to the Chairman for any of the policy decisions. Therefore, he opined that they are performing managerial functions of the trust and, hence, comes under the term manager as defined under section 13(3)(cc). From going through the letter of appointment issued by the trust to two individuals it is found that those two individuals has been hired with a specific task of getting approval for starting a new medical college and also getting approval for deemed university status for the trust. From the letter of appointment, except providing consultancy services with regard to specific project, they are not involved in any kind of day to day activities of the trust. They had been never given any kind of services to existing institutions of the trust like engineering college and other institutions run by the trust. From the above, it is clear that services required to be provided by them to the trust are in the nature of external consultancy providers, who often comes to the client business place for providing consultancy services in respect of specialized knowledge which is required by any person. In this case, evidences filed by the assessee including letter of appointment clearly shows that those two individuals are appointed for a specific period of 5 years for a specific remuneration and further they have tasked with the work of setting up of new medical college and getting deemed university status for the institutions, which has nothing to do with the existing activities carried out by the assessee and, hence, those two individuals cannot be considered as managers of the trust, who are involved in day to day managerial functions. Thus, the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) were erred in considering two persons within the ambit of section 13(3)(cc). [Para 16]

a business of manufacture, sale and distribution of pharmaceutical, medicinal and other preparations. Therefore that particular object of the trust was neither charitable nor religious in character. If the trustees could under a trust held validly, spend the entire income of the trust on this non-charitable object, it was difficult to hold that the trust property was held under a trust or other legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the Act, 1922. Having regard to the language of paragraph 2 of the trust deed in the context of other paragraphs of the document, the trust deed, on a proper interpretation, gave an absolute power of selection to the trustees to choose between charitable and non-charitable objects of the trust for spending the entire income of the trust properties. It followed that the trust did not fulfil the conditions imposed by section 4(3)(i) of the Act, 1922 and the donation made by the assessee to the trust could not therefore be exempted under section 15B of the Act, 1922.

The contention of the appellants that the question whether section 4(3)(i) applied to the trust was not within the scope of the question referred to the High Court by the Appellate Tribunal or that the High Court went beyond its jurisdiction in answering that question could not be accepted. In CIT v. Scindia Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. [1961] 42 ITR 589, it was held that even where a question of law was not raised before the Tribunal but the Tribunal dealt with it, it must be deemed to be one arising out of its order. Applying the principle to the instant case, it was to be held that the High Court was within its jurisdiction in examining the question whether the trust was eligible for exemption from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of the Act, 1922.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

after the expiry of the period of 18 years the net income derived from the investments was to be utilised for all or any one of the four objects mentioned in the deed. However, on the assessment made upon the trustees, the income-tax authorities rejected the trustees’ claim that the dividend and interest income derived from the trust property was exempt under the first half of section 4(3)(i).

On appeal to the Tribunal the claim of the assessee-trust was allowed.

On reference : HELD: Analysing the provisions of the trust deed, the scheme which emerges was clear. The settler did not wish the trustees to spend the income of the trust on the charitable objects immediately. He wanted the trust fund to increase and expand, and after the trust fund had expanded, he wanted the income of that trust fund to be spent on the charitable objects. In other words, the trust deed contained a scheme for accumulation of income and for the accumulated income to form part of the trust fund; and there was also a provision for the accumulation to go on for a specific period of time and on the expiry of that time the income of the enlarged trust fund to be spent on the charitable objects. If the property was impressed with a charitable trust or the object of the trust is charitable or religious, then the income derived from such trust or property would be income which would fall within the ambit of section 4(3)(i). It is fallacious to suggest that the object of the trust for the first 18 years was to invest monies in a particular manner. That was not the object: it was a mode of investment; it was a direction given by the settler how the income was to be utilized for the ultimate object of its being spent on the object of the trust. It was entirely untenable, to suggest that a direction with regard to investment could be looked upon as an object of the trust. An object of the trust is something definite and unvarying; it is the intention that the settler has for settling his property; it is an object with which the court can rarely interfere. Except when question of the cypress doctrine comes in, the court exercising charitable jurisdiction must always respect the charitable intention disclosed by the settler and help the trustees to carry out the charitable intention. But the direction with regard to its investment is entirely different. No court exercising equity jurisdiction-and the charity commissioner exercising his jurisdiction under the Bombay Public Trust Act under which this trust was registered-was ever tied down by the directions of the settler with regard to investments. If at any time within the 18 years the court or the charity commissioner was satisfied that the investments directed by the settler were not prudent investments and were not beneficial to the trust, it was perfectly competent to the charity commissioner or the court to direct that the investments should be made in a different manner. This clearly explains the dividing line between what are strictly the objects of the trust and the procedural matters, if one might say so, contained in the trust deed which may deal with detail like the accumulation of income, the investment of income.

It was not necessary that that intention must be immediately carried out. So long as the income from the trust property was not spent on any non-charitable object and it was saved, as it were, or set apart or accumulated for the ultimate object of carrying out the charitable purpose, then even in the intervening period the trust continues to be a charitable trust, the property is held on a charitable trust and the income from that trust is exempt from tax.

If the trust is to benefit the employees, even though they are to be benefited for purposes which are charitable, the trust would not come within the ambit of section 4(3)(i). What section 4(3)(i) has in view is not merely a religious or charitable purpose, but also that the object of the trust must be an object of general public utility. In other words, the bounty of the settler must be directed towards the public as a whole or a section of the public. If the object of his bounty is neither the public nor a section of the public but merely a conglomeration of men who constitute a mere group and the nexus which ties them is not a nexus which constitutes them a section of the public, then the trust would not be a trust which would fall within the ambit of section 4(3)(i).

'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation. It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

[Matter remanded to High Court]

On the other hand, it was clear that trusts for the benefit of a particular political party, or for the advancement of particular political opinions, were not regarded as charitable. The objects specified in the trust deed, were clearly distributive. The whole of the trust fund could be applied for any one or more of the objects specified, and if any of those objects do not fall within the purview of the legal definition of "charity", the trust could not be regarded as a good charitable trust. Sub-clause (a) of clause 11 of the deed of the deed includes the advancement of any purpose which might in the uncontrolled opinion of the Managing Committee be national or of national importance for the inhabitants of British India by any means which in the like opinion of the Managing Committee be constitutional. It is impossible to say that the Managing Committee might not regard purposes which were not according to law charitable, as being nevertheless of national importance for the inhabitants of British India, and the Committee might regard methods as constitutional which the law would not regard as constitutional. Assuming the objects specified in sub-clause (a) to be charitable, this was not the case of a gift for such charitable purposes as the Managing Committee may think fit. A gift of that sort would, no doubt, be good, because the Managing Committee would be bound to keep within the ambit of charity, and if they go beyond the legal boundary, they could be controlled by the Court. There are many purposes which an individual, acting quite bona fide , may regard as charitable, but which the law does not so regard. Therefore, sub-clause (a) goes too far; and sub-clause (b) goes too far also, because it was really a gift for political purposes. Assuming that the attainment of national autonomy may be regarded as a national purpose accepted generally by, and for the good of, the inhabitants of British India, there was a very keen divergence of opinion as to the methods by which that national autonomy should be attained; and it was impossible, to avoid the conclusion that a gift for the attainment of that object by such methods as the Managing Committee may approve was really a gift for political purposes. Therefore, it was impossible to say that the ITO was wrong in holding that the income of the trust did not fall within the purview of section 4(3)(i ).

The first proviso to section 41(1) of the 1922 Act is perfectly plain. It provides in connection with funds held by a trust that where income, profits or gains or any part thereof are not specifically receivable on behalf of any one person, or where the individual shares of the persons on whose behalf they are receivable are indeterminate or unknown, the tax shall be levied and recoverable at the maximum rate. It may be rather hard on this trust fund that it should be charged at a higher rate than the amount of its income would attract if it belonged to an individual. But that is not a matter with which the Court can deal. It is perfectly plain that the case fell within the first proviso to section 41(1), and, therefore, the ITO was correct in levying income-tax at the maximum rate under the first proviso to section 41(1) of 1922 Act.

Concurrent view (as per Kania, J.)

In section 4(3)(i) the words used are that the income should be derived from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes. By the explanation added at the end, the term "charitable purpose" is stated to include an object of general public utility. Even so, it is for the assessee to show that his case falls within that extended meaning.

Certain propositions of law now appear to be well settled as a result of authorities. First, that when there is a general charitable intention, the Court will uphold it, and if within that limit discretion is given to the trustees to select an object the trust will not fail because of the discretion so given. If a trustee selects an object, which is not charitable according to law, the Court can intervene and rectify the error.

The objects in the trust deed have to be separately read, and if any of those objects is not charity, the whole gift must fail, because if the trustees choose to apply the whole of the fund to the particular object, which according to the law of the land is not charitable, then they will not be committing a breach of trust, and the trust could be said to be properly administered. The law does not permit the administration of a trust which can be so used entirely for a non-charitable object and hold it as charitable on construction. Therefore, clause 11 of this trust deed, which defines the objects of the trust, was not charitable within section 4(3)(i ) of 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

FACT: The assessee was a charitable trust. During the course of assessment, the ITO found that certain sum had been paid to the manager of the trust as loan. HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Religious or charitable trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies created a trust and purported to endow it with share held by him in certain transport companies - Contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately but companies in which N was interested were to have benefit of assets set apart by him - N was managing trustee and empowered to borrow to any extent on properties conveyed to trust not only for trust but for his own use trustees were empowered, so long as N held office of managing trustee, to sell immovable properties belonging to trust for purpose of floating other companies - Foundation of institution was apparently to be left over until companies had made sufficient money for purpose - N also reserved right to revoke trust at any time - Whether on facts properties in question were not held under trust for charitable purpose within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The settlor N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies, created a trust and purported to endow it with the shares held by him in six transport companies. He constituted himself the managing trustee of the trust and gave himself full power to deal with its assets. The managing trustees claimed refund of tax paid in respect of dividends declared on the shares held in these transport companies. The income-tax authorities refused to allow a refund. Their reason was that the shares were not held under trust wholly for charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i).

On reference:

HELD: If the assets which N purported to set apart were to be devoted directly to such objects, no doubt the trust would be entitled to the refund claimed; but the deed clearly showed that the contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately and that the companies in which N was interested were to have the benefit of these assets set apart by him. Clause 54 of the deed provided that so long as N held the office of the managing trustee he shall have the power to borrow to any extent on the properties conveyed to the trust and that the board of trustees shall be able to borrow moneys which were necessary to discharge debts contracted by N. The power given to him was not limited to borrowing for the purpose of the trust. Apparently he could borrow moneys for his own purposes on the security of the assets set apart by him. By clause 55 the trustees were empowered, so long as N held the office of managing trustee, to sell immoveable properties belonging to the trust" in expanding or floating industrial institutions," in other words for the purpose of floating other companies. Clause 59 provided that the trustees may advance to the companies in which N was interested money for (a) discharging their liabilities (b) purchasing and substituting diesel or other more economical engines for the petrol engines on buses run by them and (c ) constructing passenger sheds and garages and other "amenities and facilities" for the use of the transport services "wherever the Trust is interested".

The foundation of the institution was apparently to be left over until the companies had made sufficient money for the purpose. By clause 71, 'N' reserved to himself the power to revoke the trust at any time.

In view of the provisions of the deed by which the assets could be utilised for N’s own purposes or the purposes of his companies, it was impossible for him to contend with reason that the deed created a trust wholly for charitable purposes. The idea that some day the institution contemplated by the deed might be founded was not sufficient compliance with the section.

It was said that in 1939 N made considerable alterations in the trust deed and that these alterations removed the objections now referred to. Whether the deed as it now stood created a trust which was entitled to the benefits of section 4(3)(i) was a question with which the High Court was not concerned. It was concerned only with the question whether a trust was created wholly for charitable purposes in the year of account, 1937-38, and it was obvious that this was not the case.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

On reference : HELD: By the Insurance Act, 1938, a "principal agent" is defined as meaning "a person, who, not being a salaried employee of an insurer, in consideration of any commission, (i) performs any administrative and organizing functions for the insurer and (ii) procures general insurance business whether wholly or in part by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents of behalf of the insurer". Evidently a principal agent by the definition does not merely render personal service but is concerned with performing certain administrative and organizing functions and the procuring of general insurance business by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents. Such an agent by the very definition will be regarded as carrying on the business of a principal agent. He is not merely an employee engaged for rendering services of a personal nature: he is invested with the right as an agent to perform the administrative organizing functions for the insurer and to procure general insurance business by employing, directly or indirectly, insurance agents. By section 42A of the Insurance Act principal agents are required to obtain a certificate from the Controller of Insurance or an officer authorized by him entitling them to conduct the business of principal agency, and the certificate remains in operation for a period of twelve months only from the date of issue but is liable to be renewed. It is also true that under Part A of the Sixth Schedule to the Insurance Act certain terms are deemed to be included in every contract between an insurer carrying on general insurance business and a principal agent. Under clause 2 of Part A of the Sixth Schedule the principal agent has to procure or cause to be procured through insurance agents such an amount of general insurance business as will yield a gross premium income of not less than Rs. 20,000 in each calendar year. Under clause 4, in the event of the principal agent failing to comply with the requirements of clause 2 in any two successive calendar years, the contract shall, without prejudice to the provisions of clause 3, terminate on the 31st day of March immediately following the second calendar year. Under clause 3 the agency is also liable to be forfeited in the events set out in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) thereof. By clause 5 certain restriction are placed upon the principal agent but an account of these provisions, which impose certain restrictive conditions upon the principal agent it could not be said that the appointment of a principal agent gave rise to a bare service agreement and that the remuneration paid was not for the conduct of a business but for performance of personal service. The circumstance that the appointment was liable to be terminated at short notice and the agency was not permanent and was liable to be forfeited in the events set out hereinbefore would not, affect the character of the agency as business. Following the observation made by the Supreme Court in J.K. Trust's case [1957] 32 ITR 535 the principal agency conducted by the assessee was a business and, therefore, "property" within the meaning of section 4(3)(i). Being property which was capable of being settled upon trust by the deed of trust, dated 17-2-1951, it was lawfully settled upon trust for charitable purposes. The taxing authorities are primarily concerned with the question whether the income sought to be taxed in income from property, which is held on trust for religious or charitable purpose. If the business of the principal agency was transferred to the trustees under a deed of settlement, and from that business income was received, the income will fall within section 4(3)(i) and be exempt from tax in the hands of the trustees. Therefore, under the terms of appointment made with the company firm became the principal agents conducting a business and that business was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i ) and that the alteration, sometime after their appointment as principal agents, in the constitution of the from did not alter the character of the income earned in the course of the business. The income which is liable to be included in the total income of the assessee, was income derived from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution, unless that income fulfils the conditions prescribed by clause (b). The expression "such income" in the proviso refers to the income derived from property (which expression includes a business) held for religious or charitable purposes. But that did not justify the submission that the business which was referred to in clause (b) of the proviso must be business which is held for charitable or religious purposes. The business referred to in clause (b) of the proviso need not be business which is held for religious or charitable purposes, provided it is business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) – Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under – Assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56 – Claim of assessee trust for exemption of its income under section 4(3)(i) was rejected by ITO on ground that business of trust carried on by managing trustee on behalf of trust fell within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and hence its business income was not exempt from taxation – Whether where trust carries on business and business itself is held in trust and income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for purpose of religious or charitable character, conditions prescribed under section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and income is exempt from taxation - Held, yes – Whether claim of exemption cannot be denied even if business were to be conducted by someone else acting on behalf of trust, and proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to such businesses as are not held under trust and, therefore, field of its operation is distinct and separate from that covered by main provision of section 4(3)(i) – Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, assessee being a religious and charitable trust, was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act for assessment years in question – Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a religious and charitable trust was founded by K under a deed of trust. The founder furnished the trust with a nucleus fund to be augmented and utilised for the purpose of the trust. A business in cotton yarn and cloth was started by the board of trustees or the managing trustee of the said trust. For the assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56, the assessee submitted returns showing nil income and claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) in respect of the income from the business carried on by the trust.

The ITO, however, denied the exemption to the said business income, from taxation, and completed the assessments.

The view of the ITO was that the income from the business of the trust which was carried on by the managing trustee on behalf of the trust would fall within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and would not be covered by the main provision of section 4(3)(i), and that the necessary conditions required to be fulfilled for the operation of the proviso (b) were not present.

On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's orders and observed that it was not the trust or the institution, which was carrying on the business from which the income was earned, that the business was carried on by the managing trustee on behalf of the trust, and that therefore the application of section 4(3)(i) was excluded by the operation of proviso (b) to that section. The Tribunal, on second appeal, also confirmed the assessments.

On reference :

HELD: A cursory perusal of the terms of the deed would show that the managing trustee was the heart and soul of the trust. The terms of the trust deed expressly provided for the trust funds being employed in any trade, industry or business, which meant that the trust could carry on the business just like an individual or a firm or a limited company. It was not the contention of the department that the trust was a mere fiction or that it was illusory. Thus, a valid trust had been constituted and the trust carried on the business during the relevant accounting years.

It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

HEADNOTE: Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Related party transaction) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-trust operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital - In order to address financial difficulties faced by assessee, it entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) involved in healthcare sector, for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to SCPL - In return, assessee would receive either a fixed amount of Rs. 1 crore or 40 per cent of SCPL's profit, whichever was higher, as management fees - Assessing Officer was of view that said agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for benefit of related parties - Consequently, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied - It was noted that object of transfer agreement with SCPL was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally, and in doing so, purpose of charity was not violated as a reputed hospital of such huge size required professional handling - Further, agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable property to SCPL but to counter huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals - Whether, on facts, there was no infirmity in order of Commissioner (Appeals) in allowing exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-trust was registered under section 12A(a) and operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital and a medical college. Due to financial difficulties, the assessee entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) for the transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of the hospital to SCPL. In return, the assessee would receive either a fixed amount or a percentage of SCPL''s profit as management fees. The assessee had incurred heavy debts and faced a negative net worth. The agreement was seen as a means to ensure the assessee''s survival and continued charitable activities, as SCPL took over the hospital''s operations and liabilities.

■

The Assessing Officer scrutinized the agreement and found that it violated the basic principles of charity for which the trust had been granted registration under section 12AA. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for the benefit of related parties. Consequently, the trust''s claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied. The Assessing Officer also reclassified the Trust''s income as that of an Association of Persons (AOP), which would only be allowed to deduct its expenditures.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal by revenue to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The issue under consideration has been decided by the Tribunal in favour of the assessee in earlier year’s orders and also by the recent order passed by the ITAT Ahmedabad in the assessee’s own case for assessment year 2016-17 in ITA No. 416/Ahd/2020 vide order dated 20-07-2022 wherein the Tribunal held that the agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable to SCPL but to counter the huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals. Therefore, the Commissioner(Appeals) has correctly held that the activity of the trust was carried on in accordance with its objects and in the best interest of charity, therefore, the exemption under section 11(1)(a) has rightly been allowed by the Commissioner(Appeals). Similarly, the Commissioner(Appeals) has clearly held that section 13((1)(c)(ii) could apply only if any part of the charitable income of the trust has been used or applied for the benefits of the said persons during the previous year. But, since no portion of the income of the assessee has been applied for said person, therefore, the case of the assessee fell outside the scope of this section. Further, the trust is in receipt of income by way of management charges from SCPL and also all of its liabilities have been taken over by the same therefore there is a fact that there is no undue benefits of the use of trust property have been taken by any other persons. Similarly, there is no diversion of income of the trust as per Explanation of section13(2)(d) and 13(2)(g) as the trust has been benefitted greatly and its deficit of trust duly reduced to a great extent. Thus, the Commissioner(Appeals) has analyzed the facts correctly and given a judicious finding which does not call for any interference from outside. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 64 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 16(3) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Transfer of assets - For benefit of spouse, etc. - Assessment year 1957-58 - Assessee by a settlement deed created a trust for benefit of his minor daughter - Settlement provided that when minor attained age of 21 years, trust property would vest absolutely in her and she would become entitled to receive income from settled immovable property in her own right - Managing trustees contributed trust money as capital to firm to join partnership and received share of profits in firm - ITO taking view that section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act did not speak of actual receipt of income but only of income arising and as income had arisen from firm, held that it was taxable in assessee’s hands - Tribunal, however, set aside ITO’s order - Whether in view of decision of Supreme Court in CIT v. Manilal Dhanji [1962] 44 ITR 876, it could be said that income derived by managing trustee was not taxable in hands of assessee either under section 16(1)(c) or section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, order passed by Tribunal was correct - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee settled upon trust a certain sum and some immovable property by a deed of settlement with a view to make provisions for his minor married daughter, ‘J’. The settlement provided, inter alia, for the investment of the trust moneys in any trade, commerce, etc., at the discretion of the trustees and with the consent of the settlor and for the collection of rents from immovable properties entitled upon trust. The deed also provided that the trust would cease to operate when the minor attained the age of 21 from when the trust property would vest absolutely in her, she would become entitled to receive the income from the settled immovable properties in her own right and to dispose of at her sole discretion the amount remaining in the hands of the trustees, out of the funds settled upon trust. The managing trustee contributed trust money as capital to the firm to join the partnership and received his share of profits in the firm. The ITO found that the share of income from the firm had been credited in the account of the trust in the books of accounts of the firm and so it had arisen to the trust during the year of account. Therefore, he held that of section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act did not speak of actual receipt of income but only of income arising and, as income had arisen from the firm, it was taxable in the assessee’s hands and that the minor had a right to use the trust funds and it did not matter that in fact she did not receive it. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal, however, held that section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act could not be applied because the provisions of the trust deed could not be read as authorising the receipt of any income or deriving any benefit by the minor.

On reference :

HELD: The Supreme Court in CIT v. Manilal Dhanji [1962] 44 ITR 876 : held that when section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act talks of benefit of the minor child it refers to benefit which arises or accrues to the minor in the year of account. If there be no such benefit, the income cannot be included in the total income of the individual who made the transfer. The Supreme Court further held that when, however, the minor child derives no benefit under the trust deed in the year of account, it is not consistent with the scheme of section 16 of 1922 Act to say even though there is no accrual of any income or benefit in the year of account in favour of the minor child, yet the income must be included in the total income of the individual concerned.

In the light of the decision of the Supreme Court the income derived by managing trustee was not taxable in the hands of the assessee either under section 16(1)(c) or 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from properties held under - Assessment year 1956-57 - By an indenture of trust, ‘D’ and his wife both doctors, settled upon trust an immovable property and two maternity hospitals which were run by them - Primary object of trust was to carry on and promote educational, health, cultural, social and economic interest of people particularly of backward and lower classes - Substance of indenture of trust itself was that all trust properties were transferred by both settlers to trustees and trustees made declaration that they would hold properties for objects of trust from date of deed - One of recitals clearly indicated that it was business of conducting two maternity homes that had been settled upon trust, because net annual income which was to accrue to trust from said hospitals to be arrived at after deducting all expenses for maintaining and running hospitals and after making payment to ‘D,’ s wife as provided in trust deed for managing said hospitals for and on behalf of trust during her lifetime - Whether as trust deed was duly registered it was sufficient in law to effect a valid transfer - Held, yes - Whether since business of running and conducting maternity homes itself was settled upon trust, conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act were fulfilled and, hence income from maternity homes was exempt from taxation - Held, yes - Whether for conducting maternity hospitals presence of a doctor was essential and therefore, amount paid to wife of ‘D’ was a part of normal expenditure of conducting and managing said hospitals which was allowable as admissible deduction in computation of income of trust in hands of trustees as association of persons - Held, yes

FACT: By an indenture of trust dated 23-8-1954, one ‘D’ and his wife settled upon trust two maternity hospitals which were run by them and an immovable property for the purposes and objects contained in the said deed of trust. The assessee were the trustees under the said trust. The primary object of the trust was to carry on and promote the educational, health, cultural, literary, social and economic interests of the people, particularly of the backward and poorer classes. The important recitals in the trust deed were to the effect that the net annual income from the said hospitals, after deducting all the expenses for maintaining and running the hospitals including a sum of Rs. 750 per month which should be paid regularly to ‘D’s wife for managing the said hospitals for and on behalf of the trust during her lifetime, should accrue to the trust from year to year and that Dr. Divekar and Dr. Nalini Divekar did transfer the above said property and both the hospitals to the Trustees. And that the monies and properties of the trust were to be applied, firstly in payment of the expenses of carrying out of the trust and then in carrying out the other objects. The assessee claimed exemption under section 43(1)(i) of the 1922 Act. Even though the ITO accepted that the business in maternity homes was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act, he however took the view that its income was not exempt under the said section because it did not fulfil the requirements of proviso (b) thereto. This view was arrived at by him because he took the view that the primary purpose in conducting or running the two maternity homes or hospitals was not to give free medical facilities but charge the patients and then to apply the income for certain objects. Even the amount paid to D’s wife claimed as a deduction was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that the same was paid by the association of persons to one of its own members.

On appeal, the AAC held that the income from the trust was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and that the salary paid was an allowable deduction in computation of the assessees’ income.

On revenue’s further appeal, the Tribunal took the view that there was no actual transfer of immovable properties to the trustees if regard be had to the language employed in the document. On the assumption that the properties were considered to have been managed on behalf of a charitable institution the Tribunal took the view that the conditions laid down in proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) were not satisfied in the case and the income was, therefore, not exempt from tax.

It, however, affirmed the finding of the AAC that salary to ‘D’s wife was an allowable deduction.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One 'S' and four persons, who were holding certain securities for charity purpose, executed a deed of declaration of trust - As per trust deed, trustees would give preference to poor and indigent relations or members of family of 'S' including therein distant and collateral relations - Whether since trust had been mainly formed for charitable purposes, mere provision for giving preference to poor and indigent relations or family members of 'S' did not affect validity of trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income from trust properties invested in securities was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: One 'S' and four others were holding certain securities for the purpose of charity and had been applying the same for and towards charitable purposes, executed, on 8-6-1922, a deed of declaration of trust declaring that the said trust fund would be held by them on trusts more specifically therein mentioned. Clause 13 of trust deed provided that the trust fund would be held by the trustees upon the trusts to apply the net income thereof after providing for all necessary expenses in relation to the management of the trust funds, for all or any of the following purposes (a) the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of jewish (b) the institution, maintenance and support of hospitals and schools, colleges or other educational institutions or (c) the relief of any distress caused by the elements of nature such as famine, pestilence, fire, tempest, flood, earthquake or any other such calamity or (d) the care and protection of animals useful to mankind or (e) the advancement of religion or (f) other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the foregoing purposes. The trust deed further provided that the trustees would give preference to the poor and indigent relations or members of the family of the said 'S' including there in distant and collateral relations. The trust fund had been invested by the trustees in inter alia 3½ per cent Government securities. In the year 1930, a certificate was issued by the ITO, whereby the Reserve Bank of India was authorized not to deduct at source the tax on the said securities so held by the trustees. For the assessment years 1948-49 and 1949-50, the ITO took the view that the income from the trust fund was not exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act accordingly, he assessed the appellants. On appeals, the AAC and the Tribunal confirmed the assessment made by the ITO.

On reference, the High Court also held that the trust property was not held wholly for religious or charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: Under clause 13 the trustees were at liberty to hold the trust fund and to apply the net income thereof for all or any of the six purposes mentioned therein. The relations or members of the family of the said 'S' including therein distant and collateral relations did not figure as direct recipients of any benefit under sub-clauses (b) to (f) and, therefore, in so far as those purposes were concerned the trust certainly involved an element of public utility.

It was open to the trustees to spend the net income entirely for the purpose referred to in sub-clause (a) to the exclusion of the other clauses. But the very fact that the relations or members of the family did not come in directly under any of those latter sub-clauses could not be ignored, for they certainly had some bearing on the question as to who or what were the primary objects of the trust as a whole. In the next place, the purpose of sub-clause (a) was the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of 'V' or any other community.

It followed that sub-clause (a ) constituted a valid public charitable trust having as its beneficiaries the several classes of persons referred to therein.

The circumstances that in selecting the beneficiaries under sub-clause (a) preference had to be given, under the proviso, to the relations or members of the family of 'S', could not affect that public charitable trust.

Therefore, the income from the trust properties came within the scope of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and was entitled to exemption.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the appellant/assessee.

The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision. The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The ITO held that the assessee-trusts were neither religious nor charitable trusts, and relying upon that finding, as also upon the provisions of clause 13 of the trust deeds, declined to grant the exemption. The AAC set aside the order of the ITO and held that the trusts were entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act. On appeal before the Tribunal, the revenue raised two contentions : (1) that one of the objects set out in clause 5 of the trust deed, namely, advancement of commerce and industry, was not a charitable object and since the trustees had discretion under that clause to utilize the corpus as also the income of the trust properties for any of the objects including the aforesaid objects, the trust was not a charitable trust, and (2) that clauses 12 and 13 of the trust deeds gave power to the trustees to take over other institutions and to accept donations and/or contributions, that such donations might carry with them terms and conditions inconsistent with the objects of the trust and if the trustees were under these powers to accept such donations and/or contributions, they would have to carry out such terms and conditions which might not be charitable in nature.
