On reference:

HELD: So far as the question as to whether the expression "advancement of commerce and industry" contained in clause 5 of the trust deeds was concerned, no difficulty arose because of the concession made by the revenue in view of the various decisions that such a clause could not be held to be objectionable and a trust for the advancement of commerce and industry would be a trust for a charitable purpose within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and the Explanation attached thereto and that such an object satisfied the statutory test, namely, advancement of any other object of general utility as contemplated by the Explanation of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act.

The revenue was fair enough to concede that the expression "allied objects" used in clause 12 would mean objects which were similar in nature or akin to the objects of the present trusts and such objects then would go hand in hand with the objects of the present trust. In other words, clause 12 on such a construction merely empowered the trustees to take even the superintendence, management and administration of such trust or institution whose objects were similar to, or consistent with, the objects of the assessee-trusts. The trustees would not, therefore, by reason of the power reserved to them under clause 12, be entitled to take over any trust or institution whose objects were not for charitable purposes. No objection, therefore, could be taken to such a clause if the power of the trustees, by the use of the expression, "allied objects", was clearly circumscribed to accepting administration and management of such trusts or institutions which had objects similar to those of the present trusts.

The predominant object of the trust was undoubtedly for charitable purposes and prima facie, therefore, it would appear that notwithstanding the power conferred upon the trustees by clause 13 to accept donations and/or contributions upon such terms and conditions as they might deem proper and also the power to expend any portion of the income of the trust fund for the purpose thereof, that power could only be exercised by them consistently with the objects of the trust as set out in clause 5 of the trust deeds. This conclusion was supported by the provisions of the other clauses of the trust deeds, namely clauses I, 2, 4.

On the assessee's appeal to the High Court: HELD: The provisions of section 13(1)(c) imposed certain restriction on utilization of income of the trust which claims exemption under section 11. As per clause (c) of sub-sec (1) of section 13, if any part of income or any property of the trust or the institution, is used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person referred in sub-section (3), then the trust is not entitled to exemption under section 11. Similarly, provisions of section 164(2) states that in a case where the whole or any part of the relevant income is not exempt under section 11 or section 12 by virtue of the provisions contained in clause (c) or clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 13, tax shall be charged on the relevant income or part of relevant income at the maximum marginal rate. Therefore, if the trust diverts its fund then, only part of the income is chargeable to tax at the maximum marginal rate of tax; but not the whole income of the trust. It is clear that in case there is violation referred to section 13(1)(c), then tax can be charged on such income which violates the provisions of section 13(1)(c); but not the whole income of the trust. The Commissioner (Appeals), after considering the relevant provisions has rightly upheld that the only amounts that have been diverted by the assessee trust can only be assessed to tax at the maximum marginal rate. Accordingly, there is no any infirmity in the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) and hence, the same is upheld. [Para 5.1]

Coming to the specific instances of diversion of funds, the Assessing Officer has brought out three instances of diversion of funds to the persons as specified under section 13(3). The Act prohibits persons specified under section 13(3) to get direct or indirect benefit from the trust or institution claims exemption under section 11. It is true that the only section of the public that could be benefited by this bath would be the European public in Bombay but it is well settled that an object of public utility need not be an object in which the whole of the public is interested. It is sufficient if a well defined section of the public benefits by the object, and the object of the trust in the instant case was to benefit clearly a defined section of the public living in Bombay. Now, on a casual consideration of the matter it may strike one that the most essential element of charity is to render service to the public without any charge or remuneration, but, it is clear on the authorities that the eleemosynary element is not an essential element of charity. A settlor or a donor may make a charity by setting up an institution and also providing funds by which those who take advantage of the institution can do so without paying any charge or one may have a case where the charity may not go to those limits and one may confine his charity to merely setting up the institution and providing that those who wish to take advantage of the institution must pay reasonable charges for the same. In both cases the setting up of the institution would be a charitable object if the institution serves a purpose of general public utility. The only essential factor to determine whether it is a charity or not would be whether there is any private gain by the setting up of the institution. If the gain derived by running the institution continues to be impressed with the trust which is a charitable trust, then it is immaterial whether the institution is run as a commercial institution or not, but if in the running of the institution profits are made and the profit goes to any private individual or if the institution is intended for any private gain, then undoubtedly the running of the institution could not be considered as being run for a charitable object.

Section 4(3)(ia) would only apply to an activity which was not an integral activity of the trust itself. If the trustees carried on a business which was not part of the property of the trust, then only that income of the business would be exempt from taxation which was applied solely to the purposes of the institution. If such a business made a profit, and only part was spent for religious or charitable institution and the other part was kept in surplus or in reserve, then the part which was kept in surplus or reserve would be liable to tax. Therefore, the Legislature, as far as section 4(3)(ia ) was concerned, looked upon a business falling under this sub-section as something independent of the trust itself; and looking upon that business as something independent of the trust itself; it naturally wanted to tax the income of that business to the extent that, that income was not applied solely to the purposes of the charitable or religious institution. If one takes this view of section 4(3)(i) and 4(3)(ia), then no difficulty would be experienced in the way of the trustees who were carrying on the activity as a part of the trust itself and which activity made profits which the trusts may keep in reserve in order to strengthen the financial position of the institution. As such income would fall under first part of section 4(3)(i ), no question could then arise of that income being necessarily applied for the purposes of the institution in order to earn exemption under section 4(3)(ia).

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1946-47 – Founders of assessee-press created a trust in respect of assessee-press and a weekly paper published by it – Clause (2) of trust deed provided that trust Committee could not change policy of paper which at its inception was published in its first issue and which in political matters was according to aims and objects of Indian National Congress – Policy article of paper as published in its first issue made it quite clear that paper was not brought into existence to maintain, support, protect or oppose any particular association, organization, person or creed and that would include Congress organization, but aimed at good of all mankind and good of India and putting down of evils in general and encouragement of catholicity and of all those aspects of life which an educated person would like to see encouraged - Whether policy of paper was aimed at supplying to Province an organ of educated public opinion, and to encourage all that would lead to progress of India as a part of progress of mankind, which was a charitable object – Held, yes – Whether therefore, income of assessee was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act – Held, yes

FACT: 'S' and 'G' started the assessee-press and a weekly paper. By a deed the aforementioned persons created a trust in respect of the assessee press and the weekly paper. The trust deed provided in clause that the Trust Committee could not change the policy of the papar, which at its inception was published in its first issue and which would be published in the first issue of every year and which in political matters was according to the aims and objects of the Indian National Congress. The first issue of the paper stated that the ultimate aim of the weekly paper was the good of all mankind and that a very important and indispensable way to achieve that aim was the progress of India by the development of agriculture, trade, knowledge, art, prosperity, self-respect, power, good conduct and character. Other requirements of progress were also set out, namely, national unity, propagation of a well organised, popular and comprehensive education of right policies of good and efficient administration conducive to the welfare of the people, prevention of social evils and persecutions, encouragement of propagation of self-dependence and strong faith in self-rule.

In respect of its income for the relevant previous year, the assessee claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act on the ground that the income was of a trust which was wholly for religious or charitable purposes. The revenue authorities rejected said claim and held that the objects were firstly vague and ambiguous and secondly were neither religious nor charitable within the meaning of section 4(3)(i).

On reference:

HELD: The charitable object of the trust in the instant case was that of supplying to the Province an organ of educated public opinion. Moreover clause (2) did not state that the policy in political matters of the paper would be the policy from time to time of the Indian National Congress. What the policy would be was determined by the policy article once and for all and the policy therein was described as being in accord with the then policies and objects of the Indian National Congress. Clause (2) did not imply that the paper would become the propaganda machinery of the Indian National Congress and would further the views from time to time of the Indian National Congress. The second part of clause (2 ) was merely descriptive, so far as political matters were concerned, of the policy article. On examining the policy article carefully, it was quite clear that the paper was not brought into existence to maintain, support, protect or oppose any particular association, organisation, person or creed and that would include the Congress organisation. A paper which aims at carrying out such a policy as was to be the policy of the paper in question and aims at the good of all mankind and the good of India and the putting down of evils in general and the encouragement of catholicity and of all those aspects of life which an educated person would like to see encouraged , must clearly intend to be an organ of educated public opinion. No doubt at places such sentiments as a strong faith in self-rule or faith in the intentions of the British Government and the desire to raise the status of Indians everywhere were mentioned. But it did not appear that the paper had a political battle cry or object, or was founded in order to further particular political, social, economic or other programmes. But the aim was to encourage all that would lead to the progress of India as a part of the progress of mankind.

The policy article of the paper was expressly mentioned in clause (2) and there was no reason why it should not be deemed to have become a part of the deed of trust.

Clause (i) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 1922 Act deals with income derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation for religious or charitable purposes, while clause (ia) deals with income derived from business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution. The two clauses, therefore, do not necessarily overlap. Clause (i) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 1922 Act, applies to cases where the business itself is held under trust for religious or charitable purposes, while clause (ia) applies only to such business as is carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution which was not held under trust.

The Sabha, was clearly an institution having been brought about to effect the purpose and to carry out the objects for which the trust was founded. The word "applied" in clause means actually spent while, in clause (i) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act, the words used are "income applied or finally set the words "finally set apart" had not been repeated in clause(ia) at that sub-section. The word "applied" did not necessarily mean "spent". Even if it has been earmarked and allocated for the purposes of the institution, it may, be deemed to have been applied for its purposes. Neither the word "applied" nor the word "institution" is of any importance in this case, the case was governed by income from the property held under trust as laid down in section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

Therefore, it was held that the bhents (offerings) vested in the Sabha under a legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes of the Sabha but the bhents could not be said to be income derived from property under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act. They would properly come under clause (ii) of that sub-section meaning thereby that they were income of a religious or charitable institution derived from voluntary contributions and applicable solely to religious or charitable purposes.

Further, the income derived from industrial and commercial concerns was the income from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes and was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and it was, therefore, not necessary to apply to such income section 4(3)(ia) of the 1922 Act.

Note:The case was decided against the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1952-53 to 1956-57 - Whether where business in kuries was held by assessee under a trust for religious or charitable purpose income derived from such business would be exempt from tax under provisions of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee company was a charitable trust one of its objects being to raise funds by conducting kuries with the company as the foreman; receiving donations and subscriptions; and by such other means as the company deemed fit. For the assessment years 1952-53 to 1956-57, the assessee claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act in respect of its income from kuries business. The ITO was of the view that the trust was of a charitable character but was covered under proviso to section 4(3)(i). On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the opinion of the department.

On reference :

HELD: It is settled law that a business itself can be held under trust for religious or charitable purposes and that the income derived from such a business will fall within the ambit of the exclusion granted by section 4(3) (i ) of the 1922 Act.

In the instant case, the business in kuries itself was held under trust for religious or charitable purposes and this was abundantly clear from the memorandum of association. The first object of the assessee was to raise funds by conducting kuries with the company as the foreman; receiving donations and subscriptions; and by such other means as the company deemed fit. Hence, the proviso to section 4(3)(i) was not attracted and the assessee trust was entitled to the exemption under section 4(3)(i ) as amended by Act 25 of 1953 in respect of its income derived from business in kuries.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HELD: A charitable purpose may be served in more than one way. One is to directly contribute for the promotion of that cause; the other is to contribute money to another charitable organisation, which advances that cause. In the absence of allegations of device and/or mala fides, the amount contributed to other charitable institutions out of the income accumulated under sub-section (2) is outside the mischief of sub-section (3) of section 11. In other words, such contribution does not amount to application of the income for purposes other than charitable or religious. Thus, the donations made to other charitable trusts would not be hit by the provisions of section 11(3).

Further, it is important to note that if the assessee trust had written off the amount in financial year 2012-13, when the employment was terminated with two individuals, then legally the loans given to them would have been wiped out from the trust balance sheet, and the Department could not have taken the plea of "continue to lend". In that event the trust would have logically missed the moral force to recover the amount. From the above, it is clear that interest free advance given to two individuals is not a beneficial/gracious payment made to persons referred to under section 13(3) and, thus, the same cannot be treated as payment in contravention to section 13(1)(c). As regards observations of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has given benefit to the interested persons without any interest or security, it is found that said finding of the Assessing Officer is not on sound footing, because the Assessing Officer has proceeded on the assumption that the assessee has lent the sum. But, the transactions between the trust and the consultants was under normal circumstances as a prudent businessman and hence question of charging interest or taking a security against such advance does not arise. Therefore, loans given to two consultants would not covered under section 13(3)(cc) and thus, not resulting in any benefit directly or indirectly to interested persons so as to attract provisions of section 13(1)(c). Consequently, on this ground the benefit of exemption under section 11 cannot be denied to the assessee for Assessment years 2012-13, 2013-14, 2016-17 and 2017-18. [Para 17]

According to the Assessing Officer, the transactions are clearly diversion of funds in contravention of provisions of section 13(1)(c), to the persons specified in sub-section (3) of section 13 and, thus, the trust is not entitled for exemption under section 11. He, therefore, rejected exemption claimed under section 11 and taxed income at maximum marginal rate as per proviso to section 164(2). [Para 13] The provisions of section 13(1)(c) imposed certain restriction on utilization of income of the trust which claims exemption under section 11. As per clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 13, if any part of income or any property of the trust or the institution, is used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person referred in sub-section (3), then the trust is not entitled to exemption under section 11. The specified persons has been referred to under section 13(3), and as per said section the persons specified are the 'author' or 'founder' of the trust, their relatives, any trustee of the trust or manager by whatever name called. The provisions of section 164(2), states that in a case, where the whole or any part of the relevant income is not exempt under section 11 or section 12 by virtue of the provisions contained in clause (c) or clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 13, tax shall be charged on the relevant income or part of relevant income at the maximum marginal rate. Therefore, if the trust allows any benefit to interested persons, then only that part of the income which is in violation of section13(1)(c) is chargeable to tax at the maximum marginal rate of tax; but not whole income of the trust. In view of the clear provisions of the Act, it is clear that in case there is violation referred to under section 13(1)(c), then tax can be charged on such income which violates the provisions of section 13(1)(c); but not whole income of the trust. Denial of exemption under section 11 should be restricted to the extent of income, which is in violation of section 13(1)(c) and 13(1)(d). In this case, the Assessing Officer has levied tax on total income of the trust at maximum marginal rate, contrary to settled position of law. Therefore, the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) were erred in rejecting exemption claimed under section 11 to total income of the trust. [Para 14]

Having said so, lets examine that whether under the given facts and circumstances of the case is there any violation of provisions of section 13(1)(c), and the Assessing Officer was right in denying the benefit of exemption claimed under section 11. The Assessing Officer has considered advances given to KVR and SV under section 13(3)(cc) and held that said loans are clearly in the nature of direct/indirect benefit of trust income/property to persons referred to in section 13(3). The provisions contained in section 13(1)(c) put a restriction on persons referred to in section 13(3) to take any benefit of either income or property of the trust. Therefore, in order to consider any payments to any person under section 13(1)(c), it is essential to see whether the income/property of the trust is directly or indirectly used or applied for the benefit of trustees. In this case, there was no such finding from the Assessing Officer that the income was used or applied for the benefit of trustees. The only allegations is that the trust has given loans to two persons without any security or interest and further said persons are in the nature of managers by whatever name called as referred to under section 13(3)(cc) and thus, said payments violates sections 13(1)(c). [Para 15]

and cross-subsidisation models to sustain their operations. If the mere existence of substantial receipts or premium facilities were to become a disqualifying factor, a large number of institutions historically recognised as charitable would be rendered vulnerable to cancellation of registration. The Tribunal finds no indication that Parliament intended such a result. On the contrary, the legislative scheme appears to encourage the creation and maintenance of institutions capable of delivering high-quality charitable services rather than penalising them for achieving operational excellence. [Para 110]

■ The Tribunal also finds that the CIT(E) has attached considerable significance to the magnitude of receipts and financial resources available with the institution. Here again, the reasoning appears to overlook the structure of section 11 itself. As already discussed, section 11 does not prohibit earning of income. It postulates income. The statute is concerned not with the quantum of income but with its application. A trust holding substantial property may derive substantial income. A large hospital may generate substantial receipts. A university may possess extensive assets and receive considerable contributions. None of these circumstances, by themselves, destroy the charitable character of the institution. What the law examines is whether such income remains dedicated to the charitable purposes for which the institution exists. In the present case, the Tribunal finds no finding by the CIT(E) that the income of the trust has ceased to be applied towards healthcare activities or that it has been diverted for private enrichment. The absence of such a finding is of considerable significance. [Para 111]

■

The financial analysis undertaken by the CIT(E) also appears to proceed on the assumption that surplus and profit motive are synonymous. This proposition stands directly contradicted by the consistent line of authorities rendered by the Supreme Court. In Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association (supra), the Court recognised that surplus arising incidentally from carrying out charitable activities does not alter the charitable character of the institution. Similar principles were reiterated in Aditanar Educational Institution (supra) and Queen's Educational Society (supra), where the Court emphasised that the decisive test lies not in the existence of surplus but in its destination. If the surplus is ploughed back into the institution and utilised for advancement of its charitable objects, it does not become profit in the commercial sense. The impugned order, however, frequently uses expressions such as 'surplus', 'large receipts' and 'financial strength' as though these facts are self-evident indicators of commerciality. Such an approach is inconsistent with the settled jurisprudence governing charitable institutions. [Para 112]

■

The Tribunal also finds considerable merit in the assessee's contention that the CIT(E) has not adequately distinguished between operational receipts and philanthropic support. The material placed before the Tribunal indicates that the institution has received donations, contributions and earmarked funds intended for charitable purposes and development of healthcare infrastructure. Such receipts cannot be equated with commercial profits. A charitable institution which receives substantial donations does not become less charitable because it possesses financial resources. Indeed, philanthropic support is often a hallmark of public confidence in the institution's charitable mission. The treatment of such receipts as indicators of commerciality therefore appears conceptually unsound. Equally, designated funds, earmarked contributions and statutory allocations cannot automatically be treated as unrestricted surplus available for private gain. The assessee has demonstrated that it has suffered deficit from its medical operation from FY 2021-22 to FY 2024-25 and is funded by philanthropic support. Hence the observation of CIT(E) that the assessee has earned huge surplus is factually incorrect. [Para 113]

■

The CIT(E) has also relied upon the size of the organisation, the number of employees and the structured nature of hospital administration. The Tribunal is unable to subscribe to the proposition that professional management and organisational sophistication are indicative of commercial character. A tertiary care hospital handling thousands of patients annually cannot function without a large workforce, detailed protocols, administrative systems, compliance mechanisms and specialised departments. The existence of such systems demonstrates operational necessity rather than profit motive. If efficiency and organisation are treated as evidence against charity, then the law would paradoxically reward inefficiency and penalise excellence. Such a conclusion would be wholly inconsistent with both logic and legislative intent. [Para 114]

The business in katha came into existence in the year 1972 and the production unit started production on 8-2-1973. Thus, the katha business was not even in the contemplation of the settlors and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. [Para 19] The test which emerged from the decision of the Apex Court in the case of J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 is that the business, if it is to be considered as property held under trust, should have been either acquired with the help of the fund originally settled upon trust or the original fund that was settled upon trust must have a substantial and real connection with the later acquisition or carrying on of the business by the trustees. The facts of the present case do not measure up to the test. The fund originally settled upon trust was a meagre amount of Rs. 2,100 at the time of the creation of the trust on 8-9-1971. It is undisputed that the katha unit was set up in the year 1972 with the aid and assistance of the borrowed amounts, the borrowings being both from the concerns in which the settlors/trustees held substantial interest and from commercial banks. There is thus,no nexus or integration between the amount originally settled upon trust and the later setting up and conduct of the katha business. Moreover, the distinction between the original trust fund and the later commencement of the business with the help of the borrowed funds should be kept in mind in the context of ascertaining whether the particular katha business was even in the contemplation of the settlors of the trust. It is difficult to view the original settlement of Rs. 2,100 upon trust and the setting up of the katha business as part of an integrated scheme even apart from the fact that the business was not acquired or carried on with the help of the original trust fund. It is also significant that section 11(1) starts with the expression 'subject to the provisions of sections 60 to 63……….'. These sections find place in Chapter V. Section 60 provides for the consequences of a transfer of income where there is no transfer of assets. It says that where a person transfers merely the income from an asset without transferring the asset itself, he would continue to be chargeable to income-tax. Section 61 provides for the consequences of a revocable transfer of assets and says that the same would be the position where a person is in receipt of income by virtue of a revocable transfer of assets. Section 62 provides for the consequences of a transfer of assets for specified period. It is an exception to section 61. Generally a person has to get rid of the asset itself before ceasing to be assessable in respect of the income from that asset. A mere direction that the income from the business shall be applied to the charitable objects of the trust, without there being a settlement of the business itself upon trust, does not result in any trust or legal obligation. [Para 21]

There is no connection between the carrying on of the katha business and the attainment of the objects of the trust, which are basically for the advancement of education, inculcation of patriotism, Indian culture, running of dispensaries hospitals, etc. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from katha business is ear-marked for application to the charitable objects would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The Commissioner (Appeals) in his order for the assessment year 1992-93 has rightly taken the view that the application of the income generated by the business is not the relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. The examples, appositely given by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order, clarify the position: the instance of a charitable trust established for providing medical relief running a nursing home in the process, or a trust for advancement of education running a publishing house or a newspaper. [Para 22]

On second appeal

HELD: The category of persons mentioned in clause (ii) of sub-section (1) of section 13 are mentioned in sub-section (3) of section 13, which includes the author of the trust or the founder of the institution. Undisputedly, 50 per cent income generated by the trust was being given to Dr. P and in the assessment year under consideration certain sum paid to him was against the monthly payments given to various other Doctors by way of salary besides free transport, etc. Thus, out of the income of the trust part of such income was being used directly or indirectly for the benefit of the founder member which came within the prohibited category referred to in sub-section (3) of section 13. Therefore, in so far as exemption under section 11 was concerned, this could not be granted in view of violation of provisions of clause (ii)(c ) of sub-section (1) of section 13 read with sub-section (3) of section 13.

Section 10(22A ) provides that the income of the hospital existing only for philanthropic purposes and not for the purposes of profit is entitled to exemption. The word ‘philanthropy’ is not defined in the Act. The general meaning of the word ‘philanthropy’ includes activities promoting goodwill to mankind or activities beneficial to humanity at large as opposed to activities solely for the benefit of a few individuals. When clause 10(22A ) was added to section 10 with almost similar wording as clause (22), it would only be proper to infer that the Legislature used those words in clause (22A ) taking note of the interpretation given to those words occurring in clause (22 ).

The CBDT Circular No. 45, dated 2-9-1970—See Taxmann’s Direct Taxes Circulars 1995 edn., Vol. 3 p. 2.374 clarifies the position that hospitals and other institutions which exist solely for philanthropic purposes and not for purposes of profit will be totally exempt from tax, as in the case of universities and other educational institutions.

In order to achieve the main philanthropic objects, the hospital may do some profit earning business provided such profit is appropriated towards the expansion and development of the hospital or to start another institution with the same philanthropic objectives. If the primary purpose is philanthropic, the inclusion of some objects for earning profit for the implementation of the primary object would not alter the character of that primary object.

Therefore, the very issuance of the show cause notice dated 25-10-2011, proposing to cancel the registration on examination of the modus of application of funds of the trust is without jurisdiction. [Para 64] In Tamil Nadu Kalvi Kapu Arakkattalai v. CIT [2014] 90 CCH 184 (Chennai), it was held that while considering the claim for exemption, the authority should not be solely guided by the objects set out in various clauses in the Instrument of Trust, rather should be guided by the activities of the Trust, as to how the funds are employed, since the exemption sought for is under Chapter III, which deals with incomes which do not form part of total income. Thus, under Chapter III, more particularly, sections 10 to 13A, the Act brings certain categories of exemption and incomes falling within those categories are completely exempt from the purview of the Act as they are not at all to be included in the total income of the assessee. Therefore, such type of exemption/s has/have to be distinguished from certain types of income which are included in the total income of the assessee, but in respect of which, statute provides relief by way of deduction in computing total income, by granting rebate of tax and by granting certain other reliefs to the taxpayers. [Para 65]

The last aspect to be considered is under what circumstances, the power under section 12AA(3) can be invoked. The said provision states that where a trust or an institution has been granted registration under clause (b) of sub-section (1) or has obtained registration at any time under section 12A and subsequently, the Commissioner is satisfied that the activities of such trust or institution are not genuine or are not being carried out in accordance with the objects of the trust or institution, as the case may be, he shall pass an order in writing cancelling the registration of such trust or registration. In terms of the proviso, no order under sub-section (3) shall be passed, unless such trust or institution has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Thus, the power under sub-section (3) of section 12AA would be invokable under two circumstances mentioned in the provision and upon the Commissioner being satisfied that the activities of the trust are not genuine or the activities are not in accordance with the objects of the trust. [Para 70]

In the case on hand, there is no allegation that the assessee trust has not carried on its activities in accordance with the objects of the trust as set out in the Deed of Trust and the Supplementary Deed. The Revenue has accepted the said fact. The DIT(E) seeks to bring the assessee's case in the first limb of sub-section (3) by stating that the activities of the trust are not genuine. [Para 71]

Except for stating that the activities are not genuine because of the amendment to the proviso to section 2(15), there is no other allegation, with regard to the genuineness of the trust. The amendment to section 2(15) cannot make activity of a trust not genuine, which was hitherto genuine while enjoying the registration under section 12AA prior to the amendment. Therefore, the DIT(E) failed to record his satisfaction as required to be done under sub-section (3) of section 12AA. The satisfaction should be on the activities of the trust and finding should be rendered as to how such activities are not genuine. The activities of the assessee trust have not been disputed, nor there is any allegation of non-genuine activities. Therefore, by referring to the amendment to the proviso to section 2(15) and referring to the meaning of the word 'education' as spelt out in certain decisions, cannot be construed to be a satisfaction, which is contemplated under sub-section (3) of section 12AA. [Para 72]

The jurisdiction to cancel the registration only arises if there is a change in the activity of the institution or the activities of the institution are not genuine. It was further held that Circular No. 21 of 2016 directs the Officer of Revenue not to cancel the registration only because the receipts on account of business are in excess of the limits in the proviso to section 2(15). HEADNOTE: Section 2(15), read with section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the indian Income-tax Act, 1922]-charitable purpose-Assessee-trust had a number of objects, independent of each other, including one to open, found or establish commercial concerns and start business undertakings-Whether assessee-trust was established for charitable purpose and entitled to exemption from tax-Held, on facts, no

FACT: The assessee claimed exemption from income-tax for the assessment years 1961-62, 1962-63 and 1963-64 under section 4(3)(i) of the Income-tax Act. 1922/section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Earlier, the assessee's claim for similar exemption for the assessment years 1954-55 to 1960-61 had been negatived by the Rajasthan High Court by its judgment in CIT v. Jaipur Charitable Trust [1971] 81 ITR 1 which was confirmed by the Supreme Court in Yogiraj Charity Trust v. C/r[1976] 103 ITR 777. The assessee's present claim for the assessment year 1961-62 was based on a trust deed dated 18-4-1948. There were a number of objects, a good many of which were of religious and charitable nature. Clause 5( a)(v) specified the object as: "To open, found, establish, equip, finance, assist, maintain or contribute to religious, commercial, technical, industrial or commercial concerns, institutions, associations or bodies imparting any type of training or providing employment to persons." Under clause 5(b) the trustees had power to acquire, hold, carry on and manage any trade or Business or any share thereof. The trustees also had full discretion in employing the whole or any portion of the trust property or fund in such trade or business or running business concerns or managing agencies or other investments, etc. It was also provided in clause 30 that if any object of the trust was found to be invalid or contrary to law, it would not affect the other objects of the trust. The lower authorities rejected the assessee's claim for exemption for the aforesaid assessment years.

On reference, the assessee contended, inter alia, (i) that the decision of the Supreme Court in the assessee's case for earlier years should be taken as modified by the latest Supreme Court decision in the case of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers' Association [1980] 121 ITR 1; (ii ) that the 1961 Act had brought about a change in the law and that under the 1961 Act merely an activity for profit did not by itself render the trust as non-charitable; (iii)that there were 14 objects set out in clause 5 each one of which, except that set out in sub-clause (v), was clearly a charitable purpose, and that it should be held that the running of a business, if any, was not with a view to making profits but in order to carry out the several admittedly charitable or religious purposes; (iv) that, in fact, the assessee did not carry on any business and that the trust had derived its income only from certain securities and investments; and (v ) that the income, profits and gains of the assessee trust could not be diverted for the benefit of the settlor or for any private individual but could only be utilised for the objects of the trust.

The application of the fund for charitable purposes is obligatory, the trustees being given a discretion only to choose, from amongst charitable objects as they might consider it proper to benefit, but no discretion to choose any object which is not charitable. The intention to benefit charities and charities alone is thus clear and if that be so, there is a valid trust and the courts will not allow it to fail in spite of the fact that the choice of the particular charity or charities is left to the discretion of the trustees. In the instant case, the governing direction was that the income from the trust fund should be paid and applied for the benefit of charitable purpose or purposes, although what the purpose or purposes would be, it was left to the trustees to select. There were no words in clause of the deed which postponed the operation of that direction. Having enjoined the trustees to pay and apply the income for such charitable purposes as they might choose, the trust undoubtedly gave them some discretion with regard to the time and the manner in which the actual payments were to be made. The total effect was that the trustees were to frame a scheme or arrangement, but the form of such scheme or arrangement should be as they might in their absolute discretion determine from time to time. The application of the income should have to be in accordance with such scheme or arrangement and from time to time and such times and in such manner as might be laid down in the scheme. The true purport of the whole direction, therefore, seemed to be that in the first place the trustees were directed to apply the income for the benefit of charities selected by themselves. In the second place, they were directed to frame a scheme or arrangement for the actual application of the income, although they may vary the form of the scheme or arrangement from time to time at their discretion, and, in the third place, they were enjoined to pay the income at such times and in such manner as might be laid down in the scheme framed by themselves. Therefore, the clause would not be read as giving an unfettered discretion to the trustees not to make any payment at all to any charity so long as they might wish. Although the direction was couched in language of a general character and no specific limits of time were laid down, the trustees were nevertheless required to carry out the directions in a reasonable manner. Should they fail to choose any charity or frame any scheme or make any payment for an unreasonable length of time and thereby fail to administer the trust at all, the court would be quite entitled to intervene and compel them to administer the trust by itself framing a scheme or it may be, should it be necessary, by taking over the administration of the trust in its own hands.

It was true that if the trustees be really the same as the settlor, if they deliberately refrain from administering the trust and making any payment of the income for a period of six years and if the vigilance of the court was not attracted, the result apprehended by the Commissioner might follow. It was, however, not open to make such possibilities into consideration in construing the deed of trust as it stood. A deed must be presumed to intend what it says and its provisions must be so construed whenever possible, as to give effect to that intention and so must the directions contained in the deed be held to be workable and intended to be worked if such a construction is open on the words used. In the instant case, as a matter of construction, neither the words relied on before the lower authorities nor the words relied on before the instant court could warrant the view that there was no valid trust or that there was only pretence of a trust and what the deed purported to have created was illusory.

In view of the decision in Dick v. Audsley [1908] AC 347, it could be said that a trust for charitable purposes does not become invalid, if the choice of the specific charitable objects to be benefited is left to the trustees, nor is it to be condemned as invalid or illusory, if, by the language of the deed, the trustees are given an absolute discretion to apply the fund at such time as they may think fit or retain it so long as they choose. If, however, the department wanted to impugn the trust on the ground that it was not a bona fide trust at all, it should have taken that point in a straightforward manner. The attack through the construction of the trust deed itself might fail.

For the above reasons it was held that a valid trust had been created wholly for charitable purposes and income of the trust from the shares thereby settled was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

A little historical background is necessary to be brought out in understanding the mandate of section 11. Section 11 corresponds to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. [Para 14] Under the provision as it existed prior to 1-4-1952, there was no difference maintained between application of the income of the trust within or without the taxable territories. The provision as it existed after the amendment made with effect from 1-4-1952 makes a reference to application or accumulation for application of the income of the trust 'to such religious or charitable purposes as relate to anything done within the taxable territories'. The assessee contended that the words 'as relate to anything done within the taxable territories' clearly show that the charitable purposes must be executed within the taxable territories and that it was immaterial where the income is actually applied. It is difficult to conceive of a situation under which the charitable purposes are executed within the taxable territories but the income of the trust is applied elsewhere in the implementation of such purposes. Be that as it may, the position is put beyond doubt by the proviso to section 4(3)(i ) of the old Act. It says that the income of the trust shall stand included in its total income if it is applied to religious or charitable purposes throughout/within the taxable territories. The proviso is indicative of the object of the main provision. In the main part, it was provided that the income of the trust should be applied within the taxable territories to religious or charitable purposes and in the proviso an exception was carved out to provide that if the income is applied outside the taxable territories, even though to religious or charitable purposes, the trust will not secure the exemption from tax in respect of such income. Two situations were anticipated for which provision was made in the proviso itself. In these two situations, the Central Board of Revenue (CBR, the present CBDT) was empowered to direct by general or special order, that in such cases the income of the trust shall not be included in the total income merely because the income was applied to charitable purposes outside the taxable territories. The first situation was where the property was held under a trust or other legal obligation created before 1-4-1952. The second situation was where the property was held under trust or other legal obligation created after the aforesaid date and the income therefrom is applied outside the taxable territories to charitable purposes as are done to promote international welfare in which India is interested. In these two cases the income of the trust could be applied or spent outside India without losing exemption, provided the CBR passes an appropriate order. [Para 17]

It may be noticed that sub-clause (ii ) of clause(c) of sub-section (i) of section 11, in substance provides for the same condition which was imposed by sub-clause (i ) of clause (a) of the proviso to section 4(3)(i) of the old Act. Sub-clause (i) of clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 11 is in the same terms as sub-clause (ii) of clause (a) of the proviso to section 4(3)(i) of the old Act. [Para 21]

headnotes.text: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1948-49 - Assessee executed a deed of trust whereby they settled certain amount on various charities and appointed themselves as trustees - Later, in accordance with terms of trust deed, trustees assessees were appointed as managing agents of a company - Before Income-tax authorities, trustee claimed that income derived from managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Revenue authorities, however, held that income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Whether word "property" in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend "business," and if question fell to be decided solely on terms of that sub-section, managing agency formed by assessees/trustees must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether fact that trustees had option at any time to throw up managing agency was no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether section 4(3)(i) relates to income from business held under trust and section 4(3)(ia) relates to income from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution where that business itself is not held on trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where business of managing agency was held in trust, it could be concluded that business carried on by trustees fell under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from properties held under - Assessment years 1947-48 to 1958-59 - Assessee trust was formed for benefit of public in general without distinction of caste, creed or colour in advancement of education, commerce, industry, public health and medical relief - Under trust deed, trustees were at liberty to apply corpus of said trust fund or any portion thereof as they might from time to time think fit for any one or more of above objects - Trustees might take over superintendence, management and administration of any trust or institution having allied objects whether endowed or not by settlor on such terms and conditions as trustees might in their absolute discretion think fit - Trustees were also entitled accept donations and/or contributions from any person, company, firm or institution upon such terms and conditions as they might deem proper and could apply any portion of income of trust fund for purpose thereof - Assessee claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act but same was denied by ITO - Whether trust deed merely empowered trustees to take over superintendence, management and administration such trust or institution whose object were similar or consistent with objects of assessee trust and they would not ,therefore, by reason of power reserved to them be entitled to take over any trust or institution whose objects were not charitable purposes - Held, yes - Whether donations and/or contributions that trustees might receive would be donations and contributions to trust fund and they would be received as and by way of accretions thereto, and since trust fund and trust property were themselves stamped with objects of trusts, donations and/or contributions which would be accepted by trustees as accretions to trust fund would also be similarly stamped with objects of trusts - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, trust fund as also accretions could not be used in any manner contrary to objects of trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 13, read with section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption - Whether manager of a trust can be treated as manager of institution referred to in clause (cc) of sub-section (3) of section 13 - Held, no - Whether 'trust' and 'institution' referred to in section 13 are different entities - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in holding that there was no violation of section 13 by assessee-trust in advancing money to its manager to warrant denial of benefit of section 11 - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trusts - Exemption of Income from property held under - Assessment years 1953-54 to 1958-59 - Two sisters ‘H’ and ‘K’ of Khoja community created trusts and claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Exemption was not granted on ground that trust was not created wholly for religions or charitable purposes - Whether a mere perusal of terms of two trusts which were consolidated by scheme of management sanctioned by High Court made it clear beyond doubt, that dominant intention of settlors was to establish a religious and charitable endowment - Held, yes - Whether dominant intention of trust to hold an annual majlis or a meeting in remembrance of anniversary of Imam Hussein Saheb, who is subject of highest veneration by Khojas to which sect ‘K’ belonged and words used were "majlis" and, a majlis is essentially a religious meeting in context in which it is used in instant case - Held, yes - Whether therefore, income of trusts arising from scheme of management was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Sub-section (1)(c)) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee-trust, running a multi-speciality hospital, claimed exemption of income under section 11 - Assessing Officer denied exemption on that Dr. K, managing trustee, himself alone had diverted income by using trust infrastructure for his profit/gains, in clear violation of provisions of sections 13(1)(c), read with section 13(2)(b) and 13(2)(g) - Whether in view of fact that 72 per cent of total receipt of trust were attributable to service of Dr. K, against which he was paid only consultancy fee that for looking after his patients in trust hospital, Dr. K had engaged associate doctors and he was paying for that services; that Dr. K had made available services of his laboratory to patients of trust hospital at concessional rate; and that Dr. K had made available large land to trust to carry on its activities of running hospital, amount paid to Dr. K, could not be said to be unreasonable and, therefore, provisions of section 13(1)(c) were not attracted - Held, yes [Paras 21  22] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Religious or charitable trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies created a trust and purported to endow it with share held by him in certain transport companies - Contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately but companies in which N was interested were to have benefit of assets set apart by him - N was managing trustee and empowered to borrow to any extent on properties conveyed to trust not only for trust but for his own use trustees were empowered, so long as N held office of managing trustee, to sell immovable properties belonging to trust for purpose of floating other companies - Foundation of institution was apparently to be left over until companies had made sufficient money for purpose - N also reserved right to revoke trust at any time - Whether on facts properties in question were not held under trust for charitable purpose within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) – Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under – Assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56 – Claim of assessee trust for exemption of its income under section 4(3)(i) was rejected by ITO on ground that business of trust carried on by managing trustee on behalf of trust fell within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and hence its business income was not exempt from taxation – Whether where trust carries on business and business itself is held in trust and income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for purpose of religious or charitable character, conditions prescribed under section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and income is exempt from taxation - Held, yes – Whether claim of exemption cannot be denied even if business were to be conducted by someone else acting on behalf of trust, and proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to such businesses as are not held under trust and, therefore, field of its operation is distinct and separate from that covered by main provision of section 4(3)(i) – Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, assessee being a religious and charitable trust, was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act for assessment years in question – Held, yes

Section 64 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 16(3) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Transfer of assets - For benefit of spouse, etc. - Assessment year 1957-58 - Assessee by a settlement deed created a trust for benefit of his minor daughter - Settlement provided that when minor attained age of 21 years, trust property would vest absolutely in her and she would become entitled to receive income from settled immovable property in her own right - Managing trustees contributed trust money as capital to firm to join partnership and received share of profits in firm - ITO taking view that section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act did not speak of actual receipt of income but only of income arising and as income had arisen from firm, held that it was taxable in assessee’s hands - Tribunal, however, set aside ITO’s order - Whether in view of decision of Supreme Court in CIT v. Manilal Dhanji [1962] 44 ITR 876, it could be said that income derived by managing trustee was not taxable in hands of assessee either under section 16(1)(c) or section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, order passed by Tribunal was correct - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from properties held under - Assessment year 1956-57 - By an indenture of trust, ‘D’ and his wife both doctors, settled upon trust an immovable property and two maternity hospitals which were run by them - Primary object of trust was to carry on and promote educational, health, cultural, social and economic interest of people particularly of backward and lower classes - Substance of indenture of trust itself was that all trust properties were transferred by both settlers to trustees and trustees made declaration that they would hold properties for objects of trust from date of deed - One of recitals clearly indicated that it was business of conducting two maternity homes that had been settled upon trust, because net annual income which was to accrue to trust from said hospitals to be arrived at after deducting all expenses for maintaining and running hospitals and after making payment to ‘D,’ s wife as provided in trust deed for managing said hospitals for and on behalf of trust during her lifetime - Whether as trust deed was duly registered it was sufficient in law to effect a valid transfer - Held, yes - Whether since business of running and conducting maternity homes itself was settled upon trust, conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act were fulfilled and, hence income from maternity homes was exempt from taxation - Held, yes - Whether for conducting maternity hospitals presence of a doctor was essential and therefore, amount paid to wife of ‘D’ was a part of normal expenditure of conducting and managing said hospitals which was allowable as admissible deduction in computation of income of trust in hands of trustees as association of persons - Held, yes

Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Related party transaction) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-trust operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital - In order to address financial difficulties faced by assessee, it entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) involved in healthcare sector, for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to SCPL - In return, assessee would receive either a fixed amount of Rs. 1 crore or 40 per cent of SCPL's profit, whichever was higher, as management fees - Assessing Officer was of view that said agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for benefit of related parties - Consequently, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied - It was noted that object of transfer agreement with SCPL was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally, and in doing so, purpose of charity was not violated as a reputed hospital of such huge size required professional handling - Further, agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable property to SCPL but to counter huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals - Whether, on facts, there was no infirmity in order of Commissioner (Appeals) in allowing exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1951-52 to 1954-55 - A partnership firm was formed by four brothers - Firm was appointed as chief agent of an insurance company - Subsequently, brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming trustees would hold said business of chief agency of said company and all benefits and profits to arise from said business upon trust for public charitable purposes - Whether principal agency conducted by assessee-trust was a business and, therefore, "property" within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which was capable of being settled upon trust - Held, yes - Whether income of assessee-trust not being one which was not governed by proviso to section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953, but was governed by operative part of section 4(3)(i), it was exempt from tax - Held, yes
