Section 11, read with section 12AA, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Deemed registration) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee-trust was formed for charitable purposes to attain its charitable objects - It predominantly run two schools - It filed Return of Income(ROI) at Nil - Since application of assessee under section 12AA had been rejected by Commissioner(Exemption), Assessing Officer denied exemption under section 11 to assessee and treated excess of income over expenditure as income chargeable to tax - It was noted that during pendency of appeal, assessee was granted registration under section 12AA - Whether case of assessee would be covered under deemed registration and ,thus, assessee would be entitled to claim benefit under section 11 on strength of registration obtained in subsequent year - Held, yes [Para 10.2] [In favour of assessee] II. Section 251, read with section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Commissioner (Appeals) - Powers of (Enhancement of assessment) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee-trust was formed for charitable purposes to attain its charitable objects - Since application of assessee under section 12AA had been rejected by Commissioner(Exemption), Assessing Officer treated excess of income over expenditure as income chargeable to tax - Commissioner (Appeals) endorsed action of Assessing Officer - He also found that assessee-trust had received certain amounts which had been directly credited in balance sheet under head 'Building funds' and 'Amalgamation funds' and thus, was treated as capital receipt by assessee - Commissioner (Appeals) concluded that such receipts were in nature of revenue receipts chargeable to tax and in exercise of enhancement powers conferred upon him under section 251(1)(a), he enhanced taxable income by making addition on account of money received for designated purposes in Building Fund and Amalgamation Fund - Whether Commissioner (Appeals) in directing Assessing Officer to make assessment based on new source of income had travelled beyond bandwidth provided in respect of enhancement powers - Held, yes - Whether enhancement of chargeable income towards receipts in building funds and amalgamation funds was not permissible - Held, yes [Paras 14.1, 14.3 and 14.4] [In favour of assessee] III. Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Sub-section (3)) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Whether provisions of section 13(3)(cc) would not extend to manager (or her spouse) of trust - Held, yes [Para 11.1] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Circular No. 1/2015, dated 21-1-2015

Section 11, read with section 164 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i), read with section 41(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1939-40 - Assessee trust was constituted for political advancement of India having its goal for acquisition of complete national autonomy or “Swarajya” to be obtained by all constitutional agitation or means and diffusion of political education and knowledge as to political affairs of India both in India and abroad for achievement of aforesaid goal and any object which in uncontrolled opinion of Managing Committee national or of national importance for inhabitants of British India by any means which in opinion of Managing Committee be constitutional - Objects specified in trust deed were distributive inasmuch as trusts for benefit of inhabitants of a particular locality were regarded as charitable while trusts for benefit of a particular political party, or for advancement of particular political opinions, were not regarded as charitable - Whether since whole of trust fund could be applied for any one or more of objects specified, if source of those objects did not fall within purview of legal definition of “charity”, trust could not be regarded as a good charitable trust and income of trust did not fall within purview of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether instant case fell within first proviso to section 41(1) of 1922 Act and ITO was justified in levying income-tax  at maximum rate - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1952-53 and 1953-54 - Settler created in respect of certain securities, trust for charitable and religious purposes and directed that balance of income of trust properties after meeting expanse, would be accumulated during life time of settler and added to corpus of trust fund - Whether so long as it cannot be predicated with certainty that income is wholly to be applied for religious or charitable purposes within taxable territories accumulation of income for such application cannot fall within ambit of section 4(3)(i) - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, trust was not exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) in view of provision in trust deed for accumulation of income for religious and charitable purposes outside taxable territories - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1946-47 – Founders of assessee-press created a trust in respect of assessee-press and a weekly paper published by it – Clause (2) of trust deed provided that trust Committee could not change policy of paper which at its inception was published in its first issue and which in political matters was according to aims and objects of Indian National Congress – Policy article of paper as published in its first issue made it quite clear that paper was not brought into existence to maintain, support, protect or oppose any particular association, organization, person or creed and that would include Congress organization, but aimed at good of all mankind and good of India and putting down of evils in general and encouragement of catholicity and of all those aspects of life which an educated person would like to see encouraged - Whether policy of paper was aimed at supplying to Province an organ of educated public opinion, and to encourage all that would lead to progress of India as a part of progress of mankind, which was a charitable object – Held, yes – Whether therefore, income of assessee was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act – Held, yes

Section 13,  read with section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Sub-section (1)(c)) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee-trust, registered under section 12A, claimed exemption under section 11 – Assessing Officer denied benefit of exemption for reason that assessee had debited certain amount to account of one MMPL, a company in which trustees were substantially interested and same was a diversion of funds as specified under section 13(1)(c) – It was found that amount paid to MMPL was a repayment of loan taken by assessee from one, KM who was director of Company MMPL and also managing trustee of assessee-trust – Assessee-trust had repaid loan amount by cheque in name of MMPL as per instructions of KM and debited to account of company instead of to account of KM – Said mistake was rectified by passing necessary journal entries in books of account in subsequent financial year – Whether, on facts, there was reasonableness that impugned amount represented repayment of loan availed by assessee from managing trustee, KM and said transaction could not be hit by provision of section 13(1)(c) thus, assessee was eligible for exemption under section 11 – Held, yes [Para 5.3][In favour of assessee]IT : Where amount paid by assessee trust to its trustee was found to be a repayment of loan, said transaction could not be hit by provisions of section 13(1)(c); thus, assessee was eligible for exemption under section 11  IT : Where assessee trust had entered into an agreement with a company, in which trustees were substantially interested, for providing nursing training to its students and paid an advance which was adjusted towards fee payable, there was no diversion of funds so as to get benefit to trustees as per section 13(3)  IT : Where as per agreement entered into between assessee trust and its trustees for construction of nursing college on land owned by trustees, trust had to incur total cost of construction, advance paid by trust to its trustee towards repayment of expenses incurred by trustees, same would not be a diversion of funds so as to a attract provisions of section 13(1)(c)

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1952-53 to 1956-57 - Whether where business in kuries was held by assessee under a trust for religious or charitable purpose income derived from such business would be exempt from tax under provisions of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953 - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Business expenditure-Assessee-company was trustee of religious and charitable trust-ITO paid management charges to an association for managing its affairs-ITO and ACC rejected claim for deduction of such charges paid-Tribunal allowed assessee's claim-Whether tribunal right in law-Held, yes

III. Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Sub-section (3)) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Whether provisions of section 13(3)(cc) would not extend to manager (or her spouse) of trust - Held, yes [Para 11.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 [corresponding to section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961] - Charitable or  religious trust - Exemption of income from property hold under trust - Settlor, carrying on mining business, created trust with corpus of Rs. 50,000 - Authorised trustees, inter alia, to start or carry on mining or other connected business with trust properties and funds and/or invest funds with businessmen of repute and to treat income from such business as trust property - Objects of trust were admittedly of charitable nature - Whether business of mining and/or of making loans was property held under trust and therefore impugned income from business or interest exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years 1964-65, 1965-66 and 1966-67 - Held, on facts, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Settlor “L” created a trust appointing himself and his relatives as trustees - Assessee trustees claimed exemption of income from trust properties under section 4(3)(1) of Act 1922 - However, one of effect of provision of trust deed was that trustees had full discretion to spend trust fund and in doing so they might spend their entire funds on one objects to exclusion of other and they might be able to spend entire funds for aid of settlor’s family - Whether in view of above provision of trust deed, assessees were not entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of Act 1922 - Held yes

Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether where a part of trust income was being used directly or indirectly for benefit of its founder and managing director, which came within prohibited category referred to in section 13(3), exemption under section 11 was not available in view of violation of clause (ii)(c) of section 13(1), read with section 13(3) - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1947-48 to 1956-57 - Testator provided in his will that executors would set apart specified sum out of his estate for purpose of charities which they did - Assessing authorities held that interest earned on said sum, being over and above sum specified in will must go back to estate of deceased testator as he had only authorised expenditure of only specified sum on charities - Whether since testator had given specific direction to executors to take out of his estate specified sum and set it apart for charities, and there was no provision prohibiting executors from spending anything more than said sum on charities, interest earned on said sum was accretion to that fund and, therefore, same was not assessable in hands of executors as income of estate of testator - Held, yes

Section 11 to 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Religious or Charitable Trust - Exemption of Income from Property Held Under - Assessment year 1952-53 - One D was carrying on business of lime - He made a will and bequeathed certain specified properties in favour of his two wives and residue in trustees for public charitable purposes - On his death, two wives executed a trust deed under which they entrusted entire business to trust Tribunal held that trust was valid and it enjoyed 8 annas share in lime business, other 8 annas being share of other two partners - Whether share of business income received by trustees was exempted under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1952-53 to 1957-58 - Trust was in relation to business - Objects of trust were charitable - Memorandum of association gave certain powers to trusts for achieving primary objects of charitable purpose - Whether assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

I. Section 11, read with section 12AA, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Deemed registration) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee-trust was formed for charitable purposes to attain its charitable objects - It predominantly run two schools - It filed Return of Income(ROI) at Nil - Since application of assessee under section 12AA had been rejected by Commissioner(Exemption), Assessing Officer denied exemption under section 11 to assessee and treated excess of income over expenditure as income chargeable to tax - It was noted that during pendency of appeal, assessee was granted registration under section 12AA - Whether case of assessee would be covered under deemed registration and ,thus, assessee would be entitled to claim benefit under section 11 on strength of registration obtained in subsequent year - Held, yes [Para 10.2] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust was granted registration under section 12AA during pendency of appeal, case of assessee would be covered under deemed registration and thus assessee would be entitled to claim benefit under section 11 on strength of registration obtained in subsequent year  INCOME TAX : Where Commissioner (Appeals) enhanced taxable income by making addition on account of money received for designated purposes in Building Fund and Amalgamation Fund, since said issue was not considered by Assessing Officer, Commissioner (Appeals) had travelled beyond bandwidth provided in respect of enhancement powers under section 251 and thus not sustainable  INCOME TAX : Provisions of section 13(3)(cc) would not extend to manager (or her spouse) of trust

Section 13, read with section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (sub-section (1)(c)) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-trust filed its return of income declaring nil income - Assessing Officer noted that certain amount had been advanced to a proprietary concern of wife of managing trustee and sought to disallow advances so made - Assessee claimed that amount had been advanced for purchase of timber for proposed construction of a medical college, however, it failed to produce any application or other documents which ought to have been submitted to Governmental authorities or Medical Council of India for proposal for setting up of medical college - High Court held that since assessee failed to produce any documents to prove genuineness of its claim, it could be concluded that in garb of purchase of timber, advance amounts had been diverted for personal benefit of an interested party as mentioned in section 13(3) and, thus, amounts so advanced had rightly been treated as income of assessee-trust - Whether SLP filed by assessee against order of High Court was to be dismissed as withdrawn - Held, yes [Para 2] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed as withdrawn against order of High Court that where assessee-trust failed to produce any application or other documents to prove that advance given to proprietary concern of wife of managing trustee was for purchase of timber for proposed construction of a medical college, it could be concluded that there was a diversion for personal benefit of an interested party as mentioned in section 13(3) and, thus, amounts so advanced was rightly treated as income in hands of assessee   INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed as withdrawn against order of High Court that where assessee-trust failed to prove that provisions of section 40(a)(ia) did not have any application on payment made in favour of a person towards consideration for contract works, expenditure so incurred was correctly disallowed by invoking provisions of section 40(a)(ia)

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1956-57 to 1960-61 - 'D' decided to gift Rs. 5 lakhs for charitable objects like establishment of medical or educational institutions or such similar philanthropic objects, to be credited with 'BUA' in name of assessee-trust - Pursuant to this, 'BUA' paid Rs. 60,000 to assessee-trust which invested same in shares - Assessee received dividends on those shares and claimed refund of TDS on ground that income was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act  - ITO disallowed claim on ground that objects for which trust was created were vague in view of words "such similar philanthropic objects" - Tribunal however, upheld assessee's claim, observing that objects were clear and not vague - Whether, on facts, a valid trust had been created which was entitled to exemption under sec. 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or Religious Trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1956-57 - Assessee company was formed to raise funds by conducting kuris, receiving donations and subscriptions - Object of assessee was to utilize its income for religious and charitable purposes - Whether fact that assessee spent very small amount in charity and transferred remaining amount to reserve fund or fact that business was carried on by directors themselves and not by trustees appointed by directors was not material considerations for deciding applicability of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether where it was no body’s case that any part of income had been utilized for purposes other than those specified in memorandum or articles of association, income of assessee could be exempt under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1961-62 - Whether once it is found that some of objects of trust are not of public charitable nature and trustees have discretion in spending amount over those objects, it cannot be said that property held under trust is held wholly for religious and charitable purposes and, therefore, assessee would not be entitled to claim benefit under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemptions of income from property held under - Assessment years 1957-58 to 1959-60 - Whether relief to a person would not be a charitable object unless it involves an object of general public utility - Held, yes - Two persons jointly made a declaration of trust and it was decided to devote income of trust property partly on charitable objects and partly towards members of donor’s family - Whether amount spent or provided to be spent on maintenance and support of donor’s family could not be a charitable object and could not, therefore, fall under section 4(3)(i) of Act, 1922 - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1940-41 - Settlor made settlement of immovable property for benefit of his poor relations and religious/pious objects - He gave absolute discretion to trustees to devote whole of income to his poor relatives - Whether, on facts trust was not a charitable trust within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act and no exemption could be granted to trust - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1942-43 - Assessee created a trust - As per terms of trust deed certain income arising from trust property was to be utilised for religious and charitable purposes - During relevant assessment year, surplus income arose from trust property - Up to a particular date, surplus income was paid to assessee personally but for remaining period assessee utilised said surplus income also for charitable and religious purposes - Whether, on facts, for period during which surplus income was paid to assessee personally it could not escape taxation, however, for subsequent period during which surplus income was utilised for religious and charitable purposes, it was exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One 'S' and four persons, who were holding certain securities for charity purpose, executed a deed of declaration of trust - As per trust deed, trustees would give preference to poor and indigent relations or members of family of 'S' including therein distant and collateral relations - Whether since trust had been mainly formed for charitable purposes, mere provision for giving preference to poor and indigent relations or family members of 'S' did not affect validity of trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income from trust properties invested in securities was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section  11,  read with section  154,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  341,  read with section  287,  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Charitable or religious trust  -  Exemption of income from property held under (Accumulation of income)  - Assessment years  2013-14 and 2015-16  - Assessee-trust had accumulated income under section 11(2) - During year, assessee paid certain amounts out of accumulated income to two institutions registered under section 12AA - Assessing Officer invoked section 11(3)(d) and treated said payments as deemed income of assessee - Assessee contended that payments were for project implementation and services rendered by recipient institutions under assessee's supervision and control, thus falling outside ambit of section 11(3)(d) - Whether section 11(3)(d) was recipient-centric and not purpose-centric and, thus, whether payment was made as donation, grant, project expenditure, consultancy charges, research fees, implementation cost or under any other nomenclature was legally irrelevant - Held, yes - Whether, thus, payments made by assessee-trust out of accumulated income under section 11 to institutions registered under section 12AA, though described as project/implementation would constitute amounts 'paid or credited' to another trust within meaning of section 11(3)(d) and would be taxable as deemed income of assessee-trust - Held, yes [Paras 18, 25, 29 and 30] [In favour of revenue]

Section 161 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 41 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Representative assessee - Liability of - Assessment years 1953-54 and 1954-55 - Under a scheme sanctioned by High Court, management and administration of a Durgh of a saint vested hereditarily in trustees called nattamingars from whom was elected a managing trustee - Managing trustee was to allocate surplus due to Kasupangudars (shares) who were descendants of foster son of saint - ITO assessed surplus income in hands of managing trustee as an association of persons - Whether even if nattamaigars were trustees in whom properties of Durgha vested, they should be deemed to have received income only on behalf of kasupangudars in definite shares - Held, yes - Whether in terms of section 41 of 1922 Act nattamaigars were managers of properties on behalf of others and were entitled to receive income therefrom on behalf of them and therefore income which they held on behalf of kasupangudars could be assessed only in their hands in manner prescribed thereunder - Held, yes - Whether what vests in nattamaigars was not properties of the Durgha but management and administration thereof and, therefore, provisions of section 41 of 1922 Act could be said to apply to assessee - Held, yes

II. Section 13, read with section 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Revision) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Commissioner in exercise of powers under section 263 set aside assessment order of assessee-trust inter alia on ground that payment to one 'A' managing trustee of trust routed through Tata Sons Ltd. was in violation of provisions of trust deed, and there was no effort made by Assessing Officer even to examine reasonableness of such payment - Whether payment of this nature, for someone at helm of affairs at a major philanthropic trust like assessee and an important part of India's most prestigious and credible business house, was not at all so unusual as to warrant further inquiries about its reasonableness more so when 'A' was managing trustee of assessee-trust since 2007 and all along, similar payments made to him did not invoke provisions of section 13(2)(c) - Held, yes - Whether further it is a common practice in large business groups to have centralized entities providing services to all group entities and related entities, particularly as it is not possible for each entity to have benefit of their own stand-alone units dealing with support services and, thus, there was nothing unusual about it so as to warrant detailed investigations into matter - Held, yes - Whether therefore, Commissioner was not justified in invoking jurisdiction under section 263 in respect of allegedly deficient inquiries about remuneration paid to trustees - Held, yes [Paras 28 and 29][In favour of assessee]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under trust (Business held in trust) - Assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, 2001-02 and 2005-06 to 2007-08 - Assessee-trust was created with objects of establishing and maintaining of schools, colleges and study circles, advancing education and research study on modern and ancient Indian thought, etc. - After formation of trust, a business was commenced in name of trust for manufacture of katha - Assessee claimed exemption under section 11 in respect of its income and filed a return of income on that basis - Assessing Officer denied exemption - High Court by impugned order held that since katha business was commenced by trustees with aid and assistance of borrowings from sister concerns it could not be case of 'property being held under trust' within meaning of section 11(4) but would only be a case of business being carried on by and on behalf of trust and mere fact that whole or some part of income from katha business was earmarked for application of charitable objects would not render business itself being considered as incidental to attainment of objects of trust - Whether Special Leave Petition filed against impugned order was to be granted - Held, yes [Paras 19 to 22] [In favour of assessee]IT: SLP granted against High Court's ruling that where business was commenced by trustees with aid and assistance of borrowings from sister concerns, it could not be a case of 'property being held under trust'

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to Section 4(3)(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Settlor created a trust in respect of certain shares declaring in trust deed that income from trust property was to be belonged to him during his life time and after his death to his wife and after death of both, income was to go to certain charitable trusts created by him - During his life time settlor modified said trust deed and relinquished his entire life interest in that property - Up to death of settlor income from trust fund was paid to his wife - After death of settlor, his wife also executed a deed on 20-5-1955 whereby she in turn relinquished and surrendered her life interest with a view to accelerating subsequent trust in favour of charity - After that deed that 20-5-1955, assessee, (trustees), claimed that income derived from property held under trust was wholly religious and charitable purpose and was to exempted from tax - However, ITO on observation that interest for life allowed by settlor to his wife was restricted in asmuch as it was laid down that she had no power to anticipate or alienate her interest, therefore declaration made by her in said deed was void and income of property held under trust was not for charitable purpose - Whether in view of decision of Supreme Court in CIT v. Kasturbai Walchand Trust [1967] 63 ITR 656 (SC) income that accrued or arose to trustees from trust properties from 20-5-1953 onwards, was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the Act 1922 - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether word charity, if used generally or without qualifications or limitations, necessary connotes use for public and as such falls within definition of term "charitable purpose" found in section 4 of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether where testator in his will directed trustee to utilize three fourths of income of residuary estate for charity, that part of income clearly fell within first part of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act and was, therefore, exempt from tax - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of Income from property held under - Assessee - trust was created by settler ‘W’ for purpose of maintaining uniform control over ‘P’ Ltd. - As per operative clause of trust deed, trust property and income of trust should be invested in shares of ‘P’ Ltd. for 18 years and after expiry of said period, it would be utilized for charitable purpose - There was also provisions of deed that if any member of public who came within objects of trust would be qualified to receive bounty of settler - However on assessment, authorities rejected claim of assessee-trust for exemption of dividend and interest income of trust property - Whether, on facts, trust deed did not compel trustees to make employees of ‘P’ Ltd. sole beneficiary of bounty of settler - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, it could not be struck down as a trust deed for purpose other than a charitable purpose income from which was not exempted under section 4(3)(i) - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1922) - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessee-trust had a number of religious or charitable objects - Trustees were directed to spend income on those objects, but their choice was not limited to them and they were authorized to spend income on any other religious or charitable purpose of a public nature -Deed also provided that if trustees made mistake and spent income on objects which were not charitable objects of a public nature, they would be guilty of breach of trust - Further, if discretion given to trustees to spend income on other religious objects was bad, trustees would be confined to objects mentioned in deed and only to such of objects as might be of religious or charitable nature - Whether, on facts, deed of trust was not void for either uncertainty or ambiguity - Held, yes

Section 2(15), read with  section 12AA, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable purpose (Object of general public utility) - Assessment years 2018-19, 2020-21 and 2021-22 - ICRW was a non-profit organization established with objective of promoting social and economic development with women's full participation and was incorporated as a company registered under section 25 of Companies Act, 1956 - Provisions of Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 were applicable in case of ICRW and, therefore, to protect financial interest of its employees, ICRW set up a trust, namely, 'ICRW Group Gratuity Trust' , i.e., assessee herein - This new trust applied for seeking registration under section 12AA - Commissioner (Exemptions) observed that assessee was formed only for limited purpose of managing statutory obligations in form of gratuity payable to employees of ICRW and said purpose would not fall within ambit of 'charitable purpose' as defined under section 2(15) - Accordingly, he dismissed application seeking registration - It was noted that assessee had placed on record copy of registered trust deed - Whether any trust that had been created for purpose of managing statutory obligations of employees of parent trust would certainly fall within ambit of advancement of general public utility and, hence, its activities was to be considered as a charitable as defined under section 2(15) - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 13] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Assessee-trust formed for limited purpose of managing statutory obligations in form of gratuity payable to employees of parent trust would fall within ambit of advancement of general public utility and, hence, its activities was to be considered as a charitable as defined under section 2(15) and, accordingly, assessee was to be granted registration under section 12AA

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1950-51 – Whether a trust for charitable purposes does not become invalid, if choice of specific charitable objects to be benefited is left to trustees, nor is it to be condmned as invalid or illusory if, by language of deed, trustees are given an absolute discretion to apply fund at such time as they may think fit or retain it so long as they choose – Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income form property held under - Assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Assessee was an association of persons - Constitution of assessee revealed that neither standing committee nor managing committee nor even members of assessee could use property of assessee for any purpose except that covered by object clause of assessee - Neither before ITO nor before AAC any contention was raised by revenue that object for which assessee was constituted was not charitable one - Whether property of assessee was held under trust or under legal obligation and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 13, read with  section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Sub-section (1)(c))- Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee-trust invested funds in a company where its trustee was managing director and his wife was a director - Whether it was a clear case of violation under section 13(1)(c) and assessee would not be entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee-turst invested funds in a company in which its trustee was managing director and his wife was a director, it was a case of violation of section 13(1)(c) and exemption under section 11 would not be available to assessee  IT : Where capital gain earned by assessee-trust became non-exempt under section 11 due to contravention of section 13(1)(c), such capital gain would be taxed at maximum marginal rate in terms of section 164(2) and benefit of section 112 could not be given to it

Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Benefit to specified persons) - Assessment years 2003-04 to 2008-09 - Assessee a registered charitable organization carried on work of education through four members, who worked in dual capacity i.e. as whole time administrators, as also regular time teachers, and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools - Members were not being paid separately for managerial work done by them - Members were also furnishing their income tax returns regularly as individuals and were duly showing their income received as salaries from assessee and their said returns had also been continuously accepted by revenue - Assessee was availing benefit of exemption of its income under sections 11 and 12 - Tribunal partially affirmed salaries paid to two of trustee members and rejected claim of assessee with regard to two others - Assessee claimed that once it was registered as a charitable organization and its accounts were being accepted since very beginning, it was entitled to benefits of exemption - It further claimed that all four members had not only huge teaching experience to their credit but were also whole time employees of assessee and thus were closely associated with management as also in running of schools of assessee - It also claimed that completion of assessment against assessee as a normal business entity was also wrong and misfounded - Whether since assessee trust/society was pursuing an object of general public utility, conclusion drawn by Assessing Officer that petitioner-society was not a charitable society was misfounded - Held, yes - Whether all four members were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and were also rendering administrative functions qua running of schools for which they were not being paid any extra salary - Held, yes - Whether thus, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11 - Held, yes [Paras 32, 39  40] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where all members of assessee-trust were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and as regular time teachers and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools and were not being paid any extra salary for management work, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1922) - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1952-53 to 1960-61 - Sale trustee of the wakf, mullaji Sahib was empowered under trust deed to make use of income arising out of property for religious, pious, charitable or ‘otherwise’ - Whether, expression or ‘otherwise’ occuring in trust deed would have to be read ejusdiem generis with words which precede that expression and same could not have effect of enlarging nature of purpose for which income could be spent by trustee so as to hold that trustee had been empowered to spend income for purposes other than religious, pious or charitable so as to deny exemption - Held, yes - Whether merely because trust deed used expression that trustees would hold, possess and enjoy properties for their own use’, which are normal covenant in conveyance, it could not be said that trustee had been given absolute power and discretion to use trust property and income for his own use so as to deny exemption - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religions trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1990-91 and 1991-92 - Where a particular clause of trust deed empowered trust to start educational agencies for earning income to achieve aims and objects of trust and Tribunal had further found that surplus was transferred to trust and utilized in purchase of land and construction of sabha bhavan, merely because assessee started an educational agency to earn income, it could not be said that it was running business so as to attract section 11(4A) [In favour of assessee]

facts.text:
'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

On reference:

One 'S' and four others were holding certain securities for the purpose of charity and had been applying the same for and towards charitable purposes, executed, on 8-6-1922, a deed of declaration of trust declaring that the said trust fund would be held by them on trusts more specifically therein mentioned. Clause 13 of trust deed provided that the trust fund would be held by the trustees upon the trusts to apply the net income thereof after providing for all necessary expenses in relation to the management of the trust funds, for all or any of the following purposes (a) the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of jewish (b) the institution, maintenance and support of hospitals and schools, colleges or other educational institutions or (c) the relief of any distress caused by the elements of nature such as famine, pestilence, fire, tempest, flood, earthquake or any other such calamity or (d) the care and protection of animals useful to mankind or (e) the advancement of religion or (f) other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the foregoing purposes. The trust deed further provided that the trustees would give preference to the poor and indigent relations or members of the family of the said 'S' including there in distant and collateral relations. The trust fund had been invested by the trustees in inter alia 3½ per cent Government securities. In the year 1930, a certificate was issued by the ITO, whereby the Reserve Bank of India was authorized not to deduct at source the tax on the said securities so held by the trustees. For the assessment years 1948-49 and 1949-50, the ITO took the view that the income from the trust fund was not exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act accordingly, he assessed the appellants. On appeals, the AAC and the Tribunal confirmed the assessment made by the ITO.

On reference, the High Court also held that the trust property was not held wholly for religious or charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

The settlor N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies, created a trust and purported to endow it with the shares held by him in six transport companies. He constituted himself the managing trustee of the trust and gave himself full power to deal with its assets. The managing trustees claimed refund of tax paid in respect of dividends declared on the shares held in these transport companies. The income-tax authorities refused to allow a refund. Their reason was that the shares were not held under trust wholly for charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i).

On reference:

The assessee was a charitable trust. During the course of assessment, the ITO found that certain sum had been paid to the manager of the trust as loan. The Assessing Officer treated the manager as a person referred to the section 13(3) and, hence, act of advancing loan to manager was hit by provisions of section 13(1)(c) and 13(2)(a). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the appellant-trust could not be said to have used any part of its income directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person referred to in section 13(3). Therefore, the provision of section 13(1)(c) was not applicable. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order that the assessee was a trust and not an institution.

On reference :

The assessee, a religious and charitable trust was founded by K under a deed of trust. The founder furnished the trust with a nucleus fund to be augmented and utilised for the purpose of the trust. A business in cotton yarn and cloth was started by the board of trustees or the managing trustee of the said trust. For the assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56, the assessee submitted returns showing nil income and claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) in respect of the income from the business carried on by the trust.

The ITO, however, denied the exemption to the said business income, from taxation, and completed the assessments.

The view of the ITO was that the income from the business of the trust which was carried on by the managing trustee on behalf of the trust would fall within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and would not be covered by the main provision of section 4(3)(i), and that the necessary conditions required to be fulfilled for the operation of the proviso (b) were not present.

On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's orders and observed that it was not the trust or the institution, which was carrying on the business from which the income was earned, that the business was carried on by the managing trustee on behalf of the trust, and that therefore the application of section 4(3)(i) was excluded by the operation of proviso (b) to that section. The Tribunal, on second appeal, also confirmed the assessments.

On reference :

By an indenture of trust dated 23-8-1954, one ‘D’ and his wife settled upon trust two maternity hospitals which were run by them and an immovable property for the purposes and objects contained in the said deed of trust. The assessee were the trustees under the said trust. The primary object of the trust was to carry on and promote the educational, health, cultural, literary, social and economic interests of the people, particularly of the backward and poorer classes. The important recitals in the trust deed were to the effect that the net annual income from the said hospitals, after deducting all the expenses for maintaining and running the hospitals including a sum of Rs. 750 per month which should be paid regularly to ‘D’s wife for managing the said hospitals for and on behalf of the trust during her lifetime, should accrue to the trust from year to year and that Dr. Divekar and Dr. Nalini Divekar did transfer the above said property and both the hospitals to the Trustees. And that the monies and properties of the trust were to be applied, firstly in payment of the expenses of carrying out of the trust and then in carrying out the other objects. The assessee claimed exemption under section 43(1)(i) of the 1922 Act. It was true that the assessee had made a part of his income a charge to meet the obligation created by the deed of dedication, but no property had been set apart exclusively for the maintenance of the temple. The income arising out of the profits of the fair was accruing to the assessee first, and part of it was then used or diverted for the maintenance of the deity. It was hardly possible, therefore, to hold, in the circumstances of the instant case that the income that the assessee was deriving from the fair was from property held under trust or other legal obligation.

In J.K. Trust v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 143 it was held that section 4(3)(i) did not confer any exemption upon income which was settled upon a charitable trust and that the exemption was only conferred upon income which was derived from property which was settled upon the charitable trust. It was also held that it was not sufficient for a person to make a trust of his future income to claim exemption under section 4(3)(i) and unless the property from which that income was derived was also made the subject of a trust, the mere making of a trust with regard to the income would not be sufficient to claim exemption under section 4(3)(i). The assessee was, therefore, not entitled to claim exemption under section 4(3)(i). The alleged legal obligation to allocate the sum did not accrue until the income from the fair was in the hands of the assessee. The tolls collected from the fair represented the income of the assessee and not until the whole or part of such income was in his hand was in a position to discharge that obligation. It followed, accordingly, that the sum so collected was income of the assessee in the first instance and was, therefore, attracted to tax.

The provisos to section 16(1)(c) were not attracted for the simple reason that the assets from which the temple is to be maintained remained the property of the assessee and a part of the income from these assets was applied for an obligation created by the assessee himself. Therefore, the income in the sum of Rs. 2,051 was not received under the deed of dedication to the deity and, therefore, it was assessable in the hands of the assessee.

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer has denied the benefit of exemption under section 11 for the simple reason that there is violation of section 13(1)(c) read with section 13(2), insofar as interest free advances given to KVR and SV, on the ground that the assessee has allowed direct/indirect benefit of trust income/property to interested persons referred to under section 13(3)(cc). The provisions of section 13(3)(cc) refers to any trustee of the trust or manager (by whatever name called) of the trust as interested persons under section 13(3). Therefore, it is necessary to examine whether those two individuals are managers as defined under section 13(3)(cc) or not to decide, is there any violation referred to under section 13(1)(c). The legal dictionary Bakshi's Law Lexicon has defined the term 'manager' as per which 'manager has to be a person, has to be in the overall management of the company or trust, very importantly should be noted that, manager specifically for trust is not just a word of art, it is a very serious word comprising of meaning of a overall management.' The term manager is very wide. Thus, in order to bring any persons within the term manager it is essential to see their position in the organization and duties and works performed by them. In this case, the Assessing Officer has treated those two individuals as managers of the trust in terms of section 13(3)(cc), by considering the nature of work required to be carried out by them in terms of their letter of appointment. According to the Assessing Officer, those two persons are tasked with setting up core team to explore changes that are taking place in respect of rules and regulations formulated by the Government. They are required to directly report to the Chairman for any of the policy decisions. Therefore, he opined that they are performing managerial functions of the trust and, hence, comes under the term manager as defined under section 13(3)(cc). From going through the letter of appointment issued by the trust to two individuals it is found that those two individuals has been hired with a specific task of getting approval for starting a new medical college and also getting approval for deemed university status for the trust. From the letter of appointment, except providing consultancy services with regard to specific project, they are not involved in any kind of day to day activities of the trust. They had been never given any kind of services to existing institutions of the trust like engineering college and other institutions run by the trust. From the above, it is clear that services required to be provided by them to the trust are in the nature of external consultancy providers, who often comes to the client business place for providing consultancy services in respect of specialized knowledge which is required by any person. In this case, evidences filed by the assessee including letter of appointment clearly shows that those two individuals are appointed for a specific period of 5 years for a specific remuneration and further they have tasked with the work of setting up of new medical college and getting deemed university status for the institutions, which has nothing to do with the existing activities carried out by the assessee and, hence, those two individuals cannot be considered as managers of the trust, who are involved in day to day managerial functions. Thus, the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) were erred in considering two persons within the ambit of section 13(3)(cc). [Para 16]

Analysing the provisions of the trust deed, the scheme which emerges was clear. The settler did not wish the trustees to spend the income of the trust on the charitable objects immediately. He wanted the trust fund to increase and expand, and after the trust fund had expanded, he wanted the income of that trust fund to be spent on the charitable objects. In other words, the trust deed contained a scheme for accumulation of income and for the accumulated income to form part of the trust fund; and there was also a provision for the accumulation to go on for a specific period of time and on the expiry of that time the income of the enlarged trust fund to be spent on the charitable objects. If the property was impressed with a charitable trust or the object of the trust is charitable or religious, then the income derived from such trust or property would be income which would fall within the ambit of section 4(3)(i). It is fallacious to suggest that the object of the trust for the first 18 years was to invest monies in a particular manner. That was not the object: it was a mode of investment; it was a direction given by the settler how the income was to be utilized for the ultimate object of its being spent on the object of the trust. It was entirely untenable, to suggest that a direction with regard to investment could be looked upon as an object of the trust. An object of the trust is something definite and unvarying; it is the intention that the settler has for settling his property; it is an object with which the court can rarely interfere. Except when question of the cypress doctrine comes in, the court exercising charitable jurisdiction must always respect the charitable intention disclosed by the settler and help the trustees to carry out the charitable intention. But the direction with regard to its investment is entirely different. No court exercising equity jurisdiction-and the charity commissioner exercising his jurisdiction under the Bombay Public Trust Act under which this trust was registered-was ever tied down by the directions of the settler with regard to investments. If at any time within the 18 years the court or the charity commissioner was satisfied that the investments directed by the settler were not prudent investments and were not beneficial to the trust, it was perfectly competent to the charity commissioner or the court to direct that the investments should be made in a different manner. This clearly explains the dividing line between what are strictly the objects of the trust and the procedural matters, if one might say so, contained in the trust deed which may deal with detail like the accumulation of income, the investment of income.

It was not necessary that that intention must be immediately carried out. So long as the income from the trust property was not spent on any non-charitable object and it was saved, as it were, or set apart or accumulated for the ultimate object of carrying out the charitable purpose, then even in the intervening period the trust continues to be a charitable trust, the property is held on a charitable trust and the income from that trust is exempt from tax.

If the trust is to benefit the employees, even though they are to be benefited for purposes which are charitable, the trust would not come within the ambit of section 4(3)(i). What section 4(3)(i) has in view is not merely a religious or charitable purpose, but also that the object of the trust must be an object of general public utility. In other words, the bounty of the settler must be directed towards the public as a whole or a section of the public. If the object of his bounty is neither the public nor a section of the public but merely a conglomeration of men who constitute a mere group and the nexus which ties them is not a nexus which constitutes them a section of the public, then the trust would not be a trust which would fall within the ambit of section 4(3)(i).

The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

[Matter remanded to High Court]

The first question that arose for consideration was whether the income of the assessee was "income derived from property held under trust... wholly for religious or charitable purposes". It had been found that its principal object was the promotion of trade, commerce and industry and all its other objects mentioned in clauses (a) to (m) of article 3(1) of its memorandum of association were clauses which sub served the primary object which was to promote, support, protect, maintain and increase the export of cotton cloth and yarn from the country. If that be so, the object would without any doubt be an object of general public utility and intended to benefit the public as a whole in the country. The question, moreover, was now placed beyond controversy by the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Andhra Chamber of Commerce [1965] 55 ITR 722 (SC).

The provisions of section 4(3)(i ) confer an exemption of income from property only where the property itself is held under a trust or other legal obligation. It does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created in respect of any property, but only the income derived from any particular property or source is itself held in trust as where it is set apart or charged for a charitable purpose. That is clear upon the terms of the section itself and upon the authorities.

In the instant case, all the income which the assessee derived or received was in the shape of grants and subscriptions from members which could not possibly have been received by it except from its business. Therefore, the entire income of the assessee must be held to be income derived from its business which was its property. If this contention was correct, then it was further submitted that there could be also no doubt upon the terms of its memorandum of association and its purposes and objects that the assessee was holding the business in trust for charitable purposes.

Supreme Court in J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that "Business" would undoubtedly be property in the connotation in which it is used in section 4(3)(i). In the light of this pronouncement of the Supreme Court it is clear that "business" itself can be property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) and upon that principle the business of the assessee in the instant case would be "property" held by the assessee.

Under the circumstances, the view taken by the Tribunal was the correct view and the income of the assessee would be exempt under the provisions of section 4(3)(i).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

A cursory perusal of the terms of the deed would show that the managing trustee was the heart and soul of the trust. The terms of the trust deed expressly provided for the trust funds being employed in any trade, industry or business, which meant that the trust could carry on the business just like an individual or a firm or a limited company. It was not the contention of the department that the trust was a mere fiction or that it was illusory. Thus, a valid trust had been constituted and the trust carried on the business during the relevant accounting years.

It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

There was, no doubt on the authorities that trusts for the benefit of the inhabitants of a particular locality were regarded as charitable, and that principle would apply to the inhabitants of British India. On the other hand, it was clear that trusts for the benefit of a particular political party, or for the advancement of particular political opinions, were not regarded as charitable. The objects specified in the trust deed, were clearly distributive. The whole of the trust fund could be applied for any one or more of the objects specified, and if any of those objects do not fall within the purview of the legal definition of "charity", the trust could not be regarded as a good charitable trust.

Sub-clause (a) of clause 11 of the deed of the deed includes the advancement of any purpose which might in the uncontrolled opinion of the Managing Committee be national or of national importance for the inhabitants of British India by any means which in the like opinion of the Managing Committee be constitutional. It is impossible to say that the Managing Committee might not regard purposes which were not according to law charitable, as being nevertheless of national importance for the inhabitants of British India, and the Committee might regard methods as constitutional which the law would not regard as constitutional. Assuming the objects specified in sub-clause (a) to be charitable, this was not the case of a gift for such charitable purposes as the Managing Committee may think fit. A gift of that sort would, no doubt, be good, because the Managing Committee would be bound to keep within the ambit of charity, and if they go beyond the legal boundary, they could be controlled by the Court. There are many purposes which an individual, acting quite bona fide , may regard as charitable, but which the law does not so regard. Therefore, sub-clause (a) goes too far; and sub-clause (b) goes too far also, because it was really a gift for political purposes. Assuming that the attainment of national autonomy may be regarded as a national purpose accepted generally by, and for the good of, the inhabitants of British India, there was a very keen divergence of opinion as to the methods by which that national autonomy should be attained; and it was impossible, to avoid the conclusion that a gift for the attainment of that object by such methods as the Managing Committee may approve was really a gift for political purposes. Therefore, it was impossible to say that the ITO was wrong in holding that the income of the trust did not fall within the purview of section 4(3)(i ).

The first proviso to section 41(1) of the 1922 Act is perfectly plain. It provides in connection with funds held by a trust that where income, profits or gains or any part thereof are not specifically receivable on behalf of any one person, or where the individual shares of the persons on whose behalf they are receivable are indeterminate or unknown, the tax shall be levied and recoverable at the maximum rate. It may be rather hard on this trust fund that it should be charged at a higher rate than the amount of its income would attract if it belonged to an individual. But that is not a matter with which the Court can deal. It is perfectly plain that the case fell within the first proviso to section 41(1), and, therefore, the ITO was correct in levying income-tax at the maximum rate under the first proviso to section 41(1) of 1922 Act.

Concurrent view (as per Kania, J.)

In section 4(3)(i) the words used are that the income should be derived from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes. By the explanation added at the end, the term "charitable purpose" is stated to include an object of general public utility. Even so, it is for the assessee to show that his case falls within that extended meaning.

Certain propositions of law now appear to be well settled as a result of authorities. First, that when there is a general charitable intention, the Court will uphold it, and if within that limit discretion is given to the trustees to select an object the trust will not fail because of the discretion so given. If a trustee selects an object, which is not charitable according to law, the Court can intervene and rectify the error.

The reopening cannot be sustained. This is because in the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT [2010] 103 ITR 777 (SC) the Supreme Court held that if one of the objects of the trust deed is not of a religious or charitable nature and the trust deed confers full discretion on the trustees to spend the trust funds for an object other than of a religious or charitable nature, the exemption under section 4(3)(i), of the 1922 Act is not available to assessee. If the primary or dominant purpose of a trust is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but which is merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purpose would not prevent the trust from being a valid charity. The Court also held that where in a trust deed providing for many charitable objects, the trustees were authorised to open and maintain commercial institutions where work at living wages could be provided to the poor and to contribute to commercial, technical or industrial concerns, institutions, associations or bodies imparting any type of training or providing employment to persons; and the deed gave uncontrolled discretion to the trustees to spend the whole of the trust fund on any of the non-charitable objects of the trust, then income of the trust was not exempted from tax under the said Act. There is not even an allegation that uncontrolled discretion or authority to open or maintain commercial institution was in the object of assessee. There is not even a finding to that effect. Just because there are certain receipts received by assessee while conducting its charitable activities, would not make those receipts whatever may be the quantum, to be income from commercial activities. [Para 3]

Therefore, there has to be a tangible material to come to the conclusion that there is an escapement of income from assessment to exercise the power to reopen. But if the reasons to believe indicate non-application of mind, the reasons to believe itself cannot be sustained. The reasons to believe proceeds on the basis that an assessment order under section 143(3) has been passed when the assessment has been processed only under section 143(1), and also on the basis of judgment, which according to the Assessing Officer is of Delhi High Court, when in reality is that of the Supreme Court. All these indicate that the reasons to believe has been formed mechanically and without application of mind. [Para 4]

In similar circumstances the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. P. Krishna Warriar [1964] 53 ITR 176 held that the business was 'property' held in trust and, therefore, the portion of business income which applied for charitable purpose, is exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act if a business is held in trust wholly or partially for religious or charitable purposes, it falls clearly under the substantive part of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and in that event clause (b) of the proviso could not be attracted as that clause was applicable only to a business not held in trust but carried on on behalf of religious or charitable institutions. Following the aforesaid decision in the instant case the Tribunal was right in holding that the income of the assessee trust was exempted under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

The share of wires from lime business was exempt under section 4(3)(i ) of the 1922 Act.
