15.1 Background

In case of a charitable trust registered under section 12A/12AA, its income is computed under sections 11 to 13. Section 11(1)(a) dealing with taxation of charitable institution provides that its income shall be exempt to the extent it is applied to charitable purposes in India. It has been held that the income of a charitable institution is not computed under the five heads of income specified in section 14, including profits and gains of business [CIT v. Rao Bahadur Calawala Kannan Chetty Charities [1982] 135 ITR 485 (Mad); CIT v. Estate of V. L. Ethiraj [1982] 136 ITR 12 (Mad.); Hindusthan Welfare Trust v. DIT [1993] 68 Taxman 205 (Cal.)].

Section 40(a)(ia) provides that in computation of profits and gains of business, 30% of any sum payable to a resident on which tax is not deducted/paid in accordance with the said section is not allowable as a deduction.

Section 40A(3) provides that no deduction is allowable in computation of profits and gains in respect of cash payments exceeding Rs.10,000. Section 40A(3A) provides that if a deduction is allowed in year 1 on mercantile basis and subsequently in year 2 the assessee makes cash payment, the payment so made shall be deemed to be profits and gains of business of year 2, if the payment exceeds Rs.10,000.

The aforesaid provisions, that is, section 40(a)(ia) and section 40A(3)/(3A) are not applicable to a charitable trust registered under section 12A/12AA whose income is required to be computed under sections 11 and 12 [see Bombay Stock Exchange Ltd. v. Dy. DIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 29/[2015] 228 Taxman 195 (Mag.) (Bom); Vidya Pratishthan v. Dy. CIT [2011] 44 SOT 90 (Pune) (URO); ITO v. Mother Theresa Educational Society [2016] 68 taxmann.com 320 (Visakh. - Trib.); ITO v. Haryana State Counseling Society [2016] 71 taxmann.com 274 (Chd. - Trib); Kendriya Academy Vidhyalaya Shiksha Samiti v. Asstt. CIT [2016] 73 taxmann.com 391 (Jp. - Trib.); ITO v. Kalinga Cultural Trust [2018] 61 ITR (Trib.) 24 (Hyd. - Trib.)].

A new Explanation 3 has been inserted after section 11(1) with effect from assessment year 2019-20 to provide that for the purposes of determining the amount of application of income under section 11(1)(a)/(b), the provisions of section 40(a)(ia), and of section 40A(3)/(3A), shall, mutatis mutandis, apply as they apply in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession".

15.2 Application of Explanation 3 - Steps

A careful reading of Explanation 3 shows that it involves following steps:

(a)

apply section 40(a)(ia)/40A(3)/40A(3A) in computing the income chargeable under the head "profits and gains of business or profession";

(b)

check whether a disallowance/addition to income could be made under the said sections;

(c)

if disallowance/addition could be made, then, apply the said sections in computing the amount of application of income for the purposes of section 11(1)(a)/(b);

(d)

the said sections should be applied mutatis mutandis;

(e)

on account of the words 'mutatis mutandis', even if disallowance or addition under section 40(a)(ia)/40A(3)/40A(3A) cannot be made in some cases, the quantum of application of income can still be adjusted under Explanation 3.

Amendments in sections 12 and 13 relating to taxation of charitable trusts

11.4 Hitherto, section 13 provided that the income of a charitable or religious trust would not be exempt if any part of income or the property of the trust or institution was used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person such as the author of the trust or the founder of the institution, trustee of the trust or manager or relative of such person (hereinafter referred to as a ‘specified person’) or any concern in which any such person has a substantial interest.

Section 13 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2001-02 and a new sub-section (6) has been added which provides that a trust running an educational institution or a medical institution or a hospital shall not lose the benefit of exemption of any income other than the value of benefits of educational or medical facilities provided to the specified persons, solely on the ground that such benefits have been provided to specified persons. In other words, the value of any such income received from specified persons would be taxable, however, the other income would remain exempt.

The expression ‘value’ has been defined in Explanation to section 12(2) of the Act, as ‘the value of any benefit or facility granted or provided free of cost or at concessional rate’.

The new provisions would apply only to charitable or religious trust running a hospital or a medical institution or an educational institution. They would not apply to all institutions eligible for exemption under section 11 of the Act, e.g. sanitariums, religious trusts, etc., would not get the benefits of the new provisions.

It appears that the value of facility provided to the specified persons would be taxable and no deduction shall be allowed in respect of expenses incurred in providing services to the specified person.

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill reads as follows -

“The existing provisions provide that the income of a charitable or religious trust will not be available if any part of such income or any property of the trust is used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person such as the author of the trust, trustee or any relative of such persons or any concerns in which such persons have a substantial interest (referred to as a specified person). It is proposed to insert a new sub-section in section 13 to provide that a trust running an educational institution or a medical institution or a hospital shall not lose the benefit of exemption of any income other than the value of benefits of educational or medical facilities provided to the specified persons, solely on the ground that such benefits have been provided to specified persons.”

This gives an impression that the amendment is made for all categories of interested persons including concerns.

However, the residual category specified in section 13(3)(e), namely, ‘any concern in which any person referred to in clauses (a), (b), (c), (cc) and (d) has a substantial interest’ is not specifically mentioned in sections 12(2) and 13(6). Thus, it is not clear as to whether a trust will lose tax exemption if any benefit is given directly or indirectly to the residual category in section 13(3)(e).

11.4-1 Amendment of section 12 - A new sub-section (2) has been inserted in section 12 with effect from the assessment year 2001-02. It provides that the value of any medical or educational services made available by any charitable or religious trust running a hospital or medial institution or an educational institution to any specified person shall be deemed to be the income of such trust or institution derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes during the previous year in which such services are so provided and shall be chargeable to income-tax notwithstanding the provisions of section 11(1).

Group company - Monies given by assessee-trust to sister concern purportedly for construction of hospital and which was kept lying unused with sister concern could not be regarded as having been applied for charitable purposes [CIT v. V. G. P. Foundation [2003] 134 Taxman 663 (Mad.)].

Improvement of property - Expenditure on improvement of a property held under trust would by itself not come within the scope of 'application of income' for charitable purposes [CIT v. Kannika Parameswari Devasthanam & Charities [1982] 133 ITR 779 (Mad.)].

Incomes exempt u/s 10 - While computing exempt income u/s 11, incomes which are exempt u/s 10 are to be excluded [DIT v. Jasubhai Foundation [2015] 58 taxmann.com 218 (Bom.)].

Provision - Where an amount was set apart as provision in the accounts of the assessee and the finding of fact was that the amount was not actually applied for charitable or religious purposes, assessee would not be entitled to exemption u/s 11 in respect of that amount [Nachimuthu Industrial Association v. CIT [1999] 235 ITR 190 (SC)].

Janmabhumi Press Trust [2000] 242 ITR 457 (Kar.); DIT v. Span Foundation [2009] 178 Taxman 436 (Delhi); DIT v. Govindu Naicker Estate [2009] 315 ITR 237 (Mad.)].

Salaries - Expenditure on salaries and miscellaneous expenses for purpose of carrying out objects and purposes of the trust can be considered as application of income for charitable purpose [CIT v. Birla Janahit Trust [1994] 73 Taxman 465 (Cal.)].

Scholarship - Where charitable object of assessee was advancement of higher technical education to deserving students, assessee's claim of expenditure incurred on account of scholarship paid to incumbent for pursuing engineering was allowable [CIT v. Seth Anandram Jaipuria Edu. Society Cantonment [2017] 80 taxmann.com 96 (All.)].

Statutory contributions - Statutory transfer of amount collected as mandi shulk to Mandi Parishad would constitute 'application of income' for charitable purposes [CIT v. Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti [2012] 27 taxmann.com 42/211 Taxman 32 (SC)].

Handing over of money by one trust to another having similar objects would amount to application of income. There are no weighty reasons to give a different meaning to the expression 'utilised' in section 11(3)(c) as 'spent'. The trust would be fulfilling the conditions prescribed in section 11(3)(c) of the Act, either by directly applying or spending the income for the purpose for which the income was accumulated or by handing over the same to an existing institution to be utilised for the same purpose. But, section 11(3)(c) of the Act cannot be limited to the above two situations. The words in section 11(3)(c) are also apt to cover cases of handing over the accumulated income to another trust having its objects similar to the purposes for which the income was accumulated with directions by the donor trust that the accumulated income should be applied to the purposes for which the income was accumulated.

2.4 Rationalisation of taxation regime for charitable trusts and institutions under sections 11 to 13

The existing provisions of section 11 contain a primary condition that for grant of exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust, such income should be applied for the charitable purposes in India, and where such income cannot be so applied during the previous year, it has to be accumulated in the prescribed modes.

2.4-1 New sub-section (6) - No depreciation if purchase of asset claimed as application of income

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted new sub-section (6) in section 11, with effect from 1-4-2015. The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation or otherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

2.4-2 New sub-section (7) - No exemption under any clause of sec. 10 except clauses (1) and (23C) if registration u/s 12A or 12AA in force

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. In terms of new sub-section (7), where such registration is in force for a previous year, then such trust or institution shall not be entitled to any exemption under any provision of section 10 [other than that relating to exemption of agricultural income and income exempt under section 10(23C)].

The amendment overcomes the decision of the Tribunal in Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mum. - Trib.). In Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt. DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mumbai - Trib.) the assessee claimed that dividend income on shares and unit and long term capital gain on sale of shares are exempt u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) respectively. The AO denied the exemption on the ground that section 11 exclusively deals with the income derived from the property held under trust and not u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38). Hence the AO held that there is a violation u/s 13 and as a result of the same exemption u/s 11 is denied. The assessee cannot claim the alternative claim for exemption u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) because these sections do not deal with income derived from the property held under the trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) concurred with AO’s view. On further appeal, however, ITAT ruled in favour of the assessee-trust and held that "the income which is exempt u/s 10 cannot be brought to tax by virtue of sections 11 and 13 of the Act because no such pre-condition is provided either u/s 10 or 11 to 13. Therefore, sections 11 to 13 would not operate as overriding effect to the section 10 of the Act. The language of these provisions does not suggest that either section 10 is subjected to the provisions of sections 11 to 13 or sections 11 to 13 has any overriding effect over section 10. Therefore, the benefit of section 10 cannot be denied by invoking the provisions of sections 11 to 13 of the Act. Once the conditions of section 10 are satisfied then no other condition can be fastened for denying the claim under section 10 of the Act".

Amendment to section 11 now overcomes the above judicial ruling.

The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation or otherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. ◆ Whether objects include any object, which could be classified as the Other Object? ◆ Whether it is pursuing any activity, which can be classified or has been classified as the Other Object?

◆ Whether the activity involved in pursuit of the Other Objects is in the nature of trade?

◆ Whether the activity involved in pursuit of the Other Objects amounts to rendering of services in relation to the trade? If so, whether it is for a consideration?

◆ Whether newly inserted proviso to section 2(15) is applicable?

◆ If not, the reasons thereof.

◆ If yes, the implications, if any, in respect of the specific objects (the relief of poor or education or medical relief).

Exemption to a ‘Sikkimese’ individual [Section 10(26AA)]

1.3 Section 10(26AA) has been inserted with retrospective effect from assessment year 1990-91 to provide that the following income, which accrues or arises to a Sikkemese individual, shall be exempt from income-tax—

(a) income from any source in the State of Sikkim; or

(b) income by way of dividend or interest on securities

1.3-1 Sikkimese, meaning - For this purpose, ‘Sikkimese’ shall mean —

(i) an individual, whose name is recorded in the register maintained under the Sikkim Subjects Regulation, 1961 read with the Sikkim Subject Rules, 1961 (‘Register of Sikkim Subjects’), immediately before 26th April, 1975; or

(ii) an individual, whose name is included in the Register of Sikkim Subjects by virtue of the Government of India Order No. 26030/36/90-I.C.I., dated 7th August, 1990 and Order of even number dated 8th April, 1991; or

(iii) any other individual, whose name does not appear in the Register of Sikkim Subjects but it is established beyond doubt that the name of such individual’s father or husband or paternal grandfather or brother from the same father has been recorded in that register.

However, this exemption will not be available to a Sikkimese woman who, on or after 1-4-2008, marries a non-Sikkimese individual.

1.3-2 Analysis of amendment - It may be noted that besides income from any source in the State of Sikkim exemption is also available in respect of any dividend or interest on securities even if it is sourced from outside the State of Sikkim.

Exemption of income of Agricultural Produce Market Committee [section 10(26AAB)]

1.4 A new section 10(26AAB) has been inserted with effect from assessment year 2009-10 to provide that any income of an agricultural produce market committee or board constituted under any law for the time being in force for the purpose of regulating the marketing of agricultural produce shall be exempt from income-tax.

Following relevant extracts from the reply of the Finance Minister to the debate in the Lok Sabha on 29-4-2008 on the Finance Bill, 2008 may also be noted :

“6. Clause 3 of the Finance Bill, 2008 seeks to amend the definition of ‘charitable purpose’ so as to exclude any activity in the nature of trade, commerce or business, or any activity of rendering any service in relation to any trade, commerce or business, for a cess or fee or any other consideration, irrespective of the nature or use of application, or retention, of the income from such activity. The intention is to limit the benefit to entities which are engaged in activities such as relief of the poor, education, medical relief and any other genuine charitable purpose, and to deny it to purely commercial and business entities which wear the mask of a charity. A number of Hon’ble Members have written to me expressing their concern on the possible impact of the proposal on Agricultural Produce Market Committees (APMC) or State Agricultural Marketing Boards (SAMB). Since there is no intention to tax such committees or boards, and in order to remove any doubts, I propose to insert a new clause (26AAB) in section 10 of the Income-tax Act to provide exemption to any income of an APMC or SAMB constituted under any law for the time being in force for the purpose of regulating the marketing of agricultural produce.”

Exploitation rights - The right to exploit space on either side of an overbridge for advertisements is a "property" [A. J. Patel v. CIT [1974] 97 ITR 683 (Bom.)].

Religious offerings - Offerings received by a religious teacher from his disciples would not constitute "property held under trust" [Swami Narsingh Giri v. CIT [1971] 79 ITR 544 (All.)].

INCOME

Commercial sense - It is not the 'total income' as would be assessed by the ITO that is relevant for the purpose of investing the funds of the trust or assessing the income of the trust. Taking into account the purpose for which the conditions of section 11(1)(a) are imposed, it would be clear that 'income' to be considered will be that which is arrived at in the context of what is available in the hands of the assessee subject to an adjustment of any expenses extraneous to the trust [CIT v. P. S. G. & Sons Charities [1997] 223 ITR 831 (Mad.)].

Grants - Where assessee-society was acting as a nodal agency receiving grant from Government of India and State Governments and distributed to district authorities for implementation of various schemes of Government of India and supervising execution of schemes, grants received by assessee should not be considered either as income or for ascertaining amount expanded or amount to be accumulated [CIT v. State Urban Development Society [2011] 11 taxmann.com 458 (P&H)]. Also see, DIT v. Gujarat State Council for Blood Transfusion [2014] 41 taxmann.com 449/221 Taxman 126 (Guj.).

Legal expenses - Legal expenses incurred by a charitable institution for defending its president from criminal charges are allowable as a permissible deduction while computing its income [Ananda Marga Pracharaka Sangha v. CIT [1994] 76 Taxman 88 (Cal.)].

Refund of income-tax - Refund of income-tax can by no stretch of imagination be held as income derived from property held under the trust and, hence, will not be covered u/s 11(2) [CIT v. Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) [2002] 120 Taxman 186 (Delhi)].

Returned amounts - Only the income spent on charitable or religious purposes is excluded from the total income of the trust and when that amount is returned by the beneficiaries of the trust, the receipt in the hands of the trust can only be its income of the years in which it is received; it cannot have any different character [CIT v. Cutchi Memon Union [1985] 20 Taxman 386/155 ITR 51 (Kar.)].

Taxes - Payment of taxes under VDIS is to be deducted before arriving at commercial income of assessee-trust that is available for application to charitable purposes [DIT v. National Association of Software & Services Companies [2012] 21 taxmann.com 213/208 Taxman 178 (Delhi)].

APPLICATION OF INCOME

General - If section 11(1)(a) has been fully exploited and there is still accumulated income left to be dealt with, section 11(2) can be pressed in service and if it is complied with, such additional accumulated income beyond the prescribed percentage can also earn exemption u/s 11(2) [Addl. CIT v. A. L. N. Rao Charitable Trust [1995] 83 Taxman 252 (SC)].

'Applied' need not be equated with 'spent' - The word 'applied' does not necessarily mean 'spent'. Even if the amount has been earmarked for the purposes of the institution and allocated, it may be deemed to have been applied [CIT v. Radhaswami Satsang Sabha [1954] 25 ITR 472 (All.)].

Both revenue and capital expenditure are covered - As far as the objects of the trust are concerned, the application of the amount can be for revenue or capital purposes [CIT v. Kannika Parameswari Devasthanam & Charities [1982] 133 ITR 779 (Mad.)].

Deemed income - Deemed income (i.e., tax deducted at source) is not to be taken into account for determining the application of income [CIT v. Jayashree Charity Trust [1986] 159 ITR 280 (Cal.)].

Donation - Donation of sale proceeds of capital asset made by charitable trust to another trust was to be allowed as 'application of income' for charitable purpose [PCIT v. St. Joseph's Monastery [2022] 137 taxmann.com 133 (Kar.)].

15.1 Background

In case of a charitable trust registered under section 12A/12AA, its income is computed under sections 11 to 13. Section 11(1)(a) dealing with taxation of charitable institution provides that its income shall be exempt to the extent it is applied to charitable purposes in India. It has been held that the income of a charitable institution is not computed under the five heads of income specified in section 14, including profits and gains of business [CIT v. Rao Bahadur Calawala Kannan Chetty Charities [1982] 135 ITR 485 (Mad); CIT v. Estate of V. L. Ethiraj [1982] 136 ITR 12 (Mad.); Hindusthan Welfare Trust v. DIT [1993] 68 Taxman 205 (Cal.)].

Section 40(a)(ia) provides that in computation of profits and gains of business, 30% of any sum payable to a resident on which tax is not deducted/paid in accordance with the said section is not allowable as a deduction.

Section 40A(3) provides that no deduction is allowable in computation of profits and gains in respect of cash payments exceeding Rs.10,000. Section 40A(3A) provides that if a deduction is allowed in year 1 on mercantile basis and subsequently in year 2 the assessee makes cash payment, the payment so made shall be deemed to be profits and gains of business of year 2, if the payment exceeds Rs.10,000.

The aforesaid provisions, that is, section 40(a)(ia) and section 40A(3)/(3A) are not applicable to a charitable trust registered under section 12A/12AA whose income is required to be computed under sections 11 and 12 [see Bombay Stock Exchange Ltd. v. Dy. DIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 29/[2015] 228 Taxman 195 (Mag.) (Bom); Vidya Pratishthan v. Dy. CIT [2011] 44 SOT 90 (Pune) (URO); ITO v. Mother Theresa Educational Society [2016] 68 taxmann.com 320 (Visakh. - Trib.); ITO v. Haryana State Counseling Society [2016] 71 taxmann.com 274 (Chd. - Trib); Kendriya Academy Vidhyalaya Shiksha Samiti v. Asstt. CIT [2016] 73 taxmann.com 391 (Jp. - Trib.); ITO v. Kalinga Cultural Trust [2018] 61 ITR (Trib.) 24 (Hyd. - Trib.)].

A new Explanation 3 has been inserted after section 11(1) with effect from assessment year 2019-20 to provide that for the purposes of determining the amount of application of income under section 11(1)(a)/(b), the provisions of section 40(a)(ia), and of section 40A(3)/(3A), shall, mutatis mutandis, apply as they apply in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession".

In case of an eligible trust, applicability of the first proviso to section 2(15) will have to be examined each year.

(b)

If the first proviso to section 2(15) applies to eligible trust, in any previous year, it would be implied that for that previous year alone, eligible trust does not exist for charitable purpose.

(c)

Accordingly, the previous year in which the first proviso to section 2(15) applies, eligible trust would not be eligible for the exemption either under section 11 or under section 10(23C)(iv)/(v).

(d)

Accordingly, its total income would include all the income derived by eligible trust, irrespective of its application to the objects of the Trust.

(e)

The exemption would not be available only in respect of the previous year in which the first proviso to section 2(15) applies. If, in any subsequent previous year, the first proviso to section 2(15) does not apply, eligible trust would be entitled to the exemption under section 11 or under to section 10(23C)(iv)/(v).

(f)

In the previous year in which the first proviso becomes applicable, the exemption would not be available even if the registration or approval or notification continues to operate. In other words, merely because the first proviso to section 2(15) applies, to a previous year, it does not imply that its registration can be cancelled or approval can be withdrawn or notification can be rescinded, or merely because the registration or approval or notification continues to operate, the exemption cannot be denied.

To illustrate:

An eligible trust is, inter alia, pursuing other objects.

In the course of that, in the previous year 2011-12, it renders certain services to trade, etc., sometime in January, 2012 and receives Rs. 30 lacs as consideration.

In the above case, eligible trust would not be eligible for the exemption in respect of income for the entire previous year 2011-12.

The eligible trust will not be able to contend that for the first 9 months it continued to be in existence for charitable purpose and, hence, its income for the first 9 months should not lose exemption on account of a specific provision made by the amendments to the effect that the exemption will not be available to that previous year in which the first proviso to section 2(15) applies.

In the previous year to follow after the previous year 2011-12, subject to fulfilment of the conditions and assuming the first proviso to section 2(15) does not apply, eligible trust would continue to get the exemption under section 11 or section 10(23C)(iv)/(v).

2.4 Rationalisation of taxation regime for charitable trusts and institutions under section 12

The existing provisions of section 11 contain a primary condition that for grant of exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust, such income should be applied for the charitable purposes in India, and where such income cannot be so applied during the previous year, it has to be accumulated in the prescribed modes.

2.4-1 New sub-section (6) - No depreciation if purchase of asset claimed as application of income

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted new sub-section (6) in section 11, with effect from 1-4-2015. The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation orotherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

2.4-2 New sub-section (7) - No exemption under any clause of sec. 10 except clauses (1) and (23C) if registration u/s 12A or 12AA in force

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. In terms of new sub-section (7), where such registration is in force for a previous year, then such trust or institution shall not be entitled to any exemption under any provision of section 10 [other than that relating to exemption of agricultural income and income exempt under section 10(23C)].

The amendment overcomes the decision of the Tribunal in Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mum. - Trib.). In Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt. DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mumbai - Trib.) the assessee claimed that dividend income on shares and unit and long term capital gain on sale of shares are exempt u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) respectively. The AO denied the exemption on the ground that section 11 exclusively deals with the income derived from the property held under trust and not u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38). Hence the AO held that there is a violation u/s 13 and as a result of the same exemption u/s 11 is denied. The assessee cannot claim the alternative claim for exemption u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) because these sections do not deal with income derived from the property held under the trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) concurred with AO's view. On further appeal, however, ITAT ruled in favour of the assessee-trust and held that "the income which is exempt u/s 10 cannot be brought to tax by virtue of sections 11 and 13 of the Act because no such pre-condition is provided either u/s 10 or 11 to 13. Therefore, sections 11 to 13 would not operate as overriding effect to the section 10 of the Act. The language of these provisions does not suggest that either section 10 is subjected to the provisions of sections 11 to 13 or sections 11 to 13 has any overriding effect over section 10. Therefore, the benefit of section 10 cannot be denied by invoking the provisions of sections 11 to 13 of the Act. Once the conditions of section 10 are satisfied then no other condition can be fastened for denying the claim under section 10 of the Act".

ADVANCEMENT OF ANY OTHER OBJECT OF GENERAL PUBLIC UTILITY

Definition of widest connote - The expression 'object of general public utility' includes all objects which promote the welfare of the general public. It cannot be said that a purpose would cease to be charitable even if public welfare is intended to be served. If the primary purpose and the predominant object are to promote the welfare of the general public, the purpose would be 'charitable purpose' [CIT v. Andhra Chamber of Commerce [1965] 55 ITR 722 (SC)]. However, it would exclude objects of private gain [All India Spinners' Association v. CIT[1944] 12 ITR 482 (PC)].

'General', meaning of - The word 'general', in the said expression, means pertaining to a whole class. Therefore, advancement of any object of benefit to the public or a section of the public as distinguished from benefit to an individual or a group of individuals would be a 'charitable purpose' [CIT v. Ahmedabad Rana Caste Association [1983] 140 ITR 1 (SC)]. However, it is not necessary that the object should be to benefit the whole of mankind or of persons in a country or State. It is sufficient if the intention to benefit a section of the public as distinguished from a specified individual is present. Nevertheless, the section of the community sought to be benefited must be sufficiently defined and identifiable by some common quality of a public or impersonal nature [Bangalore Urban & Rural District Co-operative Milk Producers Societies Members & Employees Welfare Trust Bangalore Milk Union Ltd. v. DIT [2017] 79 taxmann.com 320 (Kar.)].

Objects held to be of general public utility, illustrations - (1) When an object is to promote or protect the interest of a particular trade or industry, that object becomes an object of public utility, but not so, if it seeks to promote the interest of those who conduct the said trade or industry [Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1979] 2 Taxman 501 (SC); CIT v. Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industries [1981] 6 Taxman 7 (SC); CIT v. Andhra Chamber of Commerce [1981] 7 Taxman 27 (SC)].

(2) Where assessee-trust apart from propagation of Jain philosophy and ideology was also engaged in spreading religious and dharmik knowledge and providing amenities and facilities to pilgrims and renovation of Jain temples all over India, it was to be regarded as public charitable trust performing activities of general public utility [DIT v. Sheth Jivandas Godidas Shankheshwar Parshwanathji Jain [2014] 41 taxmann.com 492/221 Taxman 44 (Mag.) (Guj.)].

Such trusts or institutions will have to note the difference between deduction of expenses and application of income. To illustrate, while they were eligible for exemption, even capital expenditure could have been claimed as application of income. Finance Act, 2014

2.4 Rationalisation of taxation regime for charitable trusts and institutions under sections 11 to 13

The existing provisions of section 11 contain a primary condition that for grant of exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust, such income should be applied for the charitable purposes in India, and where such income cannot be so applied during the previous year, it has to be accumulated in the prescribed modes.

2.4-1 New sub-section (6) - No depreciation if purchase of asset claimed as application of income

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted new sub-section (6) in section 11, with effect from 1-4-2015. The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation or otherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

2.4-2 New sub-section (7) - No exemption under any clause of sec. 10 except clauses (1) and (23C) if registration u/s 12A or 12AA in force

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. In terms of new sub-section (7), where such registration is in force for a previous year, then such trust or institution shall not be entitled to any exemption under any provision of section 10 [other than that relating to exemption of agricultural income and income exempt under section 10(23C)].

The amendment overcomes the decision of the Tribunal in Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mum. - Trib.). In Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt. DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mumbai - Trib.) the assessee claimed that dividend income on shares and unit and long term capital gain on sale of shares are exempt u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) respectively. The AO denied the exemption on the ground that section 11 exclusively deals with the income derived from the property held under trust and not u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38). Hence the AO held that there is a violation u/s 13 and as a result of the same exemption u/s 11 is denied. The assessee cannot claim the alternative claim for exemption u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) because these sections do not deal with income derived from the property held under the trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) concurred with AO's view. On further appeal, however, ITAT ruled in favour of the assessee-trust and held that "the income which is exempt u/s 10 cannot be brought to tax by virtue of sections 11 and 13 of the Act because no such pre-condition is provided either u/s 10 or 11 to 13. Therefore, sections 11 to 13 would not operate as overriding effect to the section 10 of the Act. The language of these provisions does not suggest that either section 10 is subjected to the provisions of sections 11 to 13 or sections 11 to 13 has any overriding effect over section 10. Therefore, the benefit of section 10 cannot be denied by invoking the provisions of sections 11 to 13 of the Act. Once the conditions of section 10 are satisfied then no other condition can be fastened for denying the claim under section 10 of the Act".

Amendment to section 11 now overcomes the above judicial ruling.

New sub-section (7) also incorporates into the statute book the principle laid down in Bharati Vidyapeeth Medical Foundation v. Asstt. CIT [2013] 37 taxmann.com 242/144 ITD 510 that "When the law permits the assessee to claim exemption under section 10(23C) or section 11, the choice should be left to the assessee and the department cannot force the assessee to adopt only a particular provision".

10.3 Section 11(2) provides that where 75% of the income derived from property held under trust for charitable or religious purpose is not applied, or is not deemed to have been applied, and is accumulated or set apart for application to such purposes in India, it shall not be included in the total income of the previous year of the person in receipt of the income, provided such person gives a notice in writing to the Assessing Officer in the prescribed manner specifying the purposes for which the income is being accumulated or set apart (that is, specified purpose) and the money so accumulated or set apart is invested or deposited in the forms or modes specified in section 11(5). However, such period of accumulation is not to exceed ten years as provided in section 11(2).

Section 11(3) of the Income-tax Act provides, inter alia, that where the income accumulated or set apart is not utilised for the specified purpose during the period mentioned in clause (a) of section 11(2), it shall be deemed to be the income of the person of the previous year immediately following the expiry of the aforesaid period.

The aforesaid provisions create hardship in cases where the income accumulated or set apart cannot be applied for the specified purpose during the said period due to an order or injunction of any Court. Hence, section 11(2) has been amended to provide that in computing the period of ten years, the period during which the income could not be applied for the specified purpose, due to an order or injunction of any Court, shall be excluded.

This amendment has taken effect retrospectively from assessment year 1962-63.

Increasing the number of years for which approval can be granted by the Commissioner under section 80G

10.4 Under section 80G, a deduction in respect of any sum paid to any fund or institution referred in section 80G(2)(a)(iv) is allowed if the fund/institution is approved by the Commissioner. The power of approval, which was earlier based on administrative instructions, was made into a statutory provision by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1991. The provision stipulates that the approval has effect for such assessment year or years, not exceeding three assessment years, as may be specified in the approval. With a view to reducing the work related to repeated approvals and to simplify the procedures, section 80G has been amended to stipulate that the approval will have effect for such assessment year or years, not exceeding five assessment years, as may be specified in the approval. Cases where the Commissioner is convinced about the reputation of the fund or institution can, henceforth, be granted approval straightaway for five years. The Commissioner will, however, as is in the existing provisions, have the discretion to grant approval for less than five years depending upon the facts and circumstances of the case.

According to the Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill, 1993, the amendment is applicable in relation to assessment year 1993-94 and subsequent years and hence, it should apply to any application made after 1-4-1992.

and accumulating 15% at each stage, the effective application towards the charitable or religious activities is reduced significantly to a lesser percentage compared to the mandatory requirement of 85%.

3.3 In order to ensure intended application toward charitable or religious purpose, it is proposed that only 85% of the eligible donations made by a trust or institution under the first or the second regime to another trust under the first or second regime shall be treated as application only to the extent of 85% of such donation. Trusts or institutions attempt to circumvent the legislative intent by creating multiple trusts and accumulating 15% at each layer. This results in a significantly lower percentage of effective utilisation towards charitable or religious activities compared to the mandatory 85% requirement.

For example, ABC Trust received Rs. 10 lakhs as voluntary contributions. As per the regulations, the trust is obligated to use at least 85% of its income for charitable or religious purposes. Instead of utilising 85% of its income, the trust creates a new XYZ Trust, transfers 85% of its receipts (Rs. 8,50,000) to it, and claims the remaining 15% as exempt. The XYZ Trust has receipts of Rs. 8,50,000. It creates another new trust PQR Trust, transfers 85% of its income (Rs. 7,22,500) to PQR Trust, and claims the balance of 15% as exempt. Finally, PQR Trust has receipts of Rs. 7,22,500 and applies 85% of it (Rs. 6,14,125) towards charitable purposes and claims the balance of 15% as exempt. In this 3 layer structure, the effective utilisation towards charitable purposes is only Rs. 6,14,125 out of the initial Rs. 10 lakhs received by ABC Trust.

When this process continues, the percentage of income utilised for charitable or religious purposes decreases at each stage. As a result, the actual utilisation of income towards the intended purposes becomes significantly less than the mandatory 85% requirement.

3.4-4 Impact of amendment

The amendment by the Finance Act, 2023 has provided that any amount credited or paid, other than the amount referred to in Explanation 2 to Section 11(1), to any fund or trust or institution or any university or other educational institution or any hospital or other medical institution, referred to in Section 10(23C)(iv)/(v)/(vi)/(via) or other trust or institution registered under Section 12AB, as the case may be, shall be treated as application for charitable or religious purposes only to the extent of 85% of such amount credited or paid.

Pursuant to Explanation 2, any contribution by a charitable or religious trust to any other trust registered under Section 12AA or Section 12AB or approved under Section 10(23C), with a specific direction that it shall form part of the corpus of the recipient trust, it shall not be treated as application of income for the donor trust. Hence, if corpus donations are made to other trusts, it cannot be claimed as an 85% application even after this amendment.

Therefore, prior to the amendment by the Finance Act, 2023, there was a restriction on the amount contributed with a specific direction that it shall form part of the corpus of the donee. In such case, it shall not be treated as an application of income for charitable or religious purposes. However, there was no bar on giving a non-corpus donation. After this amendment, the non-corpus inter-charity donation is capped at 85% of the amount donated.

(c) In section 143, third proviso is inserted [to provide that the income of a body approved or notified under section 10(23C)(iv) or (v) can be computed without giving effect to the exemption discussed hereafter].

3.2.3 Analysis

3.2.3a New Seventeenth proviso in section 10(23C) - Section 10(23C) of the Act confers exemption on certain funds, institutions, etc., from tax if such funds, etc., are of the nature specified therein as well as notified or approved by the prescribed authority, subject to fulfilment of conditions.

Section 10(23C)(iv) confers exemption on any fund or institution established for charitable purposes, approved by the prescribed authority, having regard to its objects and importance throughout India or throughout any State or States.

Section 10(23C)(v) confers exemption on any Trust or institution, approved by the prescribed authority, wholly for the public religious purpose or wholly public religious and charitable purpose.

The provisions of section 10(23C) stipulate various conditions and also provides for withdrawal of approval or rescission of the Notification in certain circumstances.

Seventeenth proviso, as inserted stipulates:

The income of Trust or institution referred in sub-clause (iv) or (v) shall be included in its total income, of a previous year, if:

(a) It carries on, in pursuit of other objects, any activity in the nature of trade, etc., or renders services in relation to trade, etc., for a consideration exceeding the threshold limit of Rs. 25 lacs and as a result the First proviso to section 2(15) becomes applicable to it in that previous year,

(b) the aforesaid inclusion shall be made whether or not approval granted is withdrawn or notification issued is rescinded.

3.2.3b New sub-section (8) in section 13 - Sections 11 to 13 govern the exemption in case of a trust existing for charitable or religious purpose subject to fulfilment of the conditions. Section 13 provides that exemption conferred under section 11 on a Trust existing for charitable or religious purpose shall not apply in the circumstances specified in sub-sections (1) to (7).

The new sub-section (8) provides that the exemption under section 11 will not be available to a Trust, in a previous year, in which the First proviso to section 2(15) becomes applicable, for that previous year.

3.2.3c New third proviso to section 143(3) - The first proviso to section 143(3) provides that in case of a Trust, inter alia, referred in the said sub-clauses (iv) and (v) of section 10(23C), while making an assessment of total income or loss, effect to the exemption conferred by the said sub-clauses shall be given. Further, the Assessing Officer is empowered to intimate to the Central Government any contravention noticed by him of the said provision and/or sub-clauses and if the approval granted or notification issued in respect of such trust referred in the said sub-clause (iv) or (v) is withdrawn or rescinded, not to give effect to the exemption.

The third proviso, as inserted, empowers the denial of exemption under section 10(23C), in the previous year in which the First proviso to section 2(15) becomes applicable, in that previous year, irrespective of the fact that the approval is withdrawn or not or the notification is rescinded or not.

3.2.3d Position after the amendments - The effects of the above amendments for the Trusts referred in the said sub-clauses and/or sections 11 to 13 (collectively referred as 'eligible trust') are as follows:—

(a) In case of an eligible trust, applicability of the first proviso to section 2(15) will have to be examined each year.

(b) If the first proviso to section 2(15) applies to eligible trust, in any previous year, it would be implied that for that previous year alone, eligible trust does not exist for charitable purpose.

(c) Accordingly, the previous year in which the first proviso to section 2(15) applies, eligible trust would not be eligible for the exemption either under section 11 or under section 10(23C)(iv)/(v).

definition of the term 'charitable purpose' as defined in section 2(15) but in view of the fact that certification of seeds by the petitioner facilitates trade, commerce or business in the certified seeds by the client of the petitioner, the proviso to the said section would come into operation. Thus, the petitioner's activity assists the sale of certified seeds and is 'in relation to any trade, commerce or business' and therefore its activity cannot be held to be a 'charitable purpose'. Bureau of Indian Standards v. Director General of Income-tax (Exemptions) [2012] 27 taxmann.com 127/[2013] 212 Taxman 210/260 CTR 39/358 ITR 78 (Delhi)

The expressions "any activity", "rendering any service" and "in relation to any trade, commerce or business" imply that the intention of the legislature was to make the latter part of the exception broad and inclusive. It seems that the exception (the first proviso) is intended to catch with its ambit any and all commercial activity, except what falls within the second proviso (which bars application of the exception in cases where the aggregate value of the receipts from the activities mentioned therein is less than ten lakh rupees in the relevant previous year). The Bureau, it would appear at the first blush, renders service in relation to trade, commerce or business by granting certification/quality marks in return of license fee. Apparently, Parliament intended to clarify that not all activities of State agencies (some of which might be set up to carry on trading and commercial activities) can be considered charitable.

In these circumstances, "rendering any service in relation to trade, commerce or business" cannot, in the opinion of the Court, receive such a wide construction as to enfold regulatory and sovereign authorities, set up under statutory enactments, and tasked to act as agencies of the State in public duties which cannot be discharged by private bodies. Often, apart from the controlling or parent statutes, like the BIS Act, these statutory bodies (including BIS) are empowered to frame rules or regulations, exercise coercive powers, including inspection, raids; they possess search and seizure powers and are invariably subjected to Parliamentary or legislative oversight. The primary object for setting up such regulatory bodies would be to ensure general public utility. The prescribing of standards, and enforcing those standards, through accreditation and continuing supervision through inspection, etc., cannot be considered as trade, business or commercial activity, merely because the testing procedures, or accreditation involves charging of such fees. It cannot be said that the public utility activity of evolving, prescribing and enforcing standards, "involves" the carrying on of trade or commercial activity.

Ghatkopar Jolly Gymkhana v. DIT (Exemption) [2013] 40 taxmann.com 207/[2014] 147 ITD 112/160 TTJ 620 (Mum.)

First proviso to section 2(15) is a very rigorous provision which excludes the institution or trust from the definition of 'charitable trust', if such trust carries activities in the nature of trade, commerce or business, or any activity of rendering any service in relation to any trade, commerce or business, for a cess or fee or any other consideration, irrespective of the nature of use or application, or retention, of the income from such activity. So before the insertion of the second proviso from 1-4-2009, the definition of 'charitable purpose' when read with first proviso was very restrictive. However, by the insertion of the second proviso with effect from 1-4-2009 the rigour of the first proviso has been diluted and the first proviso has not been made applicable even if the trust carries on business activities and the gross receipts from such activities is Rs.10.00 lakhs or less than Rs.10.00 lakhs in the previous year. Hence, from 1-4-2009 the carrying out of the activities of trade, commerce or business even by charitable trust is not barred so as to exclude its activities from the definition of charitable purposes. However, a limitation has been imposed to the effect that the gross receipts from such activities should not exceed Rs.10.00 lakhs.

Late Shri Mohanlal Kanjibhai Pansara Education & Charitable Trust v. CIT [2013] 36 taxmann.com 338/59 SOT 169 (Rajkot)

The definition of 'Charitable Purpose' as given in section 2(15) is in the nature of inclusive definition. Charity means an act of piety and benevolence intended to benefit the society at large. Importing education would qualify to be called a charitable activity only if it is of public character directed for the benefit of the community or a section of the community and not motivated by commercial or business considerations. An activity which is motivated by commercial considerations can never qualify to be called a charitable activity. The same principle applies to education. The inherent features of 'charity' must be present in all the activities enumerated in section 2(15).

Critical Art & Media Practices v. DIT (Exemption) [2015] 56 taxmann.com 118/153 ITD 664/170 TTJ 401 (Mum.)

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether section 4(3)(i) relates to income from business held under trust and section 4(3)(ia) relates to income from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution where that business itself is not held on trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where business of managing agency was held in trust, it could be concluded that business carried on by trustees fell under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

On reference:

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1948-49 - Assessee executed a deed of trust whereby they settled certain amount on various charities and appointed themselves as trustees - Later, in accordance with terms of trust deed, trustees assessees were appointed as managing agents of a company - Before Income-tax authorities, trustee claimed that income derived from managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Revenue authorities, however, held that income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Whether word "property" in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend "business," and if question fell to be decided solely on terms of that sub-section, managing agency formed by assessees/trustees must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether fact that trustees had option at any time to throw up managing agency was no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

FACT: 'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

SC).

The provisions of section 4(3)(i ) confer an exemption of income from property only where the property itself is held under a trust or other legal obligation. It does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created in respect of any property, but only the income derived from any particular property or source is itself held in trust as where it is set apart or charged for a charitable purpose. That is clear upon the terms of the section itself and upon the authorities. In the instant case, all the income which the assessee derived or received was in the shape of grants and subscriptions from members which could not possibly have been received by it except from its business. Therefore, the entire income of the assessee must be held to be income derived from its business which was its property. If this contention was correct, then it was further submitted that there could be also no doubt upon the terms of its memorandum of association and its purposes and objects that the assessee was holding the business in trust for charitable purposes.

Supreme Court in J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that "Business" would undoubtedly be property in the connotation in which it is used in section 4(3)(i). In the light of this pronouncement of the Supreme Court it is clear that "business" itself can be property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) and upon that principle the business of the assessee in the instant case would be "property" held by the assessee.

Under the circumstances, the view taken by the Tribunal was the correct view and the income of the assessee would be exempt under the provisions of section 4(3)(i).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The legal dictionary Bakshi's Law Lexicon has defined the term 'manager' as per which 'manager has to be a person, has to be in the overall management of the company or trust, very importantly should be noted that, manager specifically for trust is not just a word of art, it is a very serious word comprising of meaning of a overall management.' after the expiry of the period of 18 years the net income derived from the investments was to be utilised for all or any one of the four objects mentioned in the deed. However, on the assessment made upon the trustees, the income-tax authorities rejected the trustees’ claim that the dividend and interest income derived from the trust property was exempt under the first half of section 4(3)(i).

On reference : HELD: Analysing the provisions of the trust deed, the scheme which emerges was clear. The settler did not wish the trustees to spend the income of the trust on the charitable objects immediately. He wanted the trust fund to increase and expand, and after the trust fund had expanded, he wanted the income of that trust fund to be spent on the charitable objects. In other words, the trust deed contained a scheme for accumulation of income and for the accumulated income to form part of the trust fund; and there was also a provision for the accumulation to go on for a specific period of time and on the expiry of that time the income of the enlarged trust fund to be spent on the charitable objects. If the property was impressed with a charitable trust or the object of the trust is charitable or religious, then the income derived from such trust or property would be income which would fall within the ambit of section 4(3)(i). It is fallacious to suggest that the object of the trust for the first 18 years was to invest monies in a particular manner. That was not the object: it was a mode of investment; it was a direction given by the settler how the income was to be utilized for the ultimate object of its being spent on the object of the trust. It was entirely untenable, to suggest that a direction with regard to investment could be looked upon as an object of the trust. An object of the trust is something definite and unvarying; it is the intention that the settler has for settling his property; it is an object with which the court can rarely interfere. Except when question of the cypress doctrine comes in, the court exercising charitable jurisdiction must always respect the charitable intention disclosed by the settler and help the trustees to carry out the charitable intention. But the direction with regard to its investment is entirely different. No court exercising equity jurisdiction-and the charity commissioner exercising his jurisdiction under the Bombay Public Trust Act under which this trust was registered-was ever tied down by the directions of the settler with regard to investments. If at any time within the 18 years the court or the charity commissioner was satisfied that the investments directed by the settler were not prudent investments and were not beneficial to the trust, it was perfectly competent to the charity commissioner or the court to direct that the investments should be made in a different manner. This clearly explains the dividing line between what are strictly the objects of the trust and the procedural matters, if one might say so, contained in the trust deed which may deal with detail like the accumulation of income, the investment of income.

It was not necessary that that intention must be immediately carried out. So long as the income from the trust property was not spent on any non-charitable object and it was saved, as it were, or set apart or accumulated for the ultimate object of carrying out the charitable purpose, then even in the intervening period the trust continues to be a charitable trust, the property is held on a charitable trust and the income from that trust is exempt from tax.

If the trust is to benefit the employees, even though they are to be benefited for purposes which are charitable, the trust would not come within the ambit of section 4(3)(i). What section 4(3)(i) has in view is not merely a religious or charitable purpose, but also that the object of the trust must be an object of general public utility. In other words, the bounty of the settler must be directed towards the public as a whole or a section of the public. If the object of his bounty is neither the public nor a section of the public but merely a conglomeration of men who constitute a mere group and the nexus which ties them is not a nexus which constitutes them a section of the public, then the trust would not be a trust which would fall within the ambit of section 4(3)(i).

'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation. It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

On the other hand, it was clear that trusts for the benefit of a particular political party, or for the advancement of particular political opinions, were not regarded as charitable. The objects specified in the trust deed, were clearly distributive. The whole of the trust fund could be applied for any one or more of the objects specified, and if any of those objects do not fall within the purview of the legal definition of "charity", the trust could not be regarded as a good charitable trust. Sub-clause (a) of clause 11 of the deed of the deed includes the advancement of any purpose which might in the uncontrolled opinion of the Managing Committee be national or of national importance for the inhabitants of British India by any means which in the like opinion of the Managing Committee be constitutional. It is impossible to say that the Managing Committee might not regard purposes which were not according to law charitable, as being nevertheless of national importance for the inhabitants of British India, and the Committee might regard methods as constitutional which the law would not regard as constitutional. Assuming the objects specified in sub-clause (a) to be charitable, this was not the case of a gift for such charitable purposes as the Managing Committee may think fit. A gift of that sort would, no doubt, be good, because the Managing Committee would be bound to keep within the ambit of charity, and if they go beyond the legal boundary, they could be controlled by the Court. There are many purposes which an individual, acting quite bona fide , may regard as charitable, but which the law does not so regard. Therefore, sub-clause (a) goes too far; and sub-clause (b) goes too far also, because it was really a gift for political purposes. Assuming that the attainment of national autonomy may be regarded as a national purpose accepted generally by, and for the good of, the inhabitants of British India, there was a very keen divergence of opinion as to the methods by which that national autonomy should be attained; and it was impossible, to avoid the conclusion that a gift for the attainment of that object by such methods as the Managing Committee may approve was really a gift for political purposes. Therefore, it was impossible to say that the ITO was wrong in holding that the income of the trust did not fall within the purview of section 4(3)(i ).

The first proviso to section 41(1) of the 1922 Act is perfectly plain. It provides in connection with funds held by a trust that where income, profits or gains or any part thereof are not specifically receivable on behalf of any one person, or where the individual shares of the persons on whose behalf they are receivable are indeterminate or unknown, the tax shall be levied and recoverable at the maximum rate. It may be rather hard on this trust fund that it should be charged at a higher rate than the amount of its income would attract if it belonged to an individual. But that is not a matter with which the Court can deal. It is perfectly plain that the case fell within the first proviso to section 41(1), and, therefore, the ITO was correct in levying income-tax at the maximum rate under the first proviso to section 41(1) of 1922 Act.

Concurrent view (as per Kania, J.)

In section 4(3)(i) the words used are that the income should be derived from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes. By the explanation added at the end, the term "charitable purpose" is stated to include an object of general public utility. Even so, it is for the assessee to show that his case falls within that extended meaning.

Certain propositions of law now appear to be well settled as a result of authorities. First, that when there is a general charitable intention, the Court will uphold it, and if within that limit discretion is given to the trustees to select an object the trust will not fail because of the discretion so given. If a trustee selects an object, which is not charitable according to law, the Court can intervene and rectify the error.

The objects in the trust deed have to be separately read, and if any of those objects is not charity, the whole gift must fail, because if the trustees choose to apply the whole of the fund to the particular object, which according to the law of the land is not charitable, then they will not be committing a breach of trust, and the trust could be said to be properly administered. The law does not permit the administration of a trust which can be so used entirely for a non-charitable object and hold it as charitable on construction. Therefore, clause 11 of this trust deed, which defines the objects of the trust, was not charitable within section 4(3)(i ) of 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 13, read with section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption - Whether manager of a trust can be treated as manager of institution referred to in clause (cc) of sub-section (3) of section 13 - Held, no - Whether 'trust' and 'institution' referred to in section 13 are different entities - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in holding that there was no violation of section 13 by assessee-trust in advancing money to its manager to warrant denial of benefit of section 11 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a charitable trust. During the course of assessment, the ITO found that certain sum had been paid to the manager of the trust as loan. The Assessing Officer treated the manager as a person referred to the section 13(3) and, hence, act of advancing loan to manager was hit by provisions of section 13(1)(c) and 13(2)(a). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the appellant-trust could not be said to have used any part of its income directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person referred to in section 13(3). Therefore, the provision of section 13(1)(c) was not applicable. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order that the assessee was a trust and not an institution.

On reference :

HELD: Sub-section (3) of section 13, clause (cc ) provides that any trustee of the trust or manager (by whatever name called) of the institution comes within the persons referred to in clause (c) of sub-section (1) and clause (a) of sub-section (2) for the purpose of exemption under section 11. The trust and institution referred to in section 13 are not one and the same thing and they are different entities. Clause (cc) of sub-section (3) of section 13 refers to the manager of the institution and not to the manager of the trust and in the instant case the advance had been given to the manager of the trust and not to the manager of the institution. In view of these admitted facts, no interference was called for in the order of the Tribunal.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Religious or charitable trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies created a trust and purported to endow it with share held by him in certain transport companies - Contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately but companies in which N was interested were to have benefit of assets set apart by him - N was managing trustee and empowered to borrow to any extent on properties conveyed to trust not only for trust but for his own use trustees were empowered, so long as N held office of managing trustee, to sell immovable properties belonging to trust for purpose of floating other companies - Foundation of institution was apparently to be left over until companies had made sufficient money for purpose - N also reserved right to revoke trust at any time - Whether on facts properties in question were not held under trust for charitable purpose within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The settlor N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies, created a trust and purported to endow it with the shares held by him in six transport companies. He constituted himself the managing trustee of the trust and gave himself full power to deal with its assets. The managing trustees claimed refund of tax paid in respect of dividends declared on the shares held in these transport companies. The income-tax authorities refused to allow a refund. Their reason was that the shares were not held under trust wholly for charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i).

On reference:

HELD: If the assets which N purported to set apart were to be devoted directly to such objects, no doubt the trust would be entitled to the refund claimed; but the deed clearly showed that the contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately and that the companies in which N was interested were to have the benefit of these assets set apart by him. Clause 54 of the deed provided that so long as N held the office of the managing trustee he shall have the power to borrow to any extent on the properties conveyed to the trust and that the board of trustees shall be able to borrow moneys which were necessary to discharge debts contracted by N. The power given to him was not limited to borrowing for the purpose of the trust. Apparently he could borrow moneys for his own purposes on the security of the assets set apart by him. By clause 55 the trustees were empowered, so long as N held the office of managing trustee, to sell immoveable properties belonging to the trust" in expanding or floating industrial institutions," in other words for the purpose of floating other companies. Clause 59 provided that the trustees may advance to the companies in which N was interested money for (a) discharging their liabilities (b) purchasing and substituting diesel or other more economical engines for the petrol engines on buses run by them and (c ) constructing passenger sheds and garages and other "amenities and facilities" for the use of the transport services "wherever the Trust is interested".

The foundation of the institution was apparently to be left over until the companies had made sufficient money for the purpose. By clause 71, 'N' reserved to himself the power to revoke the trust at any time.

In view of the provisions of the deed by which the assets could be utilised for N’s own purposes or the purposes of his companies, it was impossible for him to contend with reason that the deed created a trust wholly for charitable purposes. The idea that some day the institution contemplated by the deed might be founded was not sufficient compliance with the section.

It was said that in 1939 N made considerable alterations in the trust deed and that these alterations removed the objections now referred to. Whether the deed as it now stood created a trust which was entitled to the benefits of section 4(3)(i) was a question with which the High Court was not concerned. It was concerned only with the question whether a trust was created wholly for charitable purposes in the year of account, 1937-38, and it was obvious that this was not the case.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.
