The Tribunal also held that before the income of a trust for charitable purposes was exempt from tax, it must satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i), i.e., and in the instant case the business not being carried on the course of carrying out the primary purpose of the trust, the income was not exempt form liability to pay tax.

On reference : HELD: By the Insurance Act, 1938, a "principal agent" is defined as meaning "a person, who, not being a salaried employee of an insurer, in consideration of any commission, (i) performs any administrative and organizing functions for the insurer and (ii) procures general insurance business whether wholly or in part by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents of behalf of the insurer". Evidently a principal agent by the definition does not merely render personal service but is concerned with performing certain administrative and organizing functions and the procuring of general insurance business by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents. Such an agent by the very definition will be regarded as carrying on the business of a principal agent. He is not merely an employee engaged for rendering services of a personal nature: he is invested with the right as an agent to perform the administrative organizing functions for the insurer and to procure general insurance business by employing, directly or indirectly, insurance agents. By section 42A of the Insurance Act principal agents are required to obtain a certificate from the Controller of Insurance or an officer authorized by him entitling them to conduct the business of principal agency, and the certificate remains in operation for a period of twelve months only from the date of issue but is liable to be renewed. It is also true that under Part A of the Sixth Schedule to the Insurance Act certain terms are deemed to be included in every contract between an insurer carrying on general insurance business and a principal agent. Under clause 2 of Part A of the Sixth Schedule the principal agent has to procure or cause to be procured through insurance agents such an amount of general insurance business as will yield a gross premium income of not less than Rs. 20,000 in each calendar year. Under clause 4, in the event of the principal agent failing to comply with the requirements of clause 2 in any two successive calendar years, the contract shall, without prejudice to the provisions of clause 3, terminate on the 31st day of March immediately following the second calendar year. Under clause 3 the agency is also liable to be forfeited in the events set out in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) thereof. By clause 5 certain restriction are placed upon the principal agent but an account of these provisions, which impose certain restrictive conditions upon the principal agent it could not be said that the appointment of a principal agent gave rise to a bare service agreement and that the remuneration paid was not for the conduct of a business but for performance of personal service. The circumstance that the appointment was liable to be terminated at short notice and the agency was not permanent and was liable to be forfeited in the events set out hereinbefore would not, affect the character of the agency as business. Following the observation made by the Supreme Court in J.K. Trust's case [1957] 32 ITR 535 the principal agency conducted by the assessee was a business and, therefore, "property" within the meaning of section 4(3)(i). Being property which was capable of being settled upon trust by the deed of trust, dated 17-2-1951, it was lawfully settled upon trust for charitable purposes. The taxing authorities are primarily concerned with the question whether the income sought to be taxed in income from property, which is held on trust for religious or charitable purpose. If the business of the principal agency was transferred to the trustees under a deed of settlement, and from that business income was received, the income will fall within section 4(3)(i) and be exempt from tax in the hands of the trustees. Therefore, under the terms of appointment made with the company firm became the principal agents conducting a business and that business was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i ) and that the alteration, sometime after their appointment as principal agents, in the constitution of the from did not alter the character of the income earned in the course of the business. The income which is liable to be included in the total income of the assessee, was income derived from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution, unless that income fulfils the conditions prescribed by clause (b). The expression "such income" in the proviso refers to the income derived from property (which expression includes a business) held for religious or charitable purposes. But that did not justify the submission that the business which was referred to in clause (b) of the proviso must be business which is held for charitable or religious purposes. The business referred to in clause (b) of the proviso need not be business which is held for religious or charitable purposes, provided it is business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1951-52 to 1954-55 - A partnership firm was formed by four brothers - Firm was appointed as chief agent of an insurance company - Subsequently, brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming trustees would hold said business of chief agency of said company and all benefits and profits to arise from said business upon trust for public charitable purposes - Whether principal agency conducted by assessee-trust was a business and, therefore, "property" within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which was capable of being settled upon trust - Held, yes - Whether income of assessee-trust not being one which was not governed by proviso to section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953, but was governed by operative part of section 4(3)(i), it was exempt from tax - Held, yes

FACT: A partnership firm was formed by four brothers. No deed of partnership was said to have been executed in respect of this firm. The firm was appointed the chief agent an insurance company as from 1-9-1950. On 17-2-1951, the aforesaid brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming the trustees would hold the said business of the chief agency of the said company and all the benefits and profits to arise from the said business upon trust for public charitable purposes. The said declaration of trust was registered with the Registrar of Assurances.

The assessee claimed that as from 17-2-1951, the income from agency business should be assessed in the hands of the trustees and should be allowed exemption under section 4(3)(i). The ITO, however, made the assessment in the status of an unregistered firm. The ITO held that there was no charitable trust created by the deed dated 17-2-1951. On appeal, the AAC reversed the findings of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no proper and valid contract between the insurance company and the trustees as such; that the letter of appointment was only a service agreement; that there had been no transfer of property to the trustees wholly for charitable purposes; that the alleged transfer of the agency agreement did not amount to the transfer of property. The Tribunal also held that before the income of a trust for charitable purposes was exempt from tax, it must satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i), i.e., and in the instant case the business not being carried on the course of carrying out the primary purpose of the trust, the income was not exempt form liability to pay tax.

On reference :

Further, the trust was allowed registration as public charitable trust by the Commissioner under section 12A(a). Still further, the Commissioner had initiated proceedings under section 263 but had dropped the same accepting the claim of exemption made by the assessee. The provisions of section 11 were, thus, attracted and the Tribunal had rightly held that the assessee was entitled to exemption thereunder. [Para 23] Under section 11(1)(a), the income derived from property held under trust only for charitable or religious purpose is exempt to the extent of its utilization for that purpose. However, wherever there is accumulation or setting aside for application to such purposes in India, the accumulation or setting apart is not to be in excess of twenty-five per cent of the income from such property. However, this has been reduced to fifteen per cent by the Finance Act, 2002 with effect from 1-4-2003.

According to section 11(4A), an exemption is permissible where the activities are incidental to the attainment of the objectives of the trust and separate books of account are maintained by the trust or the institution in respect of such business. The Tribunal recorded that the only activity of the assessee was running newspaper to attaint the main object of promoting Punjab, Punjabi and Punjabiat and the conditions of section 11(4A) are thus, automatically stood satisfied.

However, the Commissioner (Appeals) had recorded that there was net income of Rs. 22,99,905 from publication of newspaper and there was nothing to show that this amount had been utilized for charitable purpose for claiming exemption under section 11. The Tribunal while allowing the appeal of the assessee had not adverted to this aspect with reference to any material on record. [Para 30]

Coming to the objection relating to non-compliance of provisions of section 13(1)(c) read with section 13(3), according to these provisions, wherever, any part of income or any property of the trust or the institution is applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person referred to in sub-section (3) of section 13, the provisions of section 11 shall not operate granting benefit of exemption to the trust. The Assessing Officer had recorded that certain payments were made to trustee and his relatives falling under section 13(3) and as such were inadmissible. These findings were affirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) on appeal. However, the Tribunal had reversed these findings primarily on the ground that there is no finding that these payments were excessive.

The Tribunal while reversing these findings had not recorded any definite and clear finding relating to violation of the provisions of section 13(3). The matter, thus, requires to be remanded to the Tribunal to readjudicate the claim of the assessee for exemption of income under section 11 with reference to provisions of section 13(3) in the light of the observations made hereinbefore. [Para 32]

In view of the above, the case is remanded to the Tribunal to readjudicate the issue relating to exemption claimed under section 11 with reference to provisions of section 11(1)(a) and also to examine the question of admissibility of deduction in respect of payments made to certain persons in terms of section 13(1)(c) read with section 13(3).

The appeal are disposed of in the above terms. [Para 34]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) – Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under – Assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56 – Claim of assessee trust for exemption of its income under section 4(3)(i) was rejected by ITO on ground that business of trust carried on by managing trustee on behalf of trust fell within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and hence its business income was not exempt from taxation – Whether where trust carries on business and business itself is held in trust and income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for purpose of religious or charitable character, conditions prescribed under section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and income is exempt from taxation - Held, yes – Whether claim of exemption cannot be denied even if business were to be conducted by someone else acting on behalf of trust, and proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to such businesses as are not held under trust and, therefore, field of its operation is distinct and separate from that covered by main provision of section 4(3)(i) – Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, assessee being a religious and charitable trust, was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act for assessment years in question – Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a religious and charitable trust was founded by K under a deed of trust. The founder furnished the trust with a nucleus fund to be augmented and utilised for the purpose of the trust. A business in cotton yarn and cloth was started by the board of trustees or the managing trustee of the said trust. For the assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56, the assessee submitted returns showing nil income and claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) in respect of the income from the business carried on by the trust.

The ITO, however, denied the exemption to the said business income, from taxation, and completed the assessments.

The view of the ITO was that the income from the business of the trust which was carried on by the managing trustee on behalf of the trust would fall within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and would not be covered by the main provision of section 4(3)(i), and that the necessary conditions required to be fulfilled for the operation of the proviso (b) were not present.

On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's orders and observed that it was not the trust or the institution, which was carrying on the business from which the income was earned, that the business was carried on by the managing trustee on behalf of the trust, and that therefore the application of section 4(3)(i) was excluded by the operation of proviso (b) to that section. The Tribunal, on second appeal, also confirmed the assessments.

On reference :

HELD: A cursory perusal of the terms of the deed would show that the managing trustee was the heart and soul of the trust. The terms of the trust deed expressly provided for the trust funds being employed in any trade, industry or business, which meant that the trust could carry on the business just like an individual or a firm or a limited company. It was not the contention of the department that the trust was a mere fiction or that it was illusory. Thus, a valid trust had been constituted and the trust carried on the business during the relevant accounting years.

It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

HEADNOTE: Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Related party transaction) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-trust operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital - In order to address financial difficulties faced by assessee, it entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) involved in healthcare sector, for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to SCPL - In return, assessee would receive either a fixed amount of Rs. 1 crore or 40 per cent of SCPL's profit, whichever was higher, as management fees - Assessing Officer was of view that said agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for benefit of related parties - Consequently, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied - It was noted that object of transfer agreement with SCPL was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally, and in doing so, purpose of charity was not violated as a reputed hospital of such huge size required professional handling - Further, agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable property to SCPL but to counter huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals - Whether, on facts, there was no infirmity in order of Commissioner (Appeals) in allowing exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-trust was registered under section 12A(a) and operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital and a medical college. Due to financial difficulties, the assessee entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) for the transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of the hospital to SCPL. In return, the assessee would receive either a fixed amount or a percentage of SCPL''s profit as management fees. The assessee had incurred heavy debts and faced a negative net worth. The agreement was seen as a means to ensure the assessee''s survival and continued charitable activities, as SCPL took over the hospital''s operations and liabilities.

■

The Assessing Officer scrutinized the agreement and found that it violated the basic principles of charity for which the trust had been granted registration under section 12AA. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for the benefit of related parties. Consequently, the trust''s claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied. The Assessing Officer also reclassified the Trust''s income as that of an Association of Persons (AOP), which would only be allowed to deduct its expenditures.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal by revenue to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The issue under consideration has been decided by the Tribunal in favour of the assessee in earlier year’s orders and also by the recent order passed by the ITAT Ahmedabad in the assessee’s own case for assessment year 2016-17 in ITA No. 416/Ahd/2020 vide order dated 20-07-2022 wherein the Tribunal held that the agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable to SCPL but to counter the huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals. Therefore, the Commissioner(Appeals) has correctly held that the activity of the trust was carried on in accordance with its objects and in the best interest of charity, therefore, the exemption under section 11(1)(a) has rightly been allowed by the Commissioner(Appeals). Similarly, the Commissioner(Appeals) has clearly held that section 13((1)(c)(ii) could apply only if any part of the charitable income of the trust has been used or applied for the benefits of the said persons during the previous year. But, since no portion of the income of the assessee has been applied for said person, therefore, the case of the assessee fell outside the scope of this section. Further, the trust is in receipt of income by way of management charges from SCPL and also all of its liabilities have been taken over by the same therefore there is a fact that there is no undue benefits of the use of trust property have been taken by any other persons. Similarly, there is no diversion of income of the trust as per Explanation of section13(2)(d) and 13(2)(g) as the trust has been benefitted greatly and its deficit of trust duly reduced to a great extent. Thus, the Commissioner(Appeals) has analyzed the facts correctly and given a judicious finding which does not call for any interference from outside. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 64 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 16(3) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Transfer of assets - For benefit of spouse, etc. - Assessment year 1957-58 - Assessee by a settlement deed created a trust for benefit of his minor daughter - Settlement provided that when minor attained age of 21 years, trust property would vest absolutely in her and she would become entitled to receive income from settled immovable property in her own right - Managing trustees contributed trust money as capital to firm to join partnership and received share of profits in firm - ITO taking view that section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act did not speak of actual receipt of income but only of income arising and as income had arisen from firm, held that it was taxable in assessee’s hands - Tribunal, however, set aside ITO’s order - Whether in view of decision of Supreme Court in CIT v. Manilal Dhanji [1962] 44 ITR 876, it could be said that income derived by managing trustee was not taxable in hands of assessee either under section 16(1)(c) or section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, order passed by Tribunal was correct - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee settled upon trust a certain sum and some immovable property by a deed of settlement with a view to make provisions for his minor married daughter, ‘J’. The settlement provided, inter alia, for the investment of the trust moneys in any trade, commerce, etc., at the discretion of the trustees and with the consent of the settlor and for the collection of rents from immovable properties entitled upon trust. The deed also provided that the trust would cease to operate when the minor attained the age of 21 from when the trust property would vest absolutely in her, she would become entitled to receive the income from the settled immovable properties in her own right and to dispose of at her sole discretion the amount remaining in the hands of the trustees, out of the funds settled upon trust. The managing trustee contributed trust money as capital to the firm to join the partnership and received his share of profits in the firm. The ITO found that the share of income from the firm had been credited in the account of the trust in the books of accounts of the firm and so it had arisen to the trust during the year of account. Therefore, he held that of section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act did not speak of actual receipt of income but only of income arising and, as income had arisen from the firm, it was taxable in the assessee’s hands and that the minor had a right to use the trust funds and it did not matter that in fact she did not receive it. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal, however, held that section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act could not be applied because the provisions of the trust deed could not be read as authorising the receipt of any income or deriving any benefit by the minor.

On reference :

HELD: The Supreme Court in CIT v. Manilal Dhanji [1962] 44 ITR 876 : held that when section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act talks of benefit of the minor child it refers to benefit which arises or accrues to the minor in the year of account. If there be no such benefit, the income cannot be included in the total income of the individual who made the transfer. The Supreme Court further held that when, however, the minor child derives no benefit under the trust deed in the year of account, it is not consistent with the scheme of section 16 of 1922 Act to say even though there is no accrual of any income or benefit in the year of account in favour of the minor child, yet the income must be included in the total income of the individual concerned.

In the light of the decision of the Supreme Court the income derived by managing trustee was not taxable in the hands of the assessee either under section 16(1)(c) or 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

■ A perusal of section 13 would indicate that if the assessee society has availed the services or purchased any object from any specified person contemplated in sub-clause (3) and paid to such specified person in excess of what may be paid reasonably for such service in open market, then excess would be disallowed. In other words, for example, if assessee society has availed the services of an Engineer who happened to be a specified person under sub-clause (3) and paid him the service charges which he could not command in the open market, then such excess amount will be disallowed to the assessee and benefit of Section 11 would not be available on such an amount. Similarly, it has provided traveling facility to them which was only for fulfilling the objects of the Society. In other words, in assessment year 2015-16, a little higher amount is being incurred by the assessee because the member of the Management Committee has to travel outside India for inspection of a plane which was to be used in Aviation Wing of the Engineering College. The Assessing Officer has not examined this aspect as to how this type of facilities can be availed from the open market and the price of such services. He has simply narrated that these persons are gainfully implied in their other activities also and therefore, payment of honorarium to these persons is not in accordance with law. This cannot be a logic for denying the benefit to them. The intention of the section is not as such. It is the assessee who has to manage its affairs and to decide what is necessary for its functioning. The Assessing Officer can only examine whether excess is being paid or not, but he has not carried out any Investigation in that area. The Assessing Officer has not assigned any reason as to why he is departing from the principle of consistency where such honorarium has been allowed to these per sons. Similarly Traveling Expenses has been allowed to the assessee in earlier years. The Commissioner (Appeals) failed to record any finding qua this aspect in right perspective and blindly up held the assessment order. Therefore, all these grounds of appeal are allowed.[Para 12.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from properties held under - Assessment year 1956-57 - By an indenture of trust, ‘D’ and his wife both doctors, settled upon trust an immovable property and two maternity hospitals which were run by them - Primary object of trust was to carry on and promote educational, health, cultural, social and economic interest of people particularly of backward and lower classes - Substance of indenture of trust itself was that all trust properties were transferred by both settlers to trustees and trustees made declaration that they would hold properties for objects of trust from date of deed - One of recitals clearly indicated that it was business of conducting two maternity homes that had been settled upon trust, because net annual income which was to accrue to trust from said hospitals to be arrived at after deducting all expenses for maintaining and running hospitals and after making payment to ‘D,’ s wife as provided in trust deed for managing said hospitals for and on behalf of trust during her lifetime - Whether as trust deed was duly registered it was sufficient in law to effect a valid transfer - Held, yes - Whether since business of running and conducting maternity homes itself was settled upon trust, conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act were fulfilled and, hence income from maternity homes was exempt from taxation - Held, yes - Whether for conducting maternity hospitals presence of a doctor was essential and therefore, amount paid to wife of ‘D’ was a part of normal expenditure of conducting and managing said hospitals which was allowable as admissible deduction in computation of income of trust in hands of trustees as association of persons - Held, yes

FACT: By an indenture of trust dated 23-8-1954, one ‘D’ and his wife settled upon trust two maternity hospitals which were run by them and an immovable property for the purposes and objects contained in the said deed of trust. The assessee were the trustees under the said trust. The primary object of the trust was to carry on and promote the educational, health, cultural, literary, social and economic interests of the people, particularly of the backward and poorer classes. The important recitals in the trust deed were to the effect that the net annual income from the said hospitals, after deducting all the expenses for maintaining and running the hospitals including a sum of Rs. 750 per month which should be paid regularly to ‘D’s wife for managing the said hospitals for and on behalf of the trust during her lifetime, should accrue to the trust from year to year and that Dr. Divekar and Dr. Nalini Divekar did transfer the above said property and both the hospitals to the Trustees. And that the monies and properties of the trust were to be applied, firstly in payment of the expenses of carrying out of the trust and then in carrying out the other objects. The assessee claimed exemption under section 43(1)(i) of the 1922 Act. Even though the ITO accepted that the business in maternity homes was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act, he however took the view that its income was not exempt under the said section because it did not fulfil the requirements of proviso (b) thereto. This view was arrived at by him because he took the view that the primary purpose in conducting or running the two maternity homes or hospitals was not to give free medical facilities but charge the patients and then to apply the income for certain objects. Even the amount paid to D’s wife claimed as a deduction was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that the same was paid by the association of persons to one of its own members.

On appeal, the AAC held that the income from the trust was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and that the salary paid was an allowable deduction in computation of the assessees’ income.

On revenue’s further appeal, the Tribunal took the view that there was no actual transfer of immovable properties to the trustees if regard be had to the language employed in the document. On the assumption that the properties were considered to have been managed on behalf of a charitable institution the Tribunal took the view that the conditions laid down in proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) were not satisfied in the case and the income was, therefore, not exempt from tax.

It, however, affirmed the finding of the AAC that salary to ‘D’s wife was an allowable deduction.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One 'S' and four persons, who were holding certain securities for charity purpose, executed a deed of declaration of trust - As per trust deed, trustees would give preference to poor and indigent relations or members of family of 'S' including therein distant and collateral relations - Whether since trust had been mainly formed for charitable purposes, mere provision for giving preference to poor and indigent relations or family members of 'S' did not affect validity of trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income from trust properties invested in securities was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: One 'S' and four others were holding certain securities for the purpose of charity and had been applying the same for and towards charitable purposes, executed, on 8-6-1922, a deed of declaration of trust declaring that the said trust fund would be held by them on trusts more specifically therein mentioned. Clause 13 of trust deed provided that the trust fund would be held by the trustees upon the trusts to apply the net income thereof after providing for all necessary expenses in relation to the management of the trust funds, for all or any of the following purposes (a) the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of jewish (b) the institution, maintenance and support of hospitals and schools, colleges or other educational institutions or (c) the relief of any distress caused by the elements of nature such as famine, pestilence, fire, tempest, flood, earthquake or any other such calamity or (d) the care and protection of animals useful to mankind or (e) the advancement of religion or (f) other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the foregoing purposes. The trust deed further provided that the trustees would give preference to the poor and indigent relations or members of the family of the said 'S' including there in distant and collateral relations. The trust fund had been invested by the trustees in inter alia 3½ per cent Government securities. In the year 1930, a certificate was issued by the ITO, whereby the Reserve Bank of India was authorized not to deduct at source the tax on the said securities so held by the trustees. For the assessment years 1948-49 and 1949-50, the ITO took the view that the income from the trust fund was not exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act accordingly, he assessed the appellants. On appeals, the AAC and the Tribunal confirmed the assessment made by the ITO.

On reference, the High Court also held that the trust property was not held wholly for religious or charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: Under clause 13 the trustees were at liberty to hold the trust fund and to apply the net income thereof for all or any of the six purposes mentioned therein. The relations or members of the family of the said 'S' including therein distant and collateral relations did not figure as direct recipients of any benefit under sub-clauses (b) to (f) and, therefore, in so far as those purposes were concerned the trust certainly involved an element of public utility.

It was open to the trustees to spend the net income entirely for the purpose referred to in sub-clause (a) to the exclusion of the other clauses. But the very fact that the relations or members of the family did not come in directly under any of those latter sub-clauses could not be ignored, for they certainly had some bearing on the question as to who or what were the primary objects of the trust as a whole. In the next place, the purpose of sub-clause (a) was the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of 'V' or any other community.

It followed that sub-clause (a ) constituted a valid public charitable trust having as its beneficiaries the several classes of persons referred to therein.

The circumstances that in selecting the beneficiaries under sub-clause (a) preference had to be given, under the proviso, to the relations or members of the family of 'S', could not affect that public charitable trust.

Therefore, the income from the trust properties came within the scope of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and was entitled to exemption.

The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision. The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

It is true that the only section of the public that could be benefited by this bath would be the European public in Bombay but it is well settled that an object of public utility need not be an object in which the whole of the public is interested. It is sufficient if a well defined section of the public benefits by the object, and the object of the trust in the instant case was to benefit clearly a defined section of the public living in Bombay. Now, on a casual consideration of the matter it may strike one that the most essential element of charity is to render service to the public without any charge or remuneration, but, it is clear on the authorities that the eleemosynary element is not an essential element of charity. A settlor or a donor may make a charity by setting up an institution and also providing funds by which those who take advantage of the institution can do so without paying any charge or one may have a case where the charity may not go to those limits and one may confine his charity to merely setting up the institution and providing that those who wish to take advantage of the institution must pay reasonable charges for the same. In both cases the setting up of the institution would be a charitable object if the institution serves a purpose of general public utility. The only essential factor to determine whether it is a charity or not would be whether there is any private gain by the setting up of the institution. If the gain derived by running the institution continues to be impressed with the trust which is a charitable trust, then it is immaterial whether the institution is run as a commercial institution or not, but if in the running of the institution profits are made and the profit goes to any private individual or if the institution is intended for any private gain, then undoubtedly the running of the institution could not be considered as being run for a charitable object.

Section 4(3)(ia) would only apply to an activity which was not an integral activity of the trust itself. If the trustees carried on a business which was not part of the property of the trust, then only that income of the business would be exempt from taxation which was applied solely to the purposes of the institution. If such a business made a profit, and only part was spent for religious or charitable institution and the other part was kept in surplus or in reserve, then the part which was kept in surplus or reserve would be liable to tax. Therefore, the Legislature, as far as section 4(3)(ia ) was concerned, looked upon a business falling under this sub-section as something independent of the trust itself; and looking upon that business as something independent of the trust itself; it naturally wanted to tax the income of that business to the extent that, that income was not applied solely to the purposes of the charitable or religious institution. If one takes this view of section 4(3)(i) and 4(3)(ia), then no difficulty would be experienced in the way of the trustees who were carrying on the activity as a part of the trust itself and which activity made profits which the trusts may keep in reserve in order to strengthen the financial position of the institution. As such income would fall under first part of section 4(3)(i ), no question could then arise of that income being necessarily applied for the purposes of the institution in order to earn exemption under section 4(3)(ia).

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1946-47 – Founders of assessee-press created a trust in respect of assessee-press and a weekly paper published by it – Clause (2) of trust deed provided that trust Committee could not change policy of paper which at its inception was published in its first issue and which in political matters was according to aims and objects of Indian National Congress – Policy article of paper as published in its first issue made it quite clear that paper was not brought into existence to maintain, support, protect or oppose any particular association, organization, person or creed and that would include Congress organization, but aimed at good of all mankind and good of India and putting down of evils in general and encouragement of catholicity and of all those aspects of life which an educated person would like to see encouraged - Whether policy of paper was aimed at supplying to Province an organ of educated public opinion, and to encourage all that would lead to progress of India as a part of progress of mankind, which was a charitable object – Held, yes – Whether therefore, income of assessee was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act – Held, yes

FACT: 'S' and 'G' started the assessee-press and a weekly paper. By a deed the aforementioned persons created a trust in respect of the assessee press and the weekly paper. The trust deed provided in clause that the Trust Committee could not change the policy of the papar, which at its inception was published in its first issue and which would be published in the first issue of every year and which in political matters was according to the aims and objects of the Indian National Congress. The first issue of the paper stated that the ultimate aim of the weekly paper was the good of all mankind and that a very important and indispensable way to achieve that aim was the progress of India by the development of agriculture, trade, knowledge, art, prosperity, self-respect, power, good conduct and character. Other requirements of progress were also set out, namely, national unity, propagation of a well organised, popular and comprehensive education of right policies of good and efficient administration conducive to the welfare of the people, prevention of social evils and persecutions, encouragement of propagation of self-dependence and strong faith in self-rule.

In respect of its income for the relevant previous year, the assessee claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act on the ground that the income was of a trust which was wholly for religious or charitable purposes. The revenue authorities rejected said claim and held that the objects were firstly vague and ambiguous and secondly were neither religious nor charitable within the meaning of section 4(3)(i).

On reference:

HELD: The charitable object of the trust in the instant case was that of supplying to the Province an organ of educated public opinion. Moreover clause (2) did not state that the policy in political matters of the paper would be the policy from time to time of the Indian National Congress. What the policy would be was determined by the policy article once and for all and the policy therein was described as being in accord with the then policies and objects of the Indian National Congress. Clause (2) did not imply that the paper would become the propaganda machinery of the Indian National Congress and would further the views from time to time of the Indian National Congress. The second part of clause (2 ) was merely descriptive, so far as political matters were concerned, of the policy article. On examining the policy article carefully, it was quite clear that the paper was not brought into existence to maintain, support, protect or oppose any particular association, organisation, person or creed and that would include the Congress organisation. A paper which aims at carrying out such a policy as was to be the policy of the paper in question and aims at the good of all mankind and the good of India and the putting down of evils in general and the encouragement of catholicity and of all those aspects of life which an educated person would like to see encouraged , must clearly intend to be an organ of educated public opinion. No doubt at places such sentiments as a strong faith in self-rule or faith in the intentions of the British Government and the desire to raise the status of Indians everywhere were mentioned. But it did not appear that the paper had a political battle cry or object, or was founded in order to further particular political, social, economic or other programmes. But the aim was to encourage all that would lead to the progress of India as a part of the progress of mankind.

The policy article of the paper was expressly mentioned in clause (2) and there was no reason why it should not be deemed to have become a part of the deed of trust.

Clause (i) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 1922 Act deals with income derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation for religious or charitable purposes, while clause (ia) deals with income derived from business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution. The two clauses, therefore, do not necessarily overlap. Clause (i) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 1922 Act, applies to cases where the business itself is held under trust for religious or charitable purposes, while clause (ia) applies only to such business as is carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution which was not held under trust.

The Sabha, was clearly an institution having been brought about to effect the purpose and to carry out the objects for which the trust was founded. The word "applied" in clause means actually spent while, in clause (i) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act, the words used are "income applied or finally set the words "finally set apart" had not been repeated in clause(ia) at that sub-section. The word "applied" did not necessarily mean "spent". Even if it has been earmarked and allocated for the purposes of the institution, it may, be deemed to have been applied for its purposes. Neither the word "applied" nor the word "institution" is of any importance in this case, the case was governed by income from the property held under trust as laid down in section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

Therefore, it was held that the bhents (offerings) vested in the Sabha under a legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes of the Sabha but the bhents could not be said to be income derived from property under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act. They would properly come under clause (ii) of that sub-section meaning thereby that they were income of a religious or charitable institution derived from voluntary contributions and applicable solely to religious or charitable purposes.

Further, the income derived from industrial and commercial concerns was the income from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes and was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and it was, therefore, not necessary to apply to such income section 4(3)(ia) of the 1922 Act.

Note:The case was decided against the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1952-53 to 1956-57 - Whether where business in kuries was held by assessee under a trust for religious or charitable purpose income derived from such business would be exempt from tax under provisions of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee company was a charitable trust one of its objects being to raise funds by conducting kuries with the company as the foreman; receiving donations and subscriptions; and by such other means as the company deemed fit. For the assessment years 1952-53 to 1956-57, the assessee claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act in respect of its income from kuries business. The ITO was of the view that the trust was of a charitable character but was covered under proviso to section 4(3)(i). On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the opinion of the department.

On reference :

HELD: It is settled law that a business itself can be held under trust for religious or charitable purposes and that the income derived from such a business will fall within the ambit of the exclusion granted by section 4(3) (i ) of the 1922 Act.

In the instant case, the business in kuries itself was held under trust for religious or charitable purposes and this was abundantly clear from the memorandum of association. The first object of the assessee was to raise funds by conducting kuries with the company as the foreman; receiving donations and subscriptions; and by such other means as the company deemed fit. Hence, the proviso to section 4(3)(i) was not attracted and the assessee trust was entitled to the exemption under section 4(3)(i ) as amended by Act 25 of 1953 in respect of its income derived from business in kuries.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HELD: A charitable purpose may be served in more than one way. VR and SV have been appointed for a period of 5 years. The terms of employment provides for payment of salary and other allowances. He, therefore, rejected exemption claimed under section 11 and taxed income at maximum marginal rate as per proviso to section 164(2). [Para 13] The provisions of section 13(1)(c) imposed certain restriction on utilization of income of the trust which claims exemption under section 11. As per clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 13, if any part of income or any property of the trust or the institution, is used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person referred in sub-section (3), then the trust is not entitled to exemption under section 11. The specified persons has been referred to under section 13(3), and as per said section the persons specified are the 'author' or 'founder' of the trust, their relatives, any trustee of the trust or manager by whatever name called. The provisions of section 164(2), states that in a case, where the whole or any part of the relevant income is not exempt under section 11 or section 12 by virtue of the provisions contained in clause (c) or clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 13, tax shall be charged on the relevant income or part of relevant income at the maximum marginal rate. Therefore, if the trust allows any benefit to interested persons, then only that part of the income which is in violation of section13(1)(c) is chargeable to tax at the maximum marginal rate of tax; but not whole income of the trust. In view of the clear provisions of the Act, it is clear that in case there is violation referred to under section 13(1)(c), then tax can be charged on such income which violates the provisions of section 13(1)(c); but not whole income of the trust. Denial of exemption under section 11 should be restricted to the extent of income, which is in violation of section 13(1)(c) and 13(1)(d). In this case, the Assessing Officer has levied tax on total income of the trust at maximum marginal rate, contrary to settled position of law. Therefore, the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) were erred in rejecting exemption claimed under section 11 to total income of the trust. [Para 14]

Having said so, lets examine that whether under the given facts and circumstances of the case is there any violation of provisions of section 13(1)(c), and the Assessing Officer was right in denying the benefit of exemption claimed under section 11. The Assessing Officer has considered advances given to KVR and SV under section 13(3)(cc) and held that said loans are clearly in the nature of direct/indirect benefit of trust income/property to persons referred to in section 13(3). The provisions contained in section 13(1)(c) put a restriction on persons referred to in section 13(3) to take any benefit of either income or property of the trust. Therefore, in order to consider any payments to any person under section 13(1)(c), it is essential to see whether the income/property of the trust is directly or indirectly used or applied for the benefit of trustees. In this case, there was no such finding from the Assessing Officer that the income was used or applied for the benefit of trustees. and cross-subsidisation models to sustain their operations. If the mere existence of substantial receipts or premium facilities were to become a disqualifying factor, a large number of institutions historically recognised as charitable would be rendered vulnerable to cancellation of registration. The Tribunal finds no indication that Parliament intended such a result. On the contrary, the legislative scheme appears to encourage the creation and maintenance of institutions capable of delivering high-quality charitable services rather than penalising them for achieving operational excellence. [Para 110]

■ The Tribunal also finds that the CIT(E) has attached considerable significance to the magnitude of receipts and financial resources available with the institution. Here again, the reasoning appears to overlook the structure of section 11 itself. As already discussed, section 11 does not prohibit earning of income. It postulates income. The statute is concerned not with the quantum of income but with its application. A trust holding substantial property may derive substantial income. A large hospital may generate substantial receipts. A university may possess extensive assets and receive considerable contributions. None of these circumstances, by themselves, destroy the charitable character of the institution. What the law examines is whether such income remains dedicated to the charitable purposes for which the institution exists. In the present case, the Tribunal finds no finding by the CIT(E) that the income of the trust has ceased to be applied towards healthcare activities or that it has been diverted for private enrichment. The absence of such a finding is of considerable significance. [Para 111]

■

The financial analysis undertaken by the CIT(E) also appears to proceed on the assumption that surplus and profit motive are synonymous. This proposition stands directly contradicted by the consistent line of authorities rendered by the Supreme Court. In Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association (supra), the Court recognised that surplus arising incidentally from carrying out charitable activities does not alter the charitable character of the institution. Similar principles were reiterated in Aditanar Educational Institution (supra) and Queen's Educational Society (supra), where the Court emphasised that the decisive test lies not in the existence of surplus but in its destination. If the surplus is ploughed back into the institution and utilised for advancement of its charitable objects, it does not become profit in the commercial sense. The impugned order, however, frequently uses expressions such as 'surplus', 'large receipts' and 'financial strength' as though these facts are self-evident indicators of commerciality. Such an approach is inconsistent with the settled jurisprudence governing charitable institutions. [Para 112]

■

The Tribunal also finds considerable merit in the assessee's contention that the CIT(E) has not adequately distinguished between operational receipts and philanthropic support. The material placed before the Tribunal indicates that the institution has received donations, contributions and earmarked funds intended for charitable purposes and development of healthcare infrastructure. Such receipts cannot be equated with commercial profits. A charitable institution which receives substantial donations does not become less charitable because it possesses financial resources. Indeed, philanthropic support is often a hallmark of public confidence in the institution's charitable mission. The treatment of such receipts as indicators of commerciality therefore appears conceptually unsound. Equally, designated funds, earmarked contributions and statutory allocations cannot automatically be treated as unrestricted surplus available for private gain. The assessee has demonstrated that it has suffered deficit from its medical operation from FY 2021-22 to FY 2024-25 and is funded by philanthropic support. Hence the observation of CIT(E) that the assessee has earned huge surplus is factually incorrect. [Para 113]

■

The CIT(E) has also relied upon the size of the organisation, the number of employees and the structured nature of hospital administration. The Tribunal is unable to subscribe to the proposition that professional management and organisational sophistication are indicative of commercial character. A tertiary care hospital handling thousands of patients annually cannot function without a large workforce, detailed protocols, administrative systems, compliance mechanisms and specialised departments. The existence of such systems demonstrates operational necessity rather than profit motive. If efficiency and organisation are treated as evidence against charity, then the law would paradoxically reward inefficiency and penalise excellence. Such a conclusion would be wholly inconsistent with both logic and legislative intent. [Para 114]

The business in katha came into existence in the year 1972 and the production unit started production on 8-2-1973. Thus, the katha business was not even in the contemplation of the settlors and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. [Para 19] The test which emerged from the decision of the Apex Court in the case of J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 is that the business, if it is to be considered as property held under trust, should have been either acquired with the help of the fund originally settled upon trust or the original fund that was settled upon trust must have a substantial and real connection with the later acquisition or carrying on of the business by the trustees. The facts of the present case do not measure up to the test. The fund originally settled upon trust was a meagre amount of Rs. 2,100 at the time of the creation of the trust on 8-9-1971. It is undisputed that the katha unit was set up in the year 1972 with the aid and assistance of the borrowed amounts, the borrowings being both from the concerns in which the settlors/trustees held substantial interest and from commercial banks. There is thus,no nexus or integration between the amount originally settled upon trust and the later setting up and conduct of the katha business. Moreover, the distinction between the original trust fund and the later commencement of the business with the help of the borrowed funds should be kept in mind in the context of ascertaining whether the particular katha business was even in the contemplation of the settlors of the trust. It is difficult to view the original settlement of Rs. 2,100 upon trust and the setting up of the katha business as part of an integrated scheme even apart from the fact that the business was not acquired or carried on with the help of the original trust fund. [Para 20]

It is also significant that section 11(1) starts with the expression 'subject to the provisions of sections 60 to 63……….'. These sections find place in Chapter V. Section 60 provides for the consequences of a transfer of income where there is no transfer of assets. It says that where a person transfers merely the income from an asset without transferring the asset itself, he would continue to be chargeable to income-tax. Section 61 provides for the consequences of a revocable transfer of assets and says that the same would be the position where a person is in receipt of income by virtue of a revocable transfer of assets. Section 62 provides for the consequences of a transfer of assets for specified period. It is an exception to section 61. Generally a person has to get rid of the asset itself before ceasing to be assessable in respect of the income from that asset. A mere direction that the income from the business shall be applied to the charitable objects of the trust, without there being a settlement of the business itself upon trust, does not result in any trust or legal obligation. [Para 21]

There is no connection between the carrying on of the katha business and the attainment of the objects of the trust, which are basically for the advancement of education, inculcation of patriotism, Indian culture, running of dispensaries hospitals, etc. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from katha business is ear-marked for application to the charitable objects would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The Commissioner (Appeals) in his order for the assessment year 1992-93 has rightly taken the view that the application of the income generated by the business is not the relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. The examples, appositely given by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order, clarify the position: the instance of a charitable trust established for providing medical relief running a nursing home in the process, or a trust for advancement of education running a publishing house or a newspaper. [Para 22]

In view of the above, the assessee-trust was not entitled to exemption under section 11.

HEADNOTE: Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether where a part of trust income was being used directly or indirectly for benefit of its founder and managing director, which came within prohibited category referred to in section 13(3), exemption under section 11 was not available in view of violation of clause (ii)(c) of section 13(1), read with section 13(3) - Held, yes

Section 10(22A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Exemption - Income of hospital - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether where ‘P’ who was managing trustee and also founder director had participated in profit to extent of 50 per cent of income of trust and it had not been shown by trust that it had been utilised or appropriated towards expansion and development of hospital or to start any other institution with philanthropic objects, it could be said that philanthropic objectives were frustrated - Held, yes - Whether therefore, assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 10(22A) - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a registered charitable trust, was running a Skin Institute which was providing medical facility in the field of skin and also carried out research fully recognised by the Board and offered courses of dermatology. The patients were divided into three categories, being free category, subsidised category and paying category. No consultation fees was charged from free category patients. The assessee-trust filed a return for the assessment year 1992-93 declaring nil income claiming exemption under section 10(22)/11. The Assessing Officer observed that 50 per cent of income generated by the trust was given to Dr. ‘P’, founder and managing trustee, and that the assessee denied to have received any donation, whereas in the profit and loss account it had claimed to have received donation, which in fact was sale proceeds of the medicines. The Assessing Officer denied exemption claimed by the assessee. On appeal, the assessee contended that Dr. ‘P’ had no income from trust except that he was charging 50 per cent of the income for rendering medical services to the trust, but he was not charging anything for managerial or administrative services and it was by mistake that medicine sale proceeds had been shown as donation. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejecting the assessee’s contention, upheld the Assessing Officer’s order.

On second appeal

HELD: The category of persons mentioned in clause (ii) of sub-section (1) of section 13 are mentioned in sub-section (3) of section 13, which includes the author of the trust or the founder of the institution. Undisputedly, 50 per cent income generated by the trust was being given to Dr. P and in the assessment year under consideration certain sum paid to him was against the monthly payments given to various other Doctors by way of salary besides free transport, etc. Thus, out of the income of the trust part of such income was being used directly or indirectly for the benefit of the founder member which came within the prohibited category referred to in sub-section (3) of section 13. Therefore, in so far as exemption under section 11 was concerned, this could not be granted in view of violation of provisions of clause (ii)(c ) of sub-section (1) of section 13 read with sub-section (3) of section 13.

Section 10(22A ) provides that the income of the hospital existing only for philanthropic purposes and not for the purposes of profit is entitled to exemption. The word ‘philanthropy’ is not defined in the Act. The general meaning of the word ‘philanthropy’ includes activities promoting goodwill to mankind or activities beneficial to humanity at large as opposed to activities solely for the benefit of a few individuals. When clause 10(22A ) was added to section 10 with almost similar wording as clause (22), it would only be proper to infer that the Legislature used those words in clause (22A ) taking note of the interpretation given to those words occurring in clause (22 ).

The CBDT Circular No. 45, dated 2-9-1970—See Taxmann’s Direct Taxes Circulars 1995 edn., Vol. 3 p. 2.374 clarifies the position that hospitals and other institutions which exist solely for philanthropic purposes and not for purposes of profit will be totally exempt from tax, as in the case of universities and other educational institutions.

In order to achieve the main philanthropic objects, the hospital may do some profit earning business provided such profit is appropriated towards the expansion and development of the hospital or to start another institution with the same philanthropic objectives. If the primary purpose is philanthropic, the inclusion of some objects for earning profit for the implementation of the primary object would not alter the character of that primary object.

(E) while passing the impugned order dated 8-12-2011 cancelling the assessee's registration, applied a wrong test and examined with regard to the application of the funds, which the authority is not expected to do while considering an application for registration. Therefore, the very issuance of the show cause notice dated 25-10-2011, proposing to cancel the registration on examination of the modus of application of funds of the trust is without jurisdiction. [Para 64] In Tamil Nadu Kalvi Kapu Arakkattalai v. CIT [2014] 90 CCH 184 (Chennai), it was held that while considering the claim for exemption, the authority should not be solely guided by the objects set out in various clauses in the Instrument of Trust, rather should be guided by the activities of the Trust, as to how the funds are employed, since the exemption sought for is under Chapter III, which deals with incomes which do not form part of total income. Thus, under Chapter III, more particularly, sections 10 to 13A, the Act brings certain categories of exemption and incomes falling within those categories are completely exempt from the purview of the Act as they are not at all to be included in the total income of the assessee. Therefore, such type of exemption/s has/have to be distinguished from certain types of income which are included in the total income of the assessee, but in respect of which, statute provides relief by way of deduction in computing total income, by granting rebate of tax and by granting certain other reliefs to the taxpayers. [Para 65]

The last aspect to be considered is under what circumstances, the power under section 12AA(3) can be invoked. The said provision states that where a trust or an institution has been granted registration under clause (b) of sub-section (1) or has obtained registration at any time under section 12A and subsequently, the Commissioner is satisfied that the activities of such trust or institution are not genuine or are not being carried out in accordance with the objects of the trust or institution, as the case may be, he shall pass an order in writing cancelling the registration of such trust or registration. In terms of the proviso, no order under sub-section (3) shall be passed, unless such trust or institution has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Thus, the power under sub-section (3) of section 12AA would be invokable under two circumstances mentioned in the provision and upon the Commissioner being satisfied that the activities of the trust are not genuine or the activities are not in accordance with the objects of the trust. [Para 70]

In the case on hand, there is no allegation that the assessee trust has not carried on its activities in accordance with the objects of the trust as set out in the Deed of Trust and the Supplementary Deed. The Revenue has accepted the said fact. The DIT(E) seeks to bring the assessee's case in the first limb of sub-section (3) by stating that the activities of the trust are not genuine. [Para 71]

Except for stating that the activities are not genuine because of the amendment to the proviso to section 2(15), there is no other allegation, with regard to the genuineness of the trust. The amendment to section 2(15) cannot make activity of a trust not genuine, which was hitherto genuine while enjoying the registration under section 12AA prior to the amendment. Therefore, the DIT(E) failed to record his satisfaction as required to be done under sub-section (3) of section 12AA. The satisfaction should be on the activities of the trust and finding should be rendered as to how such activities are not genuine. The activities of the assessee trust have not been disputed, nor there is any allegation of non-genuine activities. Therefore, by referring to the amendment to the proviso to section 2(15) and referring to the meaning of the word 'education' as spelt out in certain decisions, cannot be construed to be a satisfaction, which is contemplated under sub-section (3) of section 12AA. [Para 72]

In DIT(E) v. Khar Gymkhana [2016] 70 taxmann.com 181/240 Taxman 407/385 ITR 162 (Bom.), the Court considered Circular No. 21/2016 and held that registration granted under section 12AA could not be cancelled merely on the ground the receipts on account of business exceeded the cut-off specified in the proviso to section 2(15). The jurisdiction to cancel the registration only arises if there is a change in the activity of the institution or the activities of the institution are not genuine. It was further held that Circular No. 21 of 2016 directs the Officer of Revenue not to cancel the registration only because the receipts on account of business are in excess of the limits in the proviso to section 2(15). [Para 75]

Charitable Trust [1991] 59 Taxman 602/196 ITR 31 (All.), it was held that contribution to another charitable trust is an application for charitable purposes, in other words, such contribution to another charitable trust by the assessee-trust cannot be treated as income of the assessee-trust in the year of contribution. [Para 79]

Merely because the trust had been amalgamated with other trusts with similar objects, it could not be held that the accumulated amounts had been applied for any purpose other than charitable, and it was nobody’s case that the amounts invested had ceased to be invested in the year in question. The trust had given a specific clarification and undertaking regarding the utilisation of the accumulated amount. Thus, the treatment of the accumulated income as the income of this year was not justified. The addition of Rs. 40,000 was, therefore, without any justification. The request for accumulation for the current year was made within a period of 6 months from the end of the accounting period, and it was stated that the intended amount was also deposited in fixed deposit. The resolution itself was no doubt vague, but considering the fact that in earlier years the trust was accumulating for the construction of the school building and Form No. 10 also gave the same purpose, the assessee’s request should be considered by the ITO.
