It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

There was, no doubt on the authorities that trusts for the benefit of the inhabitants of a particular locality were regarded as charitable, and that principle would apply to the inhabitants of British India. On the other hand, it was clear that trusts for the benefit of a particular political party, or for the advancement of particular political opinions, were not regarded as charitable. The objects specified in the trust deed, were clearly distributive. The whole of the trust fund could be applied for any one or more of the objects specified, and if any of those objects do not fall within the purview of the legal definition of "charity", the trust could not be regarded as a good charitable trust.

Sub-clause (a) of clause 11 of the deed of the deed includes the advancement of any purpose which might in the uncontrolled opinion of the Managing Committee be national or of national importance for the inhabitants of British India by any means which in the like opinion of the Managing Committee be constitutional. It is impossible to say that the Managing Committee might not regard purposes which were not according to law charitable, as being nevertheless of national importance for the inhabitants of British India, and the Committee might regard methods as constitutional which the law would not regard as constitutional. Assuming the objects specified in sub-clause (a) to be charitable, this was not the case of a gift for such charitable purposes as the Managing Committee may think fit. A gift of that sort would, no doubt, be good, because the Managing Committee would be bound to keep within the ambit of charity, and if they go beyond the legal boundary, they could be controlled by the Court. There are many purposes which an individual, acting quite bona fide , may regard as charitable, but which the law does not so regard. Therefore, sub-clause (a) goes too far; and sub-clause (b) goes too far also, because it was really a gift for political purposes. Assuming that the attainment of national autonomy may be regarded as a national purpose accepted generally by, and for the good of, the inhabitants of British India, there was a very keen divergence of opinion as to the methods by which that national autonomy should be attained; and it was impossible, to avoid the conclusion that a gift for the attainment of that object by such methods as the Managing Committee may approve was really a gift for political purposes. Therefore, it was impossible to say that the ITO was wrong in holding that the income of the trust did not fall within the purview of section 4(3)(i ).

Sub-clause (a) of clause 11 of the deed of the deed includes the advancement of any purpose which might in the uncontrolled opinion of the Managing Committee be national or of national importance for the inhabitants of British India by any means which in the like opinion of the Managing Committee be constitutional. It is impossible to say that the Managing Committee might not regard purposes which were not according to law charitable, as being nevertheless of national importance for the inhabitants of British India, and the Committee might regard methods as constitutional which the law would not regard as constitutional. Assuming the objects specified in sub-clause (a) to be charitable, this was not the case of a gift for such charitable purposes as the Managing Committee may think fit. A gift of that sort would, no doubt, be good, because the Managing Committee would be bound to keep within the ambit of charity, and if they go beyond the legal boundary, they could be controlled by the Court. There are many purposes which an individual, acting quite bona fide , may regard as charitable, but which the law does not so regard. Therefore, sub-clause (a) goes too far; and sub-clause (b) goes too far also, because it was really a gift for political purposes. Assuming that the attainment of national autonomy may be regarded as a national purpose accepted generally by, and for the good of, the inhabitants of British India, there was a very keen divergence of opinion as to the methods by which that national autonomy should be attained; and it was impossible, to avoid the conclusion that a gift for the attainment of that object by such methods as the Managing Committee may approve was really a gift for political purposes. Therefore, it was impossible to say that the ITO was wrong in holding that the income of the trust did not fall within the purview of section 4(3)(i ).

The first proviso to section 41(1) of the 1922 Act is perfectly plain. It provides in connection with funds held by a trust that where income, profits or gains or any part thereof are not specifically receivable on behalf of any one person, or where the individual shares of the persons on whose behalf they are receivable are indeterminate or unknown, the tax shall be levied and recoverable at the maximum rate. It may be rather hard on this trust fund that it should be charged at a higher rate than the amount of its income would attract if it belonged to an individual. But that is not a matter with which the Court can deal. It is perfectly plain that the case fell within the first proviso to section 41(1), and, therefore, the ITO was correct in levying income-tax at the maximum rate under the first proviso to section 41(1) of 1922 Act.

Concurrent view (as per Kania, J.)

In section 4(3)(i) the words used are that the income should be derived from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes. By the explanation added at the end, the term "charitable purpose" is stated to include an object of general public utility. Even so, it is for the assessee to show that his case falls within that extended meaning.

Certain propositions of law now appear to be well settled as a result of authorities. First, that when there is a general charitable intention, the Court will uphold it, and if within that limit discretion is given to the trustees to select an object the trust will not fail because of the discretion so given. If a trustee selects an object, which is not charitable according to law, the Court can intervene and rectify the error.

The objects in the trust deed have to be separately read, and if any of those objects is not charity, the whole gift must fail, because if the trustees choose to apply the whole of the fund to the particular object, which according to the law of the land is not charitable, then they will not be committing a breach of trust, and the trust could be said to be properly administered. The law does not permit the administration of a trust which can be so used entirely for a non-charitable object and hold it as charitable on construction. Therefore, clause 11 of this trust deed, which defines the objects of the trust, was not charitable within section 4(3)(i ) of 1922 Act.

The reopening cannot be sustained. This is because in the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT [2010] 103 ITR 777 (SC) the Supreme Court held that if one of the objects of the trust deed is not of a religious or charitable nature and the trust deed confers full discretion on the trustees to spend the trust funds for an object other than of a religious or charitable nature, the exemption under section 4(3)(i), of the 1922 Act is not available to assessee. If the primary or dominant purpose of a trust is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but which is merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purpose would not prevent the trust from being a valid charity. The Court also held that where in a trust deed providing for many charitable objects, the trustees were authorised to open and maintain commercial institutions where work at living wages could be provided to the poor and to contribute to commercial, technical or industrial concerns, institutions, associations or bodies imparting any type of training or providing employment to persons; and the deed gave uncontrolled discretion to the trustees to spend the whole of the trust fund on any of the non-charitable objects of the trust, then income of the trust was not exempted from tax under the said Act. There is not even an allegation that uncontrolled discretion or authority to open or maintain commercial institution was in the object of assessee. There is not even a finding to that effect. Just because there are certain receipts received by assessee while conducting its charitable activities, would not make those receipts whatever may be the quantum, to be income from commercial activities. HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Religious or charitable trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies created a trust and purported to endow it with share held by him in certain transport companies - Contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately but companies in which N was interested were to have benefit of assets set apart by him - N was managing trustee and empowered to borrow to any extent on properties conveyed to trust not only for trust but for his own use trustees were empowered, so long as N held office of managing trustee, to sell immovable properties belonging to trust for purpose of floating other companies - Foundation of institution was apparently to be left over until companies had made sufficient money for purpose - N also reserved right to revoke trust at any time - Whether on facts properties in question were not held under trust for charitable purpose within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The settlor N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies, created a trust and purported to endow it with the shares held by him in six transport companies. He constituted himself the managing trustee of the trust and gave himself full power to deal with its assets. The managing trustees claimed refund of tax paid in respect of dividends declared on the shares held in these transport companies. The income-tax authorities refused to allow a refund. Their reason was that the shares were not held under trust wholly for charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i).

On reference:

HELD: If the assets which N purported to set apart were to be devoted directly to such objects, no doubt the trust would be entitled to the refund claimed; but the deed clearly showed that the contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately and that the companies in which N was interested were to have the benefit of these assets set apart by him. Clause 54 of the deed provided that so long as N held the office of the managing trustee he shall have the power to borrow to any extent on the properties conveyed to the trust and that the board of trustees shall be able to borrow moneys which were necessary to discharge debts contracted by N. The power given to him was not limited to borrowing for the purpose of the trust. Apparently he could borrow moneys for his own purposes on the security of the assets set apart by him. By clause 55 the trustees were empowered, so long as N held the office of managing trustee, to sell immoveable properties belonging to the trust" in expanding or floating industrial institutions," in other words for the purpose of floating other companies. Clause 59 provided that the trustees may advance to the companies in which N was interested money for (a) discharging their liabilities (b) purchasing and substituting diesel or other more economical engines for the petrol engines on buses run by them and (c ) constructing passenger sheds and garages and other "amenities and facilities" for the use of the transport services "wherever the Trust is interested".

The foundation of the institution was apparently to be left over until the companies had made sufficient money for the purpose. By clause 71, 'N' reserved to himself the power to revoke the trust at any time.

In view of the provisions of the deed by which the assets could be utilised for N’s own purposes or the purposes of his companies, it was impossible for him to contend with reason that the deed created a trust wholly for charitable purposes. The idea that some day the institution contemplated by the deed might be founded was not sufficient compliance with the section.

It was said that in 1939 N made considerable alterations in the trust deed and that these alterations removed the objections now referred to. Whether the deed as it now stood created a trust which was entitled to the benefits of section 4(3)(i) was a question with which the High Court was not concerned. It was concerned only with the question whether a trust was created wholly for charitable purposes in the year of account, 1937-38, and it was obvious that this was not the case.

On reference : HELD: By the Insurance Act, 1938, a "principal agent" is defined as meaning "a person, who, not being a salaried employee of an insurer, in consideration of any commission, (i) performs any administrative and organizing functions for the insurer and (ii) procures general insurance business whether wholly or in part by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents of behalf of the insurer". Evidently a principal agent by the definition does not merely render personal service but is concerned with performing certain administrative and organizing functions and the procuring of general insurance business by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents. Such an agent by the very definition will be regarded as carrying on the business of a principal agent. He is not merely an employee engaged for rendering services of a personal nature: he is invested with the right as an agent to perform the administrative organizing functions for the insurer and to procure general insurance business by employing, directly or indirectly, insurance agents. By section 42A of the Insurance Act principal agents are required to obtain a certificate from the Controller of Insurance or an officer authorized by him entitling them to conduct the business of principal agency, and the certificate remains in operation for a period of twelve months only from the date of issue but is liable to be renewed. It is also true that under Part A of the Sixth Schedule to the Insurance Act certain terms are deemed to be included in every contract between an insurer carrying on general insurance business and a principal agent. Under clause 2 of Part A of the Sixth Schedule the principal agent has to procure or cause to be procured through insurance agents such an amount of general insurance business as will yield a gross premium income of not less than Rs. 20,000 in each calendar year. Under clause 4, in the event of the principal agent failing to comply with the requirements of clause 2 in any two successive calendar years, the contract shall, without prejudice to the provisions of clause 3, terminate on the 31st day of March immediately following the second calendar year. Under clause 3 the agency is also liable to be forfeited in the events set out in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) thereof. By clause 5 certain restriction are placed upon the principal agent but an account of these provisions, which impose certain restrictive conditions upon the principal agent it could not be said that the appointment of a principal agent gave rise to a bare service agreement and that the remuneration paid was not for the conduct of a business but for performance of personal service. The circumstance that the appointment was liable to be terminated at short notice and the agency was not permanent and was liable to be forfeited in the events set out hereinbefore would not, affect the character of the agency as business. Following the observation made by the Supreme Court in J.K. Trust's case [1957] 32 ITR 535 the principal agency conducted by the assessee was a business and, therefore, "property" within the meaning of section 4(3)(i). Being property which was capable of being settled upon trust by the deed of trust, dated 17-2-1951, it was lawfully settled upon trust for charitable purposes. The taxing authorities are primarily concerned with the question whether the income sought to be taxed in income from property, which is held on trust for religious or charitable purpose. If the business of the principal agency was transferred to the trustees under a deed of settlement, and from that business income was received, the income will fall within section 4(3)(i) and be exempt from tax in the hands of the trustees. Therefore, under the terms of appointment made with the company firm became the principal agents conducting a business and that business was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i ) and that the alteration, sometime after their appointment as principal agents, in the constitution of the from did not alter the character of the income earned in the course of the business. The income which is liable to be included in the total income of the assessee, was income derived from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution, unless that income fulfils the conditions prescribed by clause (b). The expression "such income" in the proviso refers to the income derived from property (which expression includes a business) held for religious or charitable purposes. But that did not justify the submission that the business which was referred to in clause (b) of the proviso must be business which is held for charitable or religious purposes. The business referred to in clause (b) of the proviso need not be business which is held for religious or charitable purposes, provided it is business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution.

It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

The charitable object of the trust in the instant case was that of supplying to the Province an organ of educated public opinion. Moreover clause (2) did not state that the policy in political matters of the paper would be the policy from time to time of the Indian National Congress. What the policy would be was determined by the policy article once and for all and the policy therein was described as being in accord with the then policies and objects of the Indian National Congress. Clause (2) did not imply that the paper would become the propaganda machinery of the Indian National Congress and would further the views from time to time of the Indian National Congress. The second part of clause (2 ) was merely descriptive, so far as political matters were concerned, of the policy article. On examining the policy article carefully, it was quite clear that the paper was not brought into existence to maintain, support, protect or oppose any particular association, organisation, person or creed and that would include the Congress organisation. A paper which aims at carrying out such a policy as was to be the policy of the paper in question and aims at the good of all mankind and the good of India and the putting down of evils in general and the encouragement of catholicity and of all those aspects of life which an educated person would like to see encouraged , must clearly intend to be an organ of educated public opinion. No doubt at places such sentiments as a strong faith in self-rule or faith in the intentions of the British Government and the desire to raise the status of Indians everywhere were mentioned. But it did not appear that the paper had a political battle cry or object, or was founded in order to further particular political, social, economic or other programmes. But the aim was to encourage all that would lead to the progress of India as a part of the progress of mankind.

The policy article of the paper was expressly mentioned in clause (2) and there was no reason why it should not be deemed to have become a part of the deed of trust.

The trustees could always be removed and fresh trustees could be appointed and it was always possible for the trustees to control the editorial policy and to see that it was in accord with the policy laid down in the first issue. In this case the policy was so clearly laid down that the trustees could effectively control the policy because they had clear guidance in regard to what the policy was to be. Even when clause (3) was given effect to, the policy of the founder would have to be continued to be carried out and so the purpose of providing an organ of educated public opinion, which was the real purpose behind this deed of trust, would not fail.

Therefore, income of the assessee was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i)

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Related party transaction) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-trust operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital - In order to address financial difficulties faced by assessee, it entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) involved in healthcare sector, for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to SCPL - In return, assessee would receive either a fixed amount of Rs. 1 crore or 40 per cent of SCPL's profit, whichever was higher, as management fees - Assessing Officer was of view that said agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for benefit of related parties - Consequently, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied - It was noted that object of transfer agreement with SCPL was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally, and in doing so, purpose of charity was not violated as a reputed hospital of such huge size required professional handling - Further, agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable property to SCPL but to counter huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals - Whether, on facts, there was no infirmity in order of Commissioner (Appeals) in allowing exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-trust was registered under section 12A(a) and operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital and a medical college. Due to financial difficulties, the assessee entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) for the transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of the hospital to SCPL. In return, the assessee would receive either a fixed amount or a percentage of SCPL''s profit as management fees. The assessee had incurred heavy debts and faced a negative net worth. The agreement was seen as a means to ensure the assessee''s survival and continued charitable activities, as SCPL took over the hospital''s operations and liabilities.

■

The Assessing Officer scrutinized the agreement and found that it violated the basic principles of charity for which the trust had been granted registration under section 12AA. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for the benefit of related parties. Consequently, the trust''s claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied. The Assessing Officer also reclassified the Trust''s income as that of an Association of Persons (AOP), which would only be allowed to deduct its expenditures.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal by revenue to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The issue under consideration has been decided by the Tribunal in favour of the assessee in earlier year’s orders and also by the recent order passed by the ITAT Ahmedabad in the assessee’s own case for assessment year 2016-17 in ITA No. 416/Ahd/2020 vide order dated 20-07-2022 wherein the Tribunal held that the agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable to SCPL but to counter the huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals. Therefore, the Commissioner(Appeals) has correctly held that the activity of the trust was carried on in accordance with its objects and in the best interest of charity, therefore, the exemption under section 11(1)(a) has rightly been allowed by the Commissioner(Appeals). Similarly, the Commissioner(Appeals) has clearly held that section 13((1)(c)(ii) could apply only if any part of the charitable income of the trust has been used or applied for the benefits of the said persons during the previous year. But, since no portion of the income of the assessee has been applied for said person, therefore, the case of the assessee fell outside the scope of this section. Further, the trust is in receipt of income by way of management charges from SCPL and also all of its liabilities have been taken over by the same therefore there is a fact that there is no undue benefits of the use of trust property have been taken by any other persons. Similarly, there is no diversion of income of the trust as per Explanation of section13(2)(d) and 13(2)(g) as the trust has been benefitted greatly and its deficit of trust duly reduced to a great extent. Thus, the Commissioner(Appeals) has analyzed the facts correctly and given a judicious finding which does not call for any interference from outside. [Para 6]

■

■

The principal dispute which is raised and canvassed in the instant appeal pertains to the deemed income which came into existence by virtue of the donations extended by the assessee to other charitable institutions and whether the same would still fall within the ambit of Section 11(1)(a). [Para 16]

■

The revenue take the position that once sub-clause (c) or (d) of Section 11(3) were violated, the entire amount diverted ostensibly for a non-charitable purpose would lose the benefit of accumulation. The said submission can not be sustained.[Para 17]

■

It has been repeatedly acknowledged that donations extended to other charitable institutions would meet the test of application of income for charitable purposes. Section 11(3)(c) and (d) essentially deal with situations where the income so accumulated is either not utilized or applied for a charitable purpose. It is only in such a situation that the deemed income would lose the sheen of protection of exemption which would otherwise be applicable by virtue of Section 11.[Para 18]

■

The question as to whether donations made to other charitable trusts would be hit by the provisions of section 11(3) arose for consideration of the Allahabad High Court in the case of CIT v. J.K. Charitable Trust [1991] 59 Taxman 602/[1992] 196 ITR 31. While answering the aforesaid question, the Allahabad High Court significantly observed that a charitable purpose may be served in more than one way. One is to directly contribute for the promotion of that cause; the other is to contribute money to another charitable organisation, which advances that cause. In the absence of allegations of device and/or mala fides, the amount contributed to other charitable institutions out of the income accumulated under section 11(2) is outside the mischief of section 11(3). In other words, such contribution does not amount to application of the income for purposes other than charitable or religious. [Para 20]

■

While on the subject of a charitable institution making donations to other charitable entities from out of income accumulated in terms of Section 11(2), it would also be apposite to note two Explanations which have come to be inserted in Section 11.[Para 21]

■

Explanation 2 to section 11(1) came to be inserted by Finance Act, 2017 with effect from 01-4-2018. Although the said provision would have no application to the facts of the present case and which is concerned with Assessment year 2009-10, it will be apt to take due notice of the same for the purposes of completeness.[Para 23]

■

The donations which are stated to have been made by the assessee in the present case however, would not be hit by Explanation 2, since the same applies only to amounts credited or paid to certain categories of institutions and those being in the nature of a contribution accompanied by a direction that the amounts extended would form part of the corpus of those entities. Although the donations were made out of the accumulated income, the money was retrieved within two months.[Para 24]

■

In terms of Finance Act, 2002, an Explanation also came to be appended to Section 11(2). The said Explanation gets attracted in a situation where income referable to clause (a) or (b) of Section 11(1) and so accumulated or set apart is credited or paid to institutions specified therein, not being liable to be treated as application of income for charitable or religious purposes. This Explanation too will not taint the donations which were made since, and undisputedly, the donations were made from out of the monies accumulated in terms of Section 11(2). Explanation 1 to Section 11(1), as is evident from a reading thereof applies to situations where the income applied to charitable causes falls short of 85 per cent of the income derived. Section 11(2) on the other hand constitutes a gateway which enables the charity to stave off the spectre of the income which is not applied for a charitable purpose coming to be included in the total income of the assessee.[Para 26]

HEADNOTE: Section 64 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 16(3) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Transfer of assets - For benefit of spouse, etc. - Assessment year 1957-58 - Assessee by a settlement deed created a trust for benefit of his minor daughter - Settlement provided that when minor attained age of 21 years, trust property would vest absolutely in her and she would become entitled to receive income from settled immovable property in her own right - Managing trustees contributed trust money as capital to firm to join partnership and received share of profits in firm - ITO taking view that section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act did not speak of actual receipt of income but only of income arising and as income had arisen from firm, held that it was taxable in assessee’s hands - Tribunal, however, set aside ITO’s order - Whether in view of decision of Supreme Court in CIT v. Manilal Dhanji [1962] 44 ITR 876, it could be said that income derived by managing trustee was not taxable in hands of assessee either under section 16(1)(c) or section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, order passed by Tribunal was correct - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee settled upon trust a certain sum and some immovable property by a deed of settlement with a view to make provisions for his minor married daughter, ‘J’. The settlement provided, inter alia, for the investment of the trust moneys in any trade, commerce, etc., at the discretion of the trustees and with the consent of the settlor and for the collection of rents from immovable properties entitled upon trust. The deed also provided that the trust would cease to operate when the minor attained the age of 21 from when the trust property would vest absolutely in her, she would become entitled to receive the income from the settled immovable properties in her own right and to dispose of at her sole discretion the amount remaining in the hands of the trustees, out of the funds settled upon trust. The managing trustee contributed trust money as capital to the firm to join the partnership and received his share of profits in the firm. The ITO found that the share of income from the firm had been credited in the account of the trust in the books of accounts of the firm and so it had arisen to the trust during the year of account. Therefore, he held that of section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act did not speak of actual receipt of income but only of income arising and, as income had arisen from the firm, it was taxable in the assessee’s hands and that the minor had a right to use the trust funds and it did not matter that in fact she did not receive it. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal, however, held that section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act could not be applied because the provisions of the trust deed could not be read as authorising the receipt of any income or deriving any benefit by the minor.

On reference :

HELD: The Supreme Court in CIT v. Manilal Dhanji [1962] 44 ITR 876 : held that when section 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act talks of benefit of the minor child it refers to benefit which arises or accrues to the minor in the year of account. If there be no such benefit, the income cannot be included in the total income of the individual who made the transfer. The Supreme Court further held that when, however, the minor child derives no benefit under the trust deed in the year of account, it is not consistent with the scheme of section 16 of 1922 Act to say even though there is no accrual of any income or benefit in the year of account in favour of the minor child, yet the income must be included in the total income of the individual concerned.

In the light of the decision of the Supreme Court the income derived by managing trustee was not taxable in the hands of the assessee either under section 16(1)(c) or 16(3)(b) of 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Section 11, read with section 164 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i), read with section 41(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1939-40 - Assessee trust was constituted for political advancement of India having its goal for acquisition of complete national autonomy or “Swarajya” to be obtained by all constitutional agitation or means and diffusion of political education and knowledge as to political affairs of India both in India and abroad for achievement of aforesaid goal and any object which in uncontrolled opinion of Managing Committee national or of national importance for inhabitants of British India by any means which in opinion of Managing Committee be constitutional - Objects specified in trust deed were distributive inasmuch as trusts for benefit of inhabitants of a particular locality were regarded as charitable while trusts for benefit of a particular political party, or for advancement of particular political opinions, were not regarded as charitable - Whether since whole of trust fund could be applied for any one or more of objects specified, if source of those objects did not fall within purview of legal definition of “charity”, trust could not be regarded as a good charitable trust and income of trust did not fall within purview of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether instant case fell within first proviso to section 41(1) of 1922 Act and ITO was justified in levying income-tax  at maximum rate - Held, yes

Sub-section (3) of section 13, clause (cc ) provides that any trustee of the trust or manager (by whatever name called) of the institution comes within the persons referred to in clause (c) of sub-section (1) and clause (a) of sub-section (2) for the purpose of exemption under section 11. The trust and institution referred to in section 13 are not one and the same thing and they are different entities. Clause (cc) of sub-section (3) of section 13 refers to the manager of the institution and not to the manager of the trust and in the instant case the advance had been given to the manager of the trust and not to the manager of the institution. In view of these admitted facts, no interference was called for in the order of the Tribunal.

In the instant case, it appeared from the deed of trust that one of the objects of the trust, was not for charitable or religious purposes. Item No. 4 was 'to manufacture, buy, sell and distribute pharmaceutical, medicinal, chemical, and other preparations and articles such as medicines, drugs, medical and surgical articles, preparations and restoratives of food'. It might be that most of the other objects of the trust were religious and charitable in nature but if item No. 4 was not charitable, then the conditions envisaged by section 4(3)(i) of Act, 1922 were not fulfilled and the exemption conferred by section 15B of the Act, 1922 could not be applied. Clause 5(i ) of the trust deed stated that 'the trustee shall have power to apply the whole or any part of the trust property or fund whether capital or income in or towards payment of the expenses of the trust or for or towards all or any of the purposes of the trust provided any property or money held in special trust shall be applied only for that purpose and not otherwise'. In the instant case, there was no special trust, that was to say, no particular item of property had been burdened with the performance of any specific object of the trust. It was therefore manifest that under clause 5(i ) of the trust deed it was open to the trustees to utilise the income for any one of the objects of the trust to the exclusion of all other objects. In other words, it would not be a violation of the trust if the trustees devoted the entire income to the carrying on of a business of manufacture, sale and distribution of pharmaceutical, medicinal and other preparations. Therefore that particular object of the trust was neither charitable nor religious in character. If the trustees could under a trust held validly, spend the entire income of the trust on this non-charitable object, it was difficult to hold that the trust property was held under a trust or other legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the Act, 1922.

Having regard to the language of paragraph 2 of the trust deed in the context of other paragraphs of the document, the trust deed, on a proper interpretation, gave an absolute power of selection to the trustees to choose between charitable and non-charitable objects of the trust for spending the entire income of the trust properties. It followed that the trust did not fulfil the conditions imposed by section 4(3)(i) of the Act, 1922 and the donation made by the assessee to the trust could not therefore be exempted under section 15B of the Act, 1922.

The contention of the appellants that the question whether section 4(3)(i) applied to the trust was not within the scope of the question referred to the High Court by the Appellate Tribunal or that the High Court went beyond its jurisdiction in answering that question could not be accepted. In CIT v. Scindia Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. [1961] 42 ITR 589, it was held that even where a question of law was not raised before the Tribunal but the Tribunal dealt with it, it must be deemed to be one arising out of its order. Applying the principle to the instant case, it was to be held that the High Court was within its jurisdiction in examining the question whether the trust was eligible for exemption from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of the Act, 1922.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The assessee-trust was empowered by its clause 2(k) to apply the income of the trust for "the advancement of any other object or general public utility as the trustees may, in their absolute discretion, deem fit and in such way as they may consider most advantageous to the recipients". For the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74, the ITO held that the donations made by the assessee-trust to other charitable trusts were hit by section 11(3). The Tribunal, however, held that such donations were not hit by section 11(3).

A trust deriving income from a property held under trust for charitable or religious purposes is not included in its total income if such income is applied for charitable purposes in India. The income of trusts and institutions is exempt under Section 11/12, provided a minimum of 85% of the income is utilised during the year for charitable or religious purposes. These trusts and institutions can accumulate 15% of their income annually. The mandatory 85% utilisation can be done by the trust or institution itself or by donating to trusts with similar objectives. Donations to other trusts or institutions should not be towards corpus to ensure that the donee trust or institutions apply the donations.

Inter-charity donation is treated at par with direct application for the purposes of Section 11(1)(a). The courts, on various occasions, have held that inter-charity donation is treated at par with the direct utilisation of funds. 'End justifies the means' is what the courts have consistently held in determining the charitable nature of an organisation. It has been held in various cases that a donation made by one charitable organisation to another shall be considered an application for the purposes of Section 11(1)(a).

In CIT v. JK Charitable Trust [1991] 59 Taxman 602 (All.), it was held that contribution to other charitable trusts was within the power and competence of the trustees. Further, in the case of CIT v. Shamnur Savithramma Kallappa Public Trust [2011] 11 taxmann.com 59 (Kar.), it was also held that inter-charity donations were a valid application of income. The Supreme Court, in the case of CIT v. Thanthi Trust [1999] 239 ITR 502 (SC), has upheld the treatment of inter-charity donations as a valid application of funds.

3.4-2 Amendment by the Finance Act, 2023

The Finance Act, 2023 inserted clause (iii) in Explanation 4 to Section 11(1) w.e.f. 01-04-2024 as under:

"(iii) any amount credited or paid, other than the amount referred to in Explanation 2, to any fund or trust or institution or any university or other educational institution or any hospital or other medical institution referred to in sub-clause (iv) or sub-clause (v) or sub-clause (vi) or sub-clause (via) of clause (23C) of section 10, as the case may be, or other trust or institution registered under section 12AB, as the case may be, shall be treated as application for charitable or religious purposes only to the extent of eighty-five per cent of such amount credited or paid.";

After the amendment by the Finance Act, 2023, only 85% of the eligible donations made by a trust or institution registered under Section 12AB to another trust or institution registered under Section 12AB or approved under Section 10(23C) shall be treated as the application. This amendment will take effect from 01-04-2024 and will accordingly apply in relation to the assessment year 2024-25 and subsequent assessment years.

It may be noted that Explanation 2 to Section 11 was inserted by Finance Act, 2017 w.e.f 01-04-2018, providing that the inter-charity donation with specific direction towards corpus to another approved/registered organization shall not be treated as applicable income. This explanation reads as under:

"Explanation 2.—Any amount credited or paid, out of income referred to in clause (a) or clause (b) read with Explanation 1, to any fund or trust or institution or any university or other educational institution or any hospital or other medical institution referred to in sub-clause (iv) or sub-clause (v) or sub-clause (vi) or sub-clause (via) of clause (23C) of section 10 or other trust or institution registered under section 12AA or section 12AB, as the case may be, being contribution with a specific direction that it shall form part of the corpus, shall not be treated as application of income for charitable or religious purposes."

Hence after the amendment, in addition to corpus donations to other approved/registered organizations, 15% of the non-corpus donation shall not be considered as an application of income.

3.4-3 Rationale behind the amendment

3.2 Instances have come to the notice that certain trusts or institutions are trying to defeat the intention of the legislature by forming multiple trusts and accumulating 15% at each layer. For continuation of the exemption, the trust or the institution will have to ensure that none of the objects is such that it cannot be considered as charitable purpose.

Courts have considered when it can be regarded that the income is applied wholly for charitable purposes or otherwise and have laid down the following principles or guidance.

In the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 777 the Supreme Court held as follows: "If one of the objects of the trust deed is not of a religious or charitable nature and the trust deed confers full discretion on the trustees to spend the trust funds for an object other than of a religious or charitable nature, the exemption from tax under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, is not available to the assessee.

If the primary or dominant purpose of a trust is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but which is merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purpose would not prevent the trust from being a valid charity." (pg. 777)

It must also be noted that the existence of a non-charitable object may not render the trust invalid if the trust deed itself provides that the trustees shall not carry out any object, which is held to be non-charitable. This concept was delivered by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case of CIT v. Mahendra Mohta Sewa Nidi [1985] 152 ITR 516 where it was held that:

"There was not only a positive command in the trust deed that the objects mentioned in it which were not found charitable should not be carried out by the trustees but also in fact no amount was actually spent on such an object. Therefore, the assessee was a charitable trust entitled to exemption under section 11." (pg. 516)

It was also very well explained in The Law and Practice of Income-tax Volume 1 by Kanga, Palkhiwala & Vyas, page no. 516

"(iv) The property may be held upon trust to apply a specified part of the income to charitable purposes and the balance of the income to non-charitable purposes.1 For instance, where a wakf is created with a direction to apply half of the income to charity and the other half for the benefit of the wakf's descendants, the property is held in part only upon charitable trusts.2 However, this type of cases where a specified part of the income is directed to be applied to charity should be distinguished from cases where a specified part of the corpus is held upon charitable trusts. Where a specified part of the income is set apart by the author of the trust for charitable purposes, the case falls within sub-section (1)(b),—property held in part only for charitable purposes. But where a definite specified part of the corpus itself is held upon charitable trust, the remainder of the corpus being settled upon non-charitable trusts, qua the portion of the corpus which is settled upon charitable trusts, the case falls within sub-seciton (1)(a), since that portion of the property is held under trust wholly for charitable purposes. In Chaturbhuj Vallabhdas v. CIT3 a testator directed that three-fourths of his estate should be utilized for charity, while the remaining one-fourth was to be given in the discretion of the trustee to the testator's descendants. Held, the three-fourths of the estate was property held in trust wholly for charitable purposes."

FACT: One 'S' and four others were holding certain securities for the purpose of charity and had been applying the same for and towards charitable purposes, executed, on 8-6-1922, a deed of declaration of trust declaring that the said trust fund would be held by them on trusts more specifically therein mentioned. Clause 13 of trust deed provided that the trust fund would be held by the trustees upon the trusts to apply the net income thereof after providing for all necessary expenses in relation to the management of the trust funds, for all or any of the following purposes (a) the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of jewish (b) the institution, maintenance and support of hospitals and schools, colleges or other educational institutions or (c) the relief of any distress caused by the elements of nature such as famine, pestilence, fire, tempest, flood, earthquake or any other such calamity or (d) the care and protection of animals useful to mankind or (e) the advancement of religion or (f) other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the foregoing purposes. The trust deed further provided that the trustees would give preference to the poor and indigent relations or members of the family of the said 'S' including there in distant and collateral relations. The trust fund had been invested by the trustees in inter alia 3½ per cent Government securities. In the year 1930, a certificate was issued by the ITO, whereby the Reserve Bank of India was authorized not to deduct at source the tax on the said securities so held by the trustees. For the assessment years 1948-49 and 1949-50, the ITO took the view that the income from the trust fund was not exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act accordingly, he assessed the appellants. On appeals, the AAC and the Tribunal confirmed the assessment made by the ITO.

On reference, the High Court also held that the trust property was not held wholly for religious or charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: Under clause 13 the trustees were at liberty to hold the trust fund and to apply the net income thereof for all or any of the six purposes mentioned therein. The relations or members of the family of the said 'S' including therein distant and collateral relations did not figure as direct recipients of any benefit under sub-clauses (b) to (f) and, therefore, in so far as those purposes were concerned the trust certainly involved an element of public utility.

It was open to the trustees to spend the net income entirely for the purpose referred to in sub-clause (a) to the exclusion of the other clauses. But the very fact that the relations or members of the family did not come in directly under any of those latter sub-clauses could not be ignored, for they certainly had some bearing on the question as to who or what were the primary objects of the trust as a whole. In the next place, the purpose of sub-clause (a) was the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of 'V' or any other community.

It followed that sub-clause (a ) constituted a valid public charitable trust having as its beneficiaries the several classes of persons referred to therein.

The circumstances that in selecting the beneficiaries under sub-clause (a) preference had to be given, under the proviso, to the relations or members of the family of 'S', could not affect that public charitable trust.

Therefore, the income from the trust properties came within the scope of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and was entitled to exemption.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the appellant/assessee.

to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision. The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

It is sufficient if a well defined section of the public benefits by the object, and the object of the trust in the instant case was to benefit clearly a defined section of the public living in Bombay. Now, on a casual consideration of the matter it may strike one that the most essential element of charity is to render service to the public without any charge or remuneration, but, it is clear on the authorities that the eleemosynary element is not an essential element of charity. A settlor or a donor may make a charity by setting up an institution and also providing funds by which those who take advantage of the institution can do so without paying any charge or one may have a case where the charity may not go to those limits and one may confine his charity to merely setting up the institution and providing that those who wish to take advantage of the institution must pay reasonable charges for the same. In both cases the setting up of the institution would be a charitable object if the institution serves a purpose of general public utility. The only essential factor to determine whether it is a charity or not would be whether there is any private gain by the setting up of the institution. If the gain derived by running the institution continues to be impressed with the trust which is a charitable trust, then it is immaterial whether the institution is run as a commercial institution or not, but if in the running of the institution profits are made and the profit goes to any private individual or if the institution is intended for any private gain, then undoubtedly the running of the institution could not be considered as being run for a charitable object.

Section 4(3)(ia) would only apply to an activity which was not an integral activity of the trust itself. If the trustees carried on a business which was not part of the property of the trust, then only that income of the business would be exempt from taxation which was applied solely to the purposes of the institution. If such a business made a profit, and only part was spent for religious or charitable institution and the other part was kept in surplus or in reserve, then the part which was kept in surplus or reserve would be liable to tax. Therefore, the Legislature, as far as section 4(3)(ia ) was concerned, looked upon a business falling under this sub-section as something independent of the trust itself; and looking upon that business as something independent of the trust itself; it naturally wanted to tax the income of that business to the extent that, that income was not applied solely to the purposes of the charitable or religious institution. If one takes this view of section 4(3)(i) and 4(3)(ia), then no difficulty would be experienced in the way of the trustees who were carrying on the activity as a part of the trust itself and which activity made profits which the trusts may keep in reserve in order to strengthen the financial position of the institution. As such income would fall under first part of section 4(3)(i ), no question could then arise of that income being necessarily applied for the purposes of the institution in order to earn exemption under section 4(3)(ia).

CIT [1997] 224 ITR 310 for adjudicating issue regarding violation of section 13(1)(c)(ii) - Tribunal (i) after taking into account fact that advance of Rs. 25 lakh was given to P during period 1-4-2001 to 31-3-2002, and (ii) also taking into account decision of Supreme Court in case of Aditanar Educational Institution (supra), held that there was a mistake apparent on record in earlier order passed by it - It further on basis of above findings held that assessee had not violated provisions of section 13(1)(c)(ii) during relevant assessment year 2003-04 and accordingly rectified order passed by it earlier - Whether, on facts and in circumstances of case, Tribunal had rightly exercised powers conferred under section 254(2) - Held, yes - Whether impugned order passed by Tribunal was justified - Held, yes. [In favour of assessee]

FACT: For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a charitable trust, claimed exemption under section 11. The Assessing Officer having found that during the current year the assessee had advanced a sum of Rs. 25 lakh to one P, who was the managing trustee of the trust, took the view that this amounted to violation of section 13(1)(c)(ii). He, therefore, asked the assessee to explain as to why the exemption claimed under section 11 should not be denied. The assessee explained (i) that in the current year no funds were given by the trust to P, (ii) that the transaction related to the earlier assessment year 2002-03, (iii) that P gave a sum of Rs. 25 lakh to one S from his individual account during the financial year ending on 31-3-2002 for purchasing a property for the trust, (iv ) that since property could not be purchased before the end of that year, a journal entry was made in the books of the trust by showing it as a debit balance and by crediting the account of P on 31-3-2002, (v) that due to litigation in the property, it could not be purchased and the amount of advance was returned back by S to P during the year ending on 31-3-2002, (vi) that as P received back his money during the current year from S, a reverse entry was made in the books of account of the trust on 31-3-2003 and (vii ) that, therefore, during the current year there was no outflow of cash from the trust. The Assessing Officer did not accept the explanation of the assessee and denied the exemption under section 11.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) having found that during the current year no funds were given by the trust to 'P' held that since no part of the income of trust was used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person referred to in section 13(3), the exemption claimed under section 11 could not be denied to the assessee. He, accordingly, granted the exemption under section 11 to the assessee.

The settlor created a trust by transferring a running business owned by him and as a sole trustee, he continued to manage the business with the object of applying the entire income for the benefit of two other public charitable trusts. The ITO, relying upon the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Indian Chamber of Commerce v. CIT [1975] 101 ITR 796 , denied exemption on the ground that the trust was carrying on activities for profit. However, he granted relief under section 10(21) on the actual cash payments, and brought the balance income to tax. The AAC held that, since one of the beneficiary trusts was an educational centre, the assessee-trust could be treated as for educational purposes, and not "for any other object of general public utility" and, hence, prohibition of carrying on business would not apply. The AAC, therefore, reversed the ITO's order and held that the entire amount credited to the beneficiary trusts would be exempt under section 11.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1946-47 – Founders of assessee-press created a trust in respect of assessee-press and a weekly paper published by it – Clause (2) of trust deed provided that trust Committee could not change policy of paper which at its inception was published in its first issue and which in political matters was according to aims and objects of Indian National Congress – Policy article of paper as published in its first issue made it quite clear that paper was not brought into existence to maintain, support, protect or oppose any particular association, organization, person or creed and that would include Congress organization, but aimed at good of all mankind and good of India and putting down of evils in general and encouragement of catholicity and of all those aspects of life which an educated person would like to see encouraged - Whether policy of paper was aimed at supplying to Province an organ of educated public opinion, and to encourage all that would lead to progress of India as a part of progress of mankind, which was a charitable object – Held, yes – Whether therefore, income of assessee was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act – Held, yes

FACT: 'S' and 'G' started the assessee-press and a weekly paper. By a deed the aforementioned persons created a trust in respect of the assessee press and the weekly paper. The trust deed provided in clause that the Trust Committee could not change the policy of the papar, which at its inception was published in its first issue and which would be published in the first issue of every year and which in political matters was according to the aims and objects of the Indian National Congress. The first issue of the paper stated that the ultimate aim of the weekly paper was the good of all mankind and that a very important and indispensable way to achieve that aim was the progress of India by the development of agriculture, trade, knowledge, art, prosperity, self-respect, power, good conduct and character. Other requirements of progress were also set out, namely, national unity, propagation of a well organised, popular and comprehensive education of right policies of good and efficient administration conducive to the welfare of the people, prevention of social evils and persecutions, encouragement of propagation of self-dependence and strong faith in self-rule.

In respect of its income for the relevant previous year, the assessee claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act on the ground that the income was of a trust which was wholly for religious or charitable purposes. The revenue authorities rejected said claim and held that the objects were firstly vague and ambiguous and secondly were neither religious nor charitable within the meaning of section 4(3)(i).

On reference:

HELD: The charitable object of the trust in the instant case was that of supplying to the Province an organ of educated public opinion. Moreover clause (2) did not state that the policy in political matters of the paper would be the policy from time to time of the Indian National Congress. What the policy would be was determined by the policy article once and for all and the policy therein was described as being in accord with the then policies and objects of the Indian National Congress. Clause (2) did not imply that the paper would become the propaganda machinery of the Indian National Congress and would further the views from time to time of the Indian National Congress. The second part of clause (2 ) was merely descriptive, so far as political matters were concerned, of the policy article. On examining the policy article carefully, it was quite clear that the paper was not brought into existence to maintain, support, protect or oppose any particular association, organisation, person or creed and that would include the Congress organisation. A paper which aims at carrying out such a policy as was to be the policy of the paper in question and aims at the good of all mankind and the good of India and the putting down of evils in general and the encouragement of catholicity and of all those aspects of life which an educated person would like to see encouraged , must clearly intend to be an organ of educated public opinion. No doubt at places such sentiments as a strong faith in self-rule or faith in the intentions of the British Government and the desire to raise the status of Indians everywhere were mentioned. But it did not appear that the paper had a political battle cry or object, or was founded in order to further particular political, social, economic or other programmes. But the aim was to encourage all that would lead to the progress of India as a part of the progress of mankind.

The policy article of the paper was expressly mentioned in clause (2) and there was no reason why it should not be deemed to have become a part of the deed of trust.

Clause (i) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 1922 Act deals with income derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation for religious or charitable purposes, while clause (ia) deals with income derived from business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution. The two clauses, therefore, do not necessarily overlap. Clause (i) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 1922 Act, applies to cases where the business itself is held under trust for religious or charitable purposes, while clause (ia) applies only to such business as is carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution which was not held under trust.

The Sabha, was clearly an institution having been brought about to effect the purpose and to carry out the objects for which the trust was founded. The word "applied" in clause means actually spent while, in clause (i) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act, the words used are "income applied or finally set the words "finally set apart" had not been repeated in clause(ia) at that sub-section. The word "applied" did not necessarily mean "spent". Even if it has been earmarked and allocated for the purposes of the institution, it may, be deemed to have been applied for its purposes. Neither the word "applied" nor the word "institution" is of any importance in this case, the case was governed by income from the property held under trust as laid down in section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

Therefore, it was held that the bhents (offerings) vested in the Sabha under a legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes of the Sabha but the bhents could not be said to be income derived from property under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act. They would properly come under clause (ii) of that sub-section meaning thereby that they were income of a religious or charitable institution derived from voluntary contributions and applicable solely to religious or charitable purposes.

Further, the income derived from industrial and commercial concerns was the income from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes and was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and it was, therefore, not necessary to apply to such income section 4(3)(ia) of the 1922 Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1952-53 to 1956-57 - Whether where business in kuries was held by assessee under a trust for religious or charitable purpose income derived from such business would be exempt from tax under provisions of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee company was a charitable trust one of its objects being to raise funds by conducting kuries with the company as the foreman; receiving donations and subscriptions; and by such other means as the company deemed fit. For the assessment years 1952-53 to 1956-57, the assessee claimed exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act in respect of its income from kuries business. The ITO was of the view that the trust was of a charitable character but was covered under proviso to section 4(3)(i). On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the opinion of the department.

On reference :

HELD: It is settled law that a business itself can be held under trust for religious or charitable purposes and that the income derived from such a business will fall within the ambit of the exclusion granted by section 4(3) (i ) of the 1922 Act.

In the instant case, the business in kuries itself was held under trust for religious or charitable purposes and this was abundantly clear from the memorandum of association. The first object of the assessee was to raise funds by conducting kuries with the company as the foreman; receiving donations and subscriptions; and by such other means as the company deemed fit. Hence, the proviso to section 4(3)(i) was not attracted and the assessee trust was entitled to the exemption under section 4(3)(i ) as amended by Act 25 of 1953 in respect of its income derived from business in kuries.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The department accepted this trust as a valid charitable trust and gave the necessary relief to the trustees in respect of the income of the trust, till the assessment year 1957-58.

The ITO, while dealing with the assessment of trust for the year 1958-59, held that the income of the trust would not be computed in the hands of the trustees but would be computed in the hands of the assessee-settlor under section 16(1)(c).

The AAC dismissed the appeals. Before him the assessee relied on section 35 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, but the AAC held that this did not assist the assessee because the income-tax law did take into consideration income derived directly or indirectly by illegal means. He felt that the assessee could not be precluded from utilizing funds of the trust directly or indirectly to his benefit since he had a right under the settlement to do so and the Bombay Public Trusts Act did not hold any fear for him as the penalties leviable were not of a deterrent nature, compared to the advantages that he could gain directly or indirectly by reassuming control over the investments or its income.

The assessee was an association of persons. The Constitution of the assessee provided for an elected standing committee, the constitution, functions and duties of the said standing committee. The Constitution also provided for a smaller body which was entitled managing committee and its constitution and other functions. The Constitution further provided that to carry out the objects of the parishad, the standing committee could raise funds and accept donations, presents charities, etc., and would have power to administer them. The issue that arose for decision was as to whether having regard to the terms of the constitution of the assessee-association, the properties of the assessee-association were held under trust or other legal obligation so as to qualify for exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

On reference:

The Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. Thanthi Trust [1982] 137 ITR 735 clearly held that handing over a gift to another trust amounts to application of the trust money within the meaning of section 11. Following the aforesaid decision of the Madras High Court, in the instant case, the whole of the amount of Rs. 17.5 lakhs gifted by the assessee to donee amounted to proper application of the trust funds and amounted to proper utilisation of the trust funds. When there was such a proper utilisation of trust funds it could not be said that the amount was not utilised for the purpose for which it was accumulated, especially when one of the objects for which the accumulation was sought for and granted was to give subsequent donations to any relief funds by way of charity. It was not the case of the revenue that the gift was made not to any relief fund or that the donee was not a charitable institution with similar objects as that of the donor trust. Therefore, the accumulated income of the donor trust was properly utilised for the purpose for which it was so accumulated and there was no contravention of the provisions of section 11(3)(c). Unless there was that contravention it was difficult to include either Rs. 17.5 lakhs or any part of it as the deemed income of the assessee for the assessment year in question. Thus, the order of the Commissioner under section 263 was not justified.

The settlor created a trust with the objects that during his lifetime the trust money would be utilised for the purpose of Haj Pilgrimage of himself and members of his family accompanying him on such pilgrimage and meeting expenses on visits to holy places outside India and also for making offerings at such places and that after his death the net income and consequent accumulations of income, if any, should be spent or utilised by the trustees for all or any of the purposes specified in clause 3(e) of the trust deed. During his lifetime, he did not spend any money for the specified purposes and after his death, the said trust became a public charitable and religious trust and the trustees held the corpus and accumulations of income in the trust thereunder. Because of the Government's restriction on remittances outside India, the trustees passed a resolution that the income of the trust property including accumulations thereof would be spent for the purposes specified in sub-clauses (v), (vi) and (vii) of clause ( e) within the territory of India. On an application, the civil court also granted relief under section 34 of the Indian Trust Act and allowed the trustees to utilise the income as per the resolution. For the assessment years 1974-75 and 1975-76, the trustees claimed exemption under section 5(1)(i) on the ground that the properties/assets were held in trust for public purpose of charitable and religious nature in India. The AAC allowed the assessee's claim. On appeal by the revenue, the Tribunal held that the assessee-trust was not entitled to exemption under section 5(1)(i).

On reference, the High Court upheld the Tribunal's findings on the ground that all the objects and purposes of the trust were intended to be performed outside India and neither the resolution of the trustees nor the order of the civil court altered that position.

In instant appeal the assessee contended that when the assessee had applied 85 percent of its income for charitable purposes as per the provisions of section 11(1)(a), then the amount in question though might not be an investment as per the modes prescribed under section 11(5), the same could not be held as application of income for non-charitable purposes.
