CASE LAWS WITH REGARD TO THE PROJECT GRANTS 7. In Society for Integrated Development in Urban and Rural Areas (SIDUR) v. Dy. CIT [2004] 90 ITD 493 (Hyd.), the issue came up before the regular bench of the Tribunal in Hyderabad. The exemptions were forfeited by virtue of section 13( l)(c ). The assessee contended that for the purposes of computing income from various projects, grants received from foreign donors could not be included in the income liable to tax, as such receipts would not be considered as income for the purposes of section 11. It was held that project grants did not form a part of the income of the assessee nor they form a part of the corpus. Voluntary contributions covered by section 12 are those contributions freely available to the assessee without any stipulation, which the assessee can utilise towards its objectives according to its own discretion and judgment. Tied-up grants for a specified purpose would only mean that the assessee which was a voluntary organisation, had agreed to act as a trustee of a special fund granted by donor with the result that it need not be pooled or integrated with the assessee’ s normal income or corpus. The Tribunal relied upon the findings of Nirmal Agricultural Society v. ITO [1999] 71 ITD 152 (Hyd.). Some relevant extracts are as under:

"The grants received from foreign donor were for specific purposes. The grants which were for specific purposes did not belong to the assessee-society, such grants did not form corpus of the assessee or its income. Those grants were not donations to the assessee so as to bring them under the purview of section 12. Voluntary contributions covered by section 12 are those contributions freely available to the assessee without any stipulation, which the assessee can utilise towards its objectives according to its own discretion and judgment. Tied-up grants for a specified purpose would only mean that the assessee which was a voluntary organisation, had agreed to act as a trustee of a special fund granted by donor with the result that it need not be pooled or integrated with the assessee ‘s normal income or corpus..." (p. 153)

Similarly, in Sukhdeo Charity v. CIT [1984] 149 ITR 470 /19 Taxman 222 (Raj.), the issue of whether specific grants were income or not was also discussed. It was observed that if the motive and intention of the donor play an important role in the utilization of the donation, then it cannot be considered as voluntary in nature. The word ‘ voluntary ’ in its very inception connotes the absence of any obligation on the part of the donor.

In the above case, the Court referred to the case of CIT v. Shri Billeswara Charitable Trust [1984] 145 ITR 29/16 Taxman 259 (Mad.).

In the above case, the Court ruled that a grant received for specific purposes cannot by any stretch of imagination be said to be income as envisaged by section 12(1). Because the word ‘ voluntary ’ in its very inception connotes the absence of an obligation on the part of the donor.

3. Generation of surplus out of gross receipts A doubt has been raised whether generation of surplus out of gross receipts would necessarily 'breach' the threshold condition that the educational institution should exist 'solely for educational purpose and not for the purpose of profit'. Perusal of prescribed provisions clearly reveal that mere generation of surplus cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) on the ground that it amounts to an activity of the nature of profit making. In fact, the third Proviso to the said clause clearly provides that accumulation of income is permissible subject to the manner prescribed therein provided such accumulation is to be applied "wholly and exclusively to the objects for which it is established". Hence, it is clarified that mere generation of surplus by educational institution from year to year cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) if it is used for educational purposes unless the accumulation is contrary to the manner prescribed under law.

4. Collection of amounts under different heads of fee from students—

It has been brought to the notice that collection of small amounts from students by way of application fee, examination fee, fee for issuing transfer certificate, subscription fee for library etc. is being treated by some Assessing Officers as profit making activity resulting in denial of exemption u/s 10(23C)(vi). Collection of small and reasonable amounts under different heads of fee, which are essentially in the nature of fee connected with imparting education and do not violate any Central or State regulation does not, in general, represent a profit making activity. Hence, there is no justification for treating the charging of small amounts under different heads of fee as profit making activity unless the amount in the nature of 'capitation fee' is charged directly or indirectly.

5.1 Doubt has been expressed whether extraordinary powers to the Managing Trustees to appoint or remove other trustees and also to nominate their successor affect the nature of charitable activity of the trust and whether in such an eventuality, exemption can be denied.

5.2 There is no provision under the Act which calls for denial of exemption merely on account of appointment or removal of trustees. 23. Prosecution under section 276BB should be non-cognisable under section 279A on the lines of Section 276B

Section 276B provides for the prosecution if the assessee fails to deposit the tax so deducted by it with the Central Government. Section 276BB provides for the prosecution if the assessee fails to deposit the tax collected by it with the Central Government.

Section 279A lists down the offences which are non-cognisable under the Income-tax Act. This provision includes section 276B but does not include section 276BB. As both the provisions deal with the situations of default in deposit of tax deducted or collected by the assessee, there should be parity in both scenarios. So, it is recommended that section 276BB should also be covered under the list of non-cognisable offences.

(Read more: Prosecution for failure to pay tax collected at source on Taxmann.com/Practice)

24. Full exemption should not be denied to the trust on violation of section 13

Section 13 of the Income-tax Act outlines the circumstances in which exemption of sections 11 and 12 shall not be allowed to a charitable or religious trust. It restricts the exemption where trust gives benefit to an interested person. As a practice, the Assessing Officer denies the exemption in respect of entire income under section 11 if there was a violation of provisions of section 13.

The Bombay High Court in the case of CIT(Exemptions), Pune v. Audyogik Shikshan Mandal [2019] 101 taxmann.com 247 (Bombay) has held that where funds of assessee-trust were utilised for purchase of a car in the name of its trustee, there was a violation of section 13(2)(b), read with section 13(3). However, denial of exemption under section 11 should be limited only to the amount which was diverted in violation of section 13(2)(b).

Thus, it is recommended that necessary amendments be made under Section 13 to ensure that the denial of exemption to trust is restricted to amount that was diverted in violation of Section 13.

25. Condition to pay emoluments by specified modes under section 80JJAA should be applicable in case of new businesses also

Section 80JJAA of the Income-tax Act provides that every assessee, earning business income and liable to the tax audit, can claim a deduction under this provision for additional employee cost. The deduction shall be allowed for 30% of the additional employee cost in three assessment years.

However, such deduction shall be allowed only if the assessee fulfils certain conditions. One of the conditions is that emoluments must be paid by any of the following modes :

(a)

An account payee cheque;

(b)

Account payee bank draft;

(c)

By use of electronic clearing systems through a bank account; or

(d)

Other prescribed electronic modes i.e. Credit/debit card, IMPS, RTGS etc.

This condition is applicable in case of an existing business only. To move towards digital India initiative, it is expected that the above condition regarding payment of emoluments through the above modes may be extended in the case of new businesses also.

The Court wanted to know whether section 80G omission for extended time limit for regularization of approval vide Circular No.6 of 2023 for new trusts and institutions was a conscious decision or a typographic omission since the first circular i.e. Circular No.8 of 2022 granted extension of time for both the existing and new trusts alike.

In response to this query of the Court, the ASG filed additional counter-affidavit wherein it was claimed that the new trusts were bound to apply within the specified time and they cannot seek extension of time as a matter of right and in respect of trusts having provisional approval, time was not extended in respect of section 80G of the Act. The Court observed that the additional counter-affidavit did not reveal any conscious decision was taken by way of application of mind at the time of issuance of the impugned Circular No.6 of 2023 or any time before.

1.4 Decision of High Court

The Court after hearing the rival submissions firstly held that the assessee does not have any vested right to claim extension of time. When the statute prescribes a time limit the assessee is expected to apply within the said date to avail the benefits. The CBDT issues circulars enlarging the time limit to mitigate the rigours of the statute and the hardship faced by the assessees in exercise of its powers under section 119(2)(b) of the Act. No discrimination or differentiation was made between the existing trusts and new trusts at the first instance when Circular No.8 of 2022 was issued. When the impugned Circular No.6 of 2023 was issued the reason was stated viz. to mitigate genuine hardship. The Circular extended the time for filing the relevant forms. On a combined reading of the Circular No.8 of 2023 and Circular No.6 of 2023 it held that the only reason was to mitigate the hardship faced by the trusts / institutions. No reason whatsoever was mentioned for omitting new trusts / institutions in respect of applying in Form No.10AB with extended time limit.

The Court held that it could not find any reason whatsoever for leaving out new trusts in respect of approval under section 80G(5)(iii). Except for reiterating that the applicant trusts do not have any vested right to claim extension of time there was no other ground put forth by the Revenue.

Even though the new trusts as well as the existing trusts have no right to demand extension of time as a matter of right when the CBDT has given extension of time for existing trusts there was no reason given as to how the new trusts did not face the hardship in respect of filing of application under section 80G(5) of the Act alone though it was given the extension of time for regularization of registration under sections 10(23C) and 12A. The Circular hence does not provide any basis for the discrimination / classification.

The Court accordingly held that the differential treatment is not based on any substantial distinction that is real and pertinent to the object of the Circular. The discrimination is artificial. The respondents (CBDT) were evasive and could not provide any rationale for such classification. Hence, the Court held that para 5 clause (ii) of the Circular No.6 of 2023 is arbitrary and accordingly ultra vires the constitution. The writ was allowed by the Court.

Thus, IIM courses cannot be said to be ‘training’ or ‘coaching’. It is education. 2.2 IIM is not ‘commercial’ training centre - Apart from fact that IIM is not ‘training’ or ‘coaching’ centre, IIM is not a ‘commercial’ institute, even if it earns surplus from its activities.

As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘Commercial’ means engaged in, or connected with, ‘commerce’ or ‘having profit as a primary aim rather than artistic etc. value’.

‘Commercial activity’ must imply some investment of capital and the activity must run the risk of profit or loss relating to or connected with trade and traffic or commerce in general- Sakharam Narayan Kherdekar v. City of Nagpur Corpn. AIR 1964 Bom. 200.

In brief, ‘commercial’ means a business organisation having profit as primary motive. In Institute of Banking Personnel Selection v. CCE [2006] 3 STT 126 (Mum. - CESTAT), a strong prima facie view was held that a charitable trust is not a ‘commercial concern’.

Thus, IIM is not ‘commercial’ centre.

2.3 Education is not ‘trade’ or ‘commerce’ - In TMA Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka 2002 AIR SCW 4957 = AIR 2003 SC 355 = (2002) 8 SCC 481 (SC 11 member Constitution Bench - Majority decision delivered by Hon’ble B. N. Kirpal, CJI), it was held that education has so far not been regarded as a trade or business where profit is the motive.

In Nitte Education Trust v. Union of India [1997] (89) Comp. Cas. 390 = (1997) 5 CTJ 229 (Kar.), it has been held that education is not a trade practice. This judgment refers to various Supreme Court judgments - particularly J.P. Unni Krishnan v. State of AP AIR 1993 SC 2178 = (1993) 1 SCC 645 = 1993 AIR SCW 863, where it was held that education is not a business. Ratio of these judgments is that education is a mission, not a trade or business.

In Ruth Soren v. Managing Committee [2000] AIR SCW 4264 = 2001 LLR 149 (SC), it was held that establishment running educational institution does not carry business, trade or profession.

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Franchise service - Courier agency

5.10 Assessee was a courier agency with a wide network of above 45 hubs located at various stations in South India. Its agents were centered around these hubs and they collected and delivered time-sensitive letters/articles to consignees. With aid of this network, assessee acted as a courier agent and transported articles between hubs. Revenue demanded service tax from assessee in category of ‘Franchise service’ and also imposed penalty. It was found that under a standard agreement entered into with each appointed agent, the assessee and each courier agent attached to the hubs had a relation as between principal and agent. Assessee controlled and administered their activities. Those agents were not conferred with any representational right by assessee. They were entitled to use name of assessee only as an ‘authorised agent’. Registration certificates issued to those agents carried endorsement that they were agents of assessee; that they returned courier charges received from clients to assessee, while retaining their expenses and remuneration and there was no payment of fee to assessee as required by section 65(47 ).

The Tribunal held that from 16-6-2005, the franchise service involves provision of a service associated with a particular person by trade mark, service mark, trade name or logo. The registration certificates issued to the agents carried the endorsement that they were agents of the assessee. The so-called franchisees being agents who undertook the work of courier agency on behalf of the assessee, it could not be held that any other service was involved in the transactions or that there was a different person receiving the service. It was further submitted that the agents were not doing business on their own account; that they were required to use consignment notes and stationery of the assessee, with the consignment notes bearing the name of the assessee; that no fee was paid by the agents and they only made a deposit with the assessee called trade deposits; that the agents paid service tax on the charges they collected from their clients, and returned the balance after retaining their expenses and remuneration; that the assessee did not impart any skill, technical know-how or managerial expertise to the agents; and, thus, there was no service rendered by the assessee to its agents to be taxed under the category ‘Franchise service’. "Franchise means an agreement by which the franchisee is granted representational right to sell or manufacture goods or to provide service or undertake any process identified with franchisor, whether or not a trade mark, service mark, trade name or logo or any such symbol as the case may be, is involved." On the basis of facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal held that it could be said that assessee undertook only courier agency’s service, engaging several agents who did not operate as ‘principals’ and, therefore, neither those agents were franchisees nor assessee, a franchisor. Accordingly, the Tribunal set aside the impugned order and allowed the appeal filed by the assessee.

[Franch Express Network (P.) Ltd. v. CST [2008] 16 STT 10 (Chennai - CESTAT)]

SECTION 65(105)(r ) - MANAGEMENT CONSULTANT SERVICES - MAINTENANCE AND OPERATION OF LIGNITE FIRED POWER PLANT

1. Tax on Management Consultant’s Services was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998. The Finance Act, 2006, w.e.f. 1-5-2006 had specified the area of consultancy. For the words "relating to conceptualising, devising, development, modification, rectification or upgradation of any working system of any organisation", the words "in relation to financial management, human resources management, marketing management, production management, logistics management, procurement and management of information technology resources or other similar areas of management" had been substituted. So, the scope of this service is made more specific in relation to certain services, which were previously undefined. The Finance Act, 2007 renamed this service as management or business consultant’s service and to explicitly include business consultancy in the definition itself.

In the clarification contained in the CBEC Circular, dated 27-6-2001, it was stated that term ‘management’ is generally understood to mean running the affairs of an organization in an organized and systematic manner. To be able to do this efficiently and effectively, management typically involves carrying out a host of activities, functions and tasks at different levels. Thus, the term ‘management’ encompasses both strategic and operational level functioning and would include tasks such as planning, organizing, staffing, directing, controlling and co-ordinating. Management also invariably involves designing organizational structure around functions such as marketing, manufacturing, research and development and finance and/or business area, such as product groups or geographical markets. Thus, management of any organization involves carrying out a wide variety of clearly defined activities across a number of organizational sub-units in a coherent and co-ordinated manner. Since the expression ‘management’ is an inclusive term, ‘management consultant’ would also be equally encompassing expression and would include any adviser, who renders services on any aspect of management.

This would result in a reduction of income chargeable to tax to Entity A. The same has been explained in the table below: From the above, it is evident that the transfer pricing adjustment with regard to the availing of management support services, would result in a reduction of the income chargeable to tax of Entity A to the extent of 60 (1200 - 1140). Hence as per the provisions of section 92(3), the revenue authorities are not empowered to disallow the cost of management support services paid to Entity B, as this would result in a reduction of the income chargeable to tax / base erosion and hence not permitted.

In addition it would be pertinent to evaluate as to whether the restriction imposed by section 92(3) has to be analysed from the perspective of the assessee alone or whether the impact has to be evaluated by considering the transaction as a whole, i.e., considering the tax impact arising from the transaction for both the assessee as well as the AE on an aggregate basis. The said issue was subjected to a detailed analysis by the Special Bench of the ITAT in the case of Instrument arium Corporation Ltd, Finland2.

The appellant, a non-resident entity had advanced interest free loan to its wholly owned subsidiary in India. The tax authorities during the course of assessment had imputed interest on the loan and subjected the same to income-tax in India.

However, the revenue authorities had considered the interest free loan to be in compliance with the arm's length requirement, while completing the transfer pricing audit of the wholly owned Indian subsidiary.

The revenue authorities, while completing the transfer pricing audit had imputed interest on the loan provided by the non-resident entity "Entity B" to the Indian resident entity "Entity A" and had recommended an adjustment.

The Special Bench of ITAT, after hearing the detailed arguments of the appellant on base erosion and other grounds of appeal, had upheld the action of tax authorities as:

The transfer pricing adjustment does not automatically provide for a corresponding adjustment in the hands of the other entity, as per the Indian transfer pricing regulations.

Hence there would not be a Base erosion and a consequent loss to the revenue due to the action of the revenue authorities in imputing interest in respect of the loan provided by Entity B to Entity A.

The principle laid down by the Special Bench of the ITAT is elaborated in the below illustration:

Illustration 3: -

Anon-resident entity "Entity B" had advanced an interest free loan to its wholly owned Indian subsidiary company "Entity A".

However, the revenue authorities in the course of audit of the non-resident entity "Entity B" had carried out a transfer pricing adjustment, to impute an arm's length interest to the interest free loan provided to Entity A, as the said loan did not satisfy the arm's length requirement.

This would be critical to note from a group perspective that:

The non-resident Entity B has been subjected to a transfer pricing adjustment in India by imputing interest on the loan provided to Entity A. The tax rate normally applicable in the case of a non-resident with regard to interest income is @ 10%.

The income-tax rate applicable for a domestic entity "Entity A" is @ 33.99%. This would result in a tax savings of around 24% on the amount of the interest imputed by the tax authorities in the hands of the non-resident entity "Entity B".

This would result in a possible scenario of base erosion from an Indian transfer pricing regulation perspective and the same is prohibited by Sub-Section 3 of Section 92.

After going through the arguments of the appellant, the Special Bench had held that the Indian transfer pricing regulations do not provide for a corresponding interest allowanceto the Indian resident entity "Entity A", in respect of the transfer pricing adjustment made in the case of the Non-resident AE entity "Entity B" with regard to the same transaction.

This would result in a double taxation for the group as a whole, i.e.:

Entity B would be paying taxes on the transfer pricing adjustment made by the tax authorities during the course of an audit

A corresponding interest allowance would not be granted to Entity A, in respect of the transfer pricing adjustment made in the course of audit of Entity B.

This would result in a tax outgo for Entity B as well the corresponding adjustment by allowing an interest debit would not be available for Entity A.

The assessee may challenge this further, however, this highlights that it is imperative that the transactions entered into by groups satisfy the arm's length requirement as laid down in the Indian transfer pricing regulations, from the perspective of both the associated enterprises involved in the international transactions.
